"Theodorus teaches us in his poem upon the Jews, that the precept of circumcision was first given to Abraham, in these verses which Eusebius has preserved in his Gosp. Prep., Bk. 9, ch. 22.


He who from home the righteous Abraham brought,
Commanded him and all his house, with knife
To circumcise their foreskin, he obeyed."

Grotius, Deveritate, Bk. 1, sec. 16, notes.Truth of Christian Religion (2nd ed., 1719), 57.

The FORESKIN that was cut off in circumcision fitly represented corruption, not only as it aptly represented lust in general, being a special spot of the lust of the flesh, and we know how often corruption in general is called THE FLESH, but because that especially is men's NAKEDNESS, and is called their SHAME, which terms are often used in Scripture to signify SIN.This and the preceding paragraph are a later addition.

Genesis 17:12. "And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised."] One reason why they were not to be circumcised till they were eight days old was because the child was legally impure till then, and it was seven days before it was clean. Both the mother and child was unclean seven days on that account, they being both defiled with that blood, as Leviticus 12:2–3.

"Eight days old." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 168.

-- 160 --

Genesis 17:14. "That soul shall be cut off from his people."] This and other parallel texts in the law of Moses ben't necessarily to be understood of death. 'Tis very agreeable to the use of such expressions elsewhere, that he that is excommunicated, deprived either by the judgment ofJE deleted "the authority of the." ecclesiastical judges, or by the immediate judgment of God, of all union and communion with the congregation or church of God's people, should be said to "be cut off from his people," and CUT OFF from the congregation of the Lord. Joshua says to the Gibeonites, Joshua 9:23, "Now therefore ye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen." In the original, it is, "There shall not be cut off from you a bondman" (The word "cut off," in the original,כָּרַת being the same as in the other case.), i.e. no one of you shall be separated from the rest of your company so as not to partake with him, or have communion with him, in servitude. So God says, Numbers 4:18, "Cut ye not off the tribe of the families of the Kohathites from among the Levites," i.e. let 'em not be separated from them, and from a participation in their privileges. Here again the word in the original is the same, as it also is, Zechariah 14:2. "Half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the city shall not be cut off from the city," where it is implied that not only those that are dead, but those who areJE deleted "expelled or." separated from the inhabitants and benefits of the city by captivity, are cut off from the city. So divorcement in Scripture is "cutting off," the word being from the same root in the original (Deuteronomy 24:1, Deuteronomy 24:3, and Isaiah 50:1). However, God's depriving his people of church privileges, or of the privileges of his visible people, [is] compared to this very thing.

Genesis 17:17.] John 8:56.

Genesis 17:25. Josephus and Origen both speak of, as the known custom of the Ishmaelites in Arabia, to circumcise their children at thirteen years of age in their time, as Grotius informs in his book, De Veritate, Bk. 1, sec. 16, notes.Truth of Christian Religion (2nd ed., 1719), 58.

Genesis 18.] See heathen traditions about the burning of Sodom, no. 431.Works, 15, 510–11. Nos. 355 and 431.These references are a separate entry. Works, 15, 341, 510–11.

-- 161 --

Genesis 18:18–19.] By these verses it is manifest: 1. That absolute promises already made may yet in a sort depend on future condition, for the promise here mentioned had been made already absolutely over and over. But yet Abraham's future commanding "his children and his household after him" is mentioned as the condition of it; and then after that, remains another condition, viz. "that they keep the way of the Lord, to do justice and judgment."

2. That the promise is absolutely made, before the performance of all the conditions, because the performance of the future conditions is so certainly connected with what was already found in Abraham, that it was certainly consequent, and taken as already fulfilled. This may illustrate the dependence of a sinner's salvation on his future universal obedience and perseverance, though it be already absolutely promised.

3. Hereby 'tis manifest that ordinarily a thorough care and endeavor in the education of children will be successful.

4. That when God admits children into covenant with their parents, and so admits 'em to be the subjects of the visible seal of the covenant, it is as it were on a dependence on the future religion and piety of those children as so ordinarily consequent on it, that it may be looked upon as virtually included in it.

Genesis 18:25 "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?"] In the title of "fudge of all the earth" is implied God's being the fountain of all right, that the universal rule of right is from him. He is the author of all laws of righteousness, revealed laws, and laws of nature, he by whom kings rule, and princes decree justice, and all the judges of the earth [judge]. He is the author of that reason and conscience that is in men, that naturally suggests what is right and wrong, that approves of right, and condemns wrong, whereby men are a law to themselves. All knowledge of right, all approbation of it, all dislike of wrong in the universe, is from him, as well as all rewards of right and punishment of wrong. And take the meaning of the phrase in this extensive sense, and so the reasoning is very strong.

Genesis 19:1. "And there came two angels," etc.] Probably from hence and other like instance which we have an account of in Scripture, came that notion among the heathen nations which Homer expresses in his Odyssey. "The gods themselves, like unto wandering strangers (seeing they are everywhere), do come and visit cities, beholding what is done right or wrong among men." See Dr. Owen, on Hebrews 13:3, pp. 210e and 211a.John Owen, Hebrews 11–13.

-- 162 --

"And Lot sat in the gate of Sodom." Where he probably sat exhorting and reproving the people. For the gate of the city seems of old to be the place of resort on all public occasions, not only the place the judges sat to judge the people, but where their teachers sat to instruct and reprove them. Isaiah 29:21, "That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate." Amos 5:10, "They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly." The judges might properly do this, but others might also do it who did not take upon the office of judges. If Lot was now reproving the people, and striving to persuade 'em to repent and reform, he thusGrosart interlined "showed that he." had no fellowship with the unfruitful, with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reproved them. And God rewarded his withstanding and resisting the stream of the general wickedness of that people by sending angels on a most kind and merciful errand to him, while in the exercise of his fortitude and opposition. And 'tis also observable that just before the destruction of the people, God used extraordinary means to reclaim 'em by Lot's reproofs (who was "a preacher of righteousness," as well as Noah, 2 Peter 2:5–9); and their destruction came upon them just on the manifestation of the highest and most desperate degree of obstinacy in them, in their despising his reproofs, and most horrid wickedness towards Lot and the angels immediately after. Lot, having lately been reproving the people in the gate, the place of judgment, made them the more ready to say, as they do in Genesis 19:9, "This fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Genesis 19:15–17.] As these angels did, so should ministers, the angels of the churches, do. They should hasten persons' escape out of the spiritual Sodom by warning of them of the great danger of their being consumed with the city. They should charge 'em to escape for their lives, and not to look behind them, nor to stay at all by the way, but escape to the mountain, lest they be consumed. Yea, they should as it were compel them while they see them linger; they should as it were lay hold on them, and hale them forth.

Genesis 19:20–22.] Zoar is a type of the church; and Lot, in that which is here mentioned of him, is a type of Christ. Lot intercedes that Zoar, one of the cities of the plain, might be saved for his sake, that he might flee

-- 163 --

thither, and that that city might not be burnt. As Lot by interceding for this little city saved it, so Christ saves the church by his intercession. And so Lot saved Zoar from being consumed by the fire and brimstone by coming to it, coming into the city, and being among the citizens. So Christ saves men by coming into the world to them, by taking on him men's nature. He saves the church by uniting himself to it, being one of the church, becoming the brother of the elect. Lot comes out of burning Sodom, out of that sink of sin and wickedness, and as it were out of the midst of the fire of God's wrath, with salvation to Zoar. So Christ was made sin for us, and comes as it were out of the fire of God's wrath, rises from the dead, and as it were from hell, and comes to his people with salvation. Zoar was a little city; so the church is a little city. Christ's people are a "little flock" [Luke 12:32]. Lot pleads this as an argument why Zoar should be saved for his sake, that it was a "little one" Genesis 19:20]. He can be more bold to ask that mercy, that a few should be saved for his sake than that many should.

Genesis 19:23–24.] No. 359.Works, 15, 344.

Genesis 19:24–28.] Concerning the manner of the destruction of Sodom and the neighboring places, see no. 276.Ibid., 232–33.

Genesis 19:26.] Concerning what was typified by Lot's wife's becoming a "pillar of salt," see no. 380.Ibid., 365.

"Looked back from behind him." No. 230.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 1 89–90.

Genesis 19:31–35.] Lot's daughters seem still to retain the prevailing disposition of the place they came from, viz. inordinate lechery.

Genesis 20:4. "Wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?"] The particle "also" is used with relation to the destruction of that wicked people, the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, etc., which had very lately come to pass.

Genesis 21:7.] The bringing forth of Christ mystical in Gentile world so late, after it had been so long confirmed in heathenism and barrenness and when the case of the heathen nations appeared desperate, was wonderful.

-- 164 --

So will the conversion of the worldJE deleted "after." at the fall of Antichrist be wonderful on the same accounts, which will be another fulfillment of the woman's bringing forth the man-child, spoken of in Revelation 12.

Genesis 21:8.] See no. 138a.Works, 15, 89.

Genesis 21:9. "And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking."] Which represents the Jews' mocking the Gentile Christians (who are represented by the free woman and her son), at the time when God weaned his church from the milk of Jewish ordinances, and also that part of the professing world that are addicted to carnal ordinances, mocking the more pure church of God in all ages. See Galatians 4:29.

Genesis 21:10–11.] No. 361.Ibid., 347–48.

Genesis 22.] Concerning Abraham's offering up his son, see no. 362.Ibid., 348–49. Fables of Saturn among the heathen taken from this story, see note on Genesis 1:27, the third paragraph of that note. See also SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 188. This reference and the preceding sentence are later additions.

Genesis 22:4. "On the third day."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, p. 104a-b.Kidder cites "a great many places of Scripture, which mention the third day, and many particulars for which the third day was remarkable." Demonstration of the Messias, Pt. 1 (2nd ed. corr., 1726), 104.

Genesis 22:6. "Took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it on Isaac his son."]

See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, p. 104a.Kidder points to the fact that Isaac "bore the wood which was to bear him, and in these things he was a remarkable type of Christ." Demonstration of the Messias, Pt. 1 (2nd ed. corr., 1726), 104.

Genesis 22:8.] See no. 7.Works, 15, 50. JE deleted this reference when he wrote the following entries.

"God will provide himself a lamb." Fulfilled in Christ.This paragraph is a separate entry.

We may observe here an instance of the harmony between the Old

-- 165 --

and New Testament, in that 'tis according to the Old Testament as well as New, that 'tis not unreasonable that God himself should provide the sacrifice by which sins against himself should [be] atoned, and his own anger appeased. Abraham did not only tell his son that God would provide himself, but he actually did provide a ram for Abraham to offer up as a burnt offering.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Again we may observe here that which may confirm us, that the prophecies of the prophets often, according to the mind of the Holy Ghost, had respect to those things which the prophets themselves had no thought of. For Abraham, when he said, "God will provide himself a lamb," had no thought of any other than that Isaac was to be the lamb that was to be offered, and that God had provided for himself. See note on John 11:51, no. 53.This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 15, 65.

Genesis 22:13.] See Genesis 22:8.

Genesis 22:14. "In the mount," etc.] Mr. Hervey translates it, "In the mount the Lord shall be seen." See Dialogues, vol. 3, pp. 190–91.James Hervey, Theron and Aspasio, 3. Hereafter cited as Dialogues. Multiple different editions of the Dialogues appeared in 1755 with different pagination. Hervey (1714–58), a popular devotional writer sympathetic to the evangelical revivals, suggests that the KJV translation obscures and spoils the proper interpretation (pp. 190–91 note).

Joshua 18:28.This reference is a separate entry.

Genesis 23.] Concerning Abraham's buying in Canaan a possession of a burying place, see no. 350.Works, 15, 335. The remainder of this entry is a later addition. Agreeable to Ecclesiastes 6:3–4 and some parallel places, burial typifies gathering the soul to everlasting rest. (See note on that place in Eccles.) So a possession of a burying place in Canaan, in one that [has] not a foot of land for a possession on earth, typifies the possession in heaven which they come to by the happy change they pass under at death, who are pilgrims and strangers on earth. See note on Genesis 33:19.

Genesis 24.] See the mystery of this story of Isaac's marriage, in my "Exposition on Revelation," in no. 21.Works, 5, 131–33.

-- 166 --

Genesis 24:2. "Put thy hand under my thigh."] That Abraham might sit on his hand. SSS.Poole, Synapsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 194.

Genesis 24:12.] Abraham's servant obtained a wife for his master's son, not merely by delivering his message, but by prayer joined with it. So the ministers of Christ win souls, not only by preaching, but by earnest prayer to God for their conversion.

Genesis 24:13. "And behold, I stand here by the well," etc.] The well of water typifies God's ordinances that are as it were the vehicles of grace and the Holy Spirit, represented by water, which also was typified by the pool of Bethesda, where impotent people waited for theJE deleted "troubling." moving of the water. Here it was that Abraham's servant waited for a wife for his master's son; so ministers are to seek for the conversion of souls in the use of ordinances. And it was by coming here to this well that Rebecca obtained her husband, and there she received her ornaments. So it is by an attendance on ordinances that souls find Christ, and are brought to a saving close with him, and are sanctified. See no. 161.Works, 15, 97.

Genesis 24:14, Genesis 24:17–20.] This is the mark by which Abraham's servant knows his master's wife, viz. her kindness to him. So love or charity is the principal mark by which the true church is distinguished, and especially do true saints respect and kindly receive Christ's ministers. And then this seems to be represented by Rebecca's giving Abraham's servant drink of the well. The well, as I have observed, represents God's ordinances; and Rebecca represents the church. The ministers of Christ themselves have spiritual supplies by the ordinances that are administered in the church; they suck the breasts of the church. And that church that is Christ's spouse, or the true church, is distinguished from all false churches, that she gives spiritual nourishment and refreshment, as Rebecca was distinguished from all the otherJE deleted "virgins." women that came out to draw water. Rebecca's pitcher signifies the cup of salvation, the same that is represented by the cup in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. Rebecca gave drink to the camels also; the saints are of a most extensive condescending charity. It extends to the meanest and most inferior, and even to the beasts. A good man regardeth the life of his beast. 'Tis a property of the true

-- 167 --

church of Christ that she affords provision, and refreshment, and entertainment for every creature. Everyone that thirsts is invited to come to the waters; the poor have the gospel preached to them. However mean and abject persons' outward condition is, yet in her they may be kindly entertained and have their spiritual wants supplied. The poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind are called to the gospel feast; here is provision for barbarian, Scythian, bond, and free.

Rebecca, in doing deeds of charity, obtained her husband, Isaac, a type of Christ, and was received into the line of the covenant, and became the mother of Christ, and received those precious ornaments. So to do deeds of charity is an hopeful way to receive Christ as a spiritual husband, and to become the spiritual mother of Christ, and to receive spiritual ornaments in our souls. Cornelius, in a way of doing deeds of charity, had Christ savingly revealed to him [Acts 10].This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 24:22.] He gave Rebecca bracelets and earrings. So Christ's ministers fitJE deleted "souls." persons to be the spouse of Christ by giving them an excellent ear to hear, and excellent hands adorned with good works.

Genesis 24:25. "We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in."] The people of God ought well to maintain the ministers of Christ; and such as are true saints are of that spirit, as Rebecca, the type of the church, was willing to receive and provide for Abraham's servant, and the men that were with him, and the camels, while they stayed there at her father's house, which typified this world. See notes on Psalms 45:10. The provision they made for him, the straw, and provender, and meat, and drink, and lodging typifies those worldly good things which the people of God ought to maintain their ministers with. Abraham's servant was well and handsomely entertained by them; so Christ's ministers should be well and comfortably supported.

Genesis 24:33. "And there was set meat before him to eat; but he said, I will not eat, till I have told mine errand."] So the ministers of Christ ought to have the doing of their master's work, and faithfully declaring that message that their master hath sent them with, before their maintenance or temporal interest.

-- 168 --

Genesis 24:63. "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field."] Hence learn that though those religious pleasures and our sweet sense of the things of religion be such as is promoted by the beauties of nature and by rural solitude, yet 'tis no sign that those pleasures and that sense of mind is not of the right kind.

Genesis 24:64–65. "And when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel,… and took a veil, and covered herself."] So those that truly come to Christ come humbly to him.

Genesis 24:65.] Isaac comes forth to meet and receive Rebecca who is coming to him; so Christ most readily receives and welcomes repenting sinners coming to him.

Genesis 24:66. "And the servant told Isaac," etc.] Thus the ministers of Christ will render up their account to Christ, how they have fulfilled their ministry. Hebrews 13:17, "For they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief."

Genesis 24:67. "And Isaac brought her into his mother's tent."] Here Rebecca represents two things. 1. She represents the soul of a believer whom Christ espouses to himself, and brings into his church, the spiritual mother of Christ, and to the enjoyment of the privileges of the church in this world, and to heaven, the habitation provided for the church in the other world. Those things are here represented by his mother's tent. 2. She represents the Gentile or new testament church. And then by Isaac's mother is represented the church of the Jews or old testament church, which was as it were Christ's mother, for he descended of the Jews. And he was in the church; it was under the old testament dispensation. He was subject to the old testament ordinances; those were the breasts he sucked.

The apostasy of the Jews, their being cut off by unbelief from being God's people, was the death of this mother of Christ. The Gentile church was called into her tent, as 'tis said of Japheth, that "he shall dwell in the tents of Shem" [Genesis 9:27]. The natural branches were broken off that these might be grafted in. Thus Christ is as it were comforted concerning the loss of the Jewish church by the calling of the Gentiles. See notes on Ephesians 5:30–32, no. 232.Works, 15, 181–82.

-- 169 --

Genesis 25:2.]JE's biblical reference here is Genesis 25:1, but the link to "Midian" is in Genesis 25:2. The country of the Midianites, by the Scripture account, seems to have been on "the southeast of the Salt Sea," reaching to the Red Sea. "Accordingly we find a city called Madana, placed in these parts by heathen writers, near the Red Sea." Wells' Sacred Geography, vol. 1, pp. 345–46.Historical Geography of the Old Testament, I, 345–46.

Genesis 25:6. "But unto the sons of the concubines."] Both Hagar and Keturah are called his concubines (1 Chronicles 1:32).

"And sent them away from Isaac his son eastward, into the east country." Therefore their posterity are called "the children of the east," and were very numerous by virtue of the blessing of Abraham. See Judges 6:3, Judges 6:5, Judges 6:33, and Judges 7:12, and Judges 8:10.This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 25:12–18.] Concerning the posterity of Ishmael, and their settlements in Arabia, see "Scripture," no. 420.Works, 15, 500.

Genesis 25:18. "And he died in the presence of all his brethren."] I.e. he died the first of them.

Genesis 25:20. "And Isaac was forty years old."] So Christ came into the world, and redeemed the church in the year of the world 4000. See notes on Exodus 24:18. So the children of Israel were forty years in the wilderness. Moses was forty years old when he visited his brethren (Acts 7:23). Saul reigned forty years, and then the kingdom of David began. David reigned forty years, and then the glorious and peaceable reign of Solomon began.

Genesis 25:22.] See no. 71.Ibid., 69.

Genesis 25:22–23. "And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to inquire of the Lord. And the Lord said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels."] Esau in this struggle represents false professors, or the false professing church, or those enemies of the people of God who were yet in some sense the children of the church, as Jacob and Esau were both the children of Rebecca, and conceived

-- 170 --

and brought forth together. And so Edom or the Edomites in the Prophets are very often put for the enemies of God's church, but not the enemies of it in general, not those enemies that are professed infidels, but the false Christian church who are the greatest persecutors of the true church of Christ; and the antichristian church seems especially to be intended.

Genesis 25:26. "His hand took hold on Esau's heel."] See notes on Genesis 38:28–29.

Genesis 25:33. "And he sold him his birthright."] See notes on Genesis 38:28–29.

Genesis 26:5.] If God had such respect to Abraham's righteousness and obedience, and particularly to his offering up his son in obedience to God, as to give the earthly Canaan to his seed, much more will God have such a respect to the righteousness of Christ, and his offering up himself in obedience to God, as for the sake of this to give his seed the heavenly Canaan.

Genesis 26:12.] Thus he was blessed for his obedience to God, when God commanded him not to go down into Egypt on that year of famine; and thus he found the way of duty to be the way to prosperity, even when the appearance of things very much threatened the contrary.

Genesis 26:18.] "Note, in our searches after truth, that fountain of living water, 'tis good to make use of the discoveries of former ages, which have been clouded by the corruptions of later times. Inquire for the old way, the wells that our fathers digged, which the adversaries of truth have stopped up. Ask thine elders, and they shall teach thee." Henry.Exposition, 1 (1725), 89.

Genesis 26:19–21.] "His servants digged new wells. Note, though we must use the light of former ages, it doth not therefore follow that we must rest in it, and make no advances. We must still be building upon their foundation, running to and fro, that knowledge may be increased. In digging these wells, he met with much opposition. Those that open the fountains of truth must expect contradiction." See Henry.Ibid. See further, no. 369.Works, 15, 359–60.

-- 171 --

Genesis 26:30–33.] "Isaac entertains Abimelech and his company, and enters into a league of friendship with him. Here see how generous the good man was. 1. In giving. He made them a feast, and bid them welcome. 2. In forgiving. He did not insist upon the diskindnesses they had done him, but freely entered into a covenant of friendship with them, and bound himself never to do them any injury. And providence smiled upon what Isaac did, for the same day that he made this covenant with Abimelech, his servants brought him tidings of a well of water they had found. He had not insisted upon the wells which the Philistines had unjustly taken from him, lest that should have broke off the treaty, but sat down silent under the injury. And to recompense him for that, immediately he is enriched with a new well, which, because it suited so well to the occurrence of the day, he called by an old name, 'Beersheba,'שֶבַע     בְּאֵר 'the well of the oath.'" Henry.Exposition, 1 (1725), 90.

Genesis 27:4.] It was probably the manner in those days for parents, when they grew old and expected to die in a little time, to make a feast, and to eat and drink with their children, when they gave them their blessing and their dying charges, and so did as it were make their will. Their dying testament or blessing was something like a covenant; but it was the manner of those, when they made a covenant with any, to make a feast, and eat and drink together (Genesis 26:30 and Genesis 31:46). When they gave their children the blessing, they then as it were took their leave of them. But when near friends took their leave one of another, they were wont to eat and drink together. So Rebecca's friends took their leave of her (Genesis 24:54). So did the Levite's father-in-law take leave of him and his daughter, the Levite's wife, in Judges 19. So God, when he makes his testament or covenant with us, doth as it were at a feast. Of old, when the people entered into solemn covenant with God, they were wont to make a feast, and feasted before the Lord; and almost all solemnities were attended with feasting.

The patriarchs' thus blessing their children before their death exhibits to us a type of the covenant of grace, which is as it were Christ's last will and testament to his people.

Genesis 27:9. "Kids of the goat."] Jacob, when he went to his father for the blessing, went with an offering of kids of the flock that had been slain. So when

-- 172 --

we go to our heavenly Father for his blessing, we should by faith carry with us the sacrifice of Christ, the Lamb slain. See notes on Genesis 27:15–16.

Genesis 27:15–16 ff.] Jacob, when he goes to his father for the blessing, goes clad in the goodly raiment of his elder brother, and with the skins of those kids that were slain to be offered to his father, and goes in the name of his elder brother. So when we go to our heavenly Father for his blessing, we must go in the name of Christ, our elder brother, and clothed with the goodly raiment of his righteousness, the best robe, and with the clothing of the Lamb slain and offered to God. Otherwise, we shall not obtain the blessing.

Genesis 27:29.] See no. 35.Works, 15, 57.

Genesis 27:33. "I have blessed him; yea, and he shall be blessed."] Isaac thus confirms the blessing he had given to Jacob, though by mistake and though notorously cheated by Jacob, because he remembered that he had been extraordinarily filled with the Holy Ghost in giving it, which probably made him recollect the divine oracle given before his birth.

Genesis 28:11–12 ff.] See no. 119.Ibid., 84. There seems to be a double representation in this story. It seems to be a type that has respect to two things. 1. By Jacob sleeping and having heaven opened to him, and God appearing in heaven as his covenant God, and "the angels of God ascending and descending" on him, seems to be represented Christ, which is confirmed by what Christ says, John 1:51, "You shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of man," in which Christ plainly alludes to what is said here in the Genesis 28:12. And Jacob's sleep here seems to represent the death of Christ. As Jacob in his sleep has the gate of heaven opened, and a ladder set on the earth on the land of Canaan, whose top reached to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it, and God appearing in heaven revealing himself as the covenant God of him and his seed, and promising that his seed "shall be as the dust of the earth" Genesis 28:14], and that in him and in his seed all the families of the earth should be blessed, so Christ by his death procured that the gate of heaven should be opened towards the earth, and that there should be an union between heaven and earth, and that

-- 173 --

there should be a way to heaven from the earth. He procured as it were a ladder by which there might be an ascent from this sinful miserable world to heaven. Christ procured this way to heaven for his covenant people, for his spiritual posterity; and therefore the foot of the ladder is set on the land of Canaan, the land of his people, on Jacob's land, or the land of Jacob's posterity. And Christ by his death procured that the angels of God might ascend and descend to and from the land of Canaan, in and through his mediation, or on his ladder, to be "ministering spirits" to the inhabitants of Canaan (Hebrews 1:14). So through the death of Christ God appears as the covenant God of him and his seed, promising to give heaven to him and his seed, as in the Genesis 28:14 he promises to give Canaan to Jacob and his seed; and also as bound in covenant to multiply his seed "as the dust of the earth," as here to Jacob—Isaiah 53:10, "When thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed"—and promising to give him the Gentiles in all parts of the world, or from the four winds of heaven to be his seed (which was accomplished soon after the death of Christ), as here he promises to Jacob that he should "spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south"; and as promising that in him "all the families of the earth" should be blessed in him, as here to Jacob. Note that Christ is evidently called by the name of "Israel," one of the names of Jacob, in Isaiah 49:3, which renders it more probable that Jacob is here a type of Christ.

2. Jacob here represents a believer, or rather all believers collective, or theJE deleted "whole." church, or spiritual Israel, of whom Jacob or Israel is the father; and the stone that he slept or rested upon represents Christ, who is from time to time compared to a stone. And that Christ is represented by this stone seems more evident because he anointed it (Genesis 28:18). Thereby he is represented that is Christ, or the anointed, and is called so, not only as he is anointed of God, but also as anointed by his people. See note on Daniel 9:25, and on Mark 14:3. And another thing that confirms that this stone is a type of Christ is what Jacob says of it in the Genesis 28:22. "And this stone, that I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house," for Christ is the house of God, in whom dwells "all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" [Colossians 2:9]. It was he that was signified by the tabernacle and temple, as is evident by what Christ says of his own body; for, says he, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will build it up" [John 2:19]. And the Lamb is said to be the temple of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22). And it is still further evident by the use that he put it to, for "he set it up for a

-- 174 --

pillar" Genesis 28:18], i.e. for an altar. See Exodus 24:4. For the oil that Jacob poured on it was to consecrate it as an altar, and also was as an offering to God on the altar, as the precious ointment was that Mary poured on the head of Christ was an offering to Christ and to God through him. And this will be more evident if we compare what is said here with Genesis 35:14, where we have an account that Jacob in the same place set up a pillar of stoneJE deleted "if it was not the same stone." (and probably it was the same stone), and "poured a drink offering thereon, and poured oil thereon."

What we are told of, Genesis 35:7, "And he built there an altar, and called it El-Beth-el, because there God appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother," this altar probably is the same spoken of in the Genesis 35:14, on which "he poured a drink offering" and oil, viz. the stone which he set up for a pillar, which was probably the same stone that is spoken of in this place, or that stone at least was a principal stone in the altar. But this he calls El-Beth-el,בֵּית־אֵל     אֵל or the God of Bethel, because it rep resented the God of Bethel, or Jesus Christ, who is that God.

Jacob promises, at the end of this chapter, that when God should return him again into his own land in peace, that this stone which he had set up for a pillar should be "God's house" [Genesis 28:22], i.e. this very place shall be that which I will make the place of worship (and therefore he set up the stone, that he slept on, for a pillar or monument whereby to remember the place). And this very stone shall be the altar on which I will worship and offer offerings to God. As we are told of David, when he had built an altar in the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, in the place where the angel appeared to him, 1 Chronicles 22:1, "Then said David, This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel," which accordingly was the place where the temple was built. And therefore when Jacob was returned to Canaan, and seemed to be negligent of his promise, God put him in mind of it, and commanded him to go, and dwell there, and make that the place of his worship (Genesis 35:1). And therefore doubtless the stone that he set up when he came there, that we have account of, Genesis 35:14–15, was in the very same place; and we have all reason to think the same stone. There God talked with him again then; and we have an account, Genesis 35:13, that "God went up Torn him in the place he talked with him," which denoted that place where God appeared then was the gate or entrance into heaven, as he

-- 175 --

says this place is, and so doubtless was the same spot. Besides that, we find Jacob calls it by the same name (Genesis 35:15).This paragraph is a later addition.

Jacob's sleeping or resting on this stone (for this stone, we are told, was his pillow) typifies God's people's believing in or resting on Christ. Christ invites the weary to come to him, and promises that in him they shall have rest [Matthew 11:28]. Jacob, while resting on this stone, has heaven's gate opened to him, and a ladder reaching from him to God in heaven. So 'tis by faith in Christ that God's people have heaven's gate opened to them, and have a way prepared for them to ascend and come to God in heaven. Jacob, while resting on this stone, has God appearing to him as his covenant God. So 'tis through faith in Christ that God becomes their covenant God, and whereby they become interested in the promises of the covenant of grace. And 'tis by faith that they become related to heaven, and have the privilege of the ministration of angels.

Jacob'sJE deleted "But whether we understand this type either one way or the other, Jacob's sleep, if we look," at the start of this paragraph. sleep here represents both death and rest. If we look on Jacob here as a type of Christ, his sleep is a type of death. If as a type of the church or of the Israel of God, then it represents spiritual rest. But let us take the type which way we will, we may observe that the great privilege and blessing is obtained of having heaven's gate opened, and a way to heaven from the earth; and the ministration is enjoyed in Bethel, in the house of God, i.e. in God's church, and in the improvement of the ordinances of his house.

Hence we may learn that their altars of old were types of Christ, especially in his divine nature. They represented him who is the rock of Israel. See Judges 13:19. And therefore it was the manner of the heathen to set up pillars or small altars instead of images, as Bedford in his Scripture ChronologyBedford writes, "So that the conversion of these pillars to an idolatrous use before the time of Moses, was the reason, that God forbad the Israelites to erect any" (p. 345). and other historians have observed, which was strictly forbidden to the children of Israel. Leviticus 26:1, "Ye shall make you no idols nor graven image; neither shall ye set up any pillar in your land, to bow down to it, for I am the Lord your God." And so Deuteronomy 16:22. And the children of Israel were required to destroy the pillars of the people of the land (Deuteronomy 7:5 and Deuteronomy 12:3). And hence the children of Israel were strictly forbidden to have any other altar but one, no other but the altar of the Lord, because God was one, and Christ was one, and because altars

-- 176 --

represented Christ. This is not the only place where the name of God is given to an altar; we have the like, Exodus 17:15.

Genesis 28:18.] Fables among the heathen derived from hence, see Gale's Court of the Gentiles, pp. 89 ff.Second edition, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 7, pp. 89–91.

"And took the stone that he had put for his pillows." No. 406,Works, 15, 414–15. SSS, and on Genesis 25:14.These references are a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 213, 200.

Genesis 28:19.] Luzלוּז signifies an almond tree. The same city is called both Bethel, or "God's house," and Luz, or "an almond tree," because that city represents the church of God which shall bring forth fruit like an almond tree. See Jeremiah 1:11–12. Thus Moses' rod was the rod of an almond tree.

Genesis 29:9–10.] Rachel was a shepherdess, as Zipporah, Moses' wife, was, herein being a type of the church. But 'tis Jacob that rolls away the stone for the watering the flock. So 'tis Christ that removes the difficulties in the way of the spiritualJE deleted "life." good of the church. 'Tis he that has set open the fountain for us.

Genesis 29:20. "And they seemed," etc.] It did not seem much to him to give such a price for that that he looked upon as so great a prize. Seven years service was a small thing to give for one that he so greatly esteemed and loved.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. What is here said of their seeming but a few days has respect to what they seemed to him when he made the bargain and agreed to serve so long for her, and not to what they seemed while he was waiting, for he did not wait the seven years before he married. This may appear by the note on Genesis 29:20–28.

Jacob was a type of Christ in his obtaining his wife by a servitude, and in his servitude's seeming light to him, and his going so cheerfully through it for the love wherewith he loved her. That Jacob might enjoy his beloved Rachel was the joy set before Jacob, for which he despised the difficulty of his servitude. And so that Christ might redeem his church, and present it to himself a glorious and blessed church to dwell

-- 177 --

with him in glory forever, was the joy that was set before Christ, for which he endured the cross and despised the shame.This paragraph is a separate entry. "But a few days." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 215.

Genesis 29:20–28.] Bedford in his Scripture Chronology, p. 294, col. 2, observes that "they who suppose that Jacob served seven years before he married Leah, and especially that he served seven years more before he married Rachel, involve themselves in insurmountable difficulties in fixing the births of the twelve patriarchs," and therefore supposes that Jacob only "served seven days as an earnest for seven years before Leah was given him to wife, and then served seven days more in the same manner before he married Rachel." And therefore when he found himself deceived by Laban's placing Leah instead of Rachel, and complains of it, Laban says, "Fulfill her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet other seven years" Genesis 29:27]. And we are told that 'Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week" Genesis 29:28]. So that it seems that it was but a week or seven days that Jacob served before he had Rachel. For however seven years is called a "week" in Daniel's prophecy of the coming of the Messiah [Daniel 9:25], yet there is no need of understanding a week here in any other than a literal sense, seeing that in order to the history's being consistent with itself, it must be so understood. 'Tis no wonder that seven years is called a week in a prophecy where all things are commonly represented under figures and images. And though we find it once so called in prophecy, yet there is no necessity of our understanding so in this history, when the history itself won't bear its being so understood, and we don't find it so called anywhere before, nor indeed anywhere at all in the whole history of the Bible. And then there was more reason why seven years should be called a week in Daniel's than in Jacob's time, for in Daniel's time years were divided and marked out into weeks, as days be, by a sabbath at every seven. There was a sabbatical year every seventh year, as there are sabbatical days every seven days; but it was not so in Jacob's time. And then there is no more difficulty in supposing that Laban should put a week for seven years than seven years for a week.

Genesis 29:25.] Jacob "had deceived his father with a suborned person, taking upon himself to be Esau when he was Jacob; and he is deceived by his father-in-law

-- 178 --

with a suborned person, and so embraces Leah whilst he thought he had embraced Rachel." Bedford, Scripture Chronology, p. 346. Hereby he was punishedMS: "Punishment." by the bitterness of the disappointment, and was obliged to keep Leah, who he did not love, and to serve seven years longer. See note on Genesis 37:31–33.

Genesis 29:27. "Fulfill her week."] By this it is evident that then in those days their time was divided out into weeks, or periods of seven days, as it is now, by which may rationally [be] argued that the sabbath was then observed among them, that it was an institution for the times before Moses, and that the remembrance of the institution was kept up in the world through the ages that preceded the Mosaic dispensation. For the weekly division of time had its rise from the appointment of one day in seven to be observed as a sabbath, and it was the observing the sabbath that upheld this division.

Genesis 30:1. "Give me children, or else I die."] 'Tis an observation in the fulfilling of the Scripture, that when God's people have an immediate desire and pressing after an outward thing, they have their desire sometimes answered, but therewith a sharp reproof from God, and usually find small satisfaction in their enjoying that about which they were so unsober in their pursuit. "Give children, or else I die," said Rachel. She got children, and she died in bringing one of them forth.

Genesis 30:3. "She shall bear upon my knees."] I.e. she shall bring forth children that I may receive and tend as my own upon my knees, or in my lap.

Genesis 30:14. "Mandrakes in the field."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 218.

Genesis 30:39.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 221–22.

Genesis 31:24. "That thou speak not unto Jacob either good or bad."] I.e. say nothing at all to him to compel him, to oblige him, to return again, or to bring him again under thy service, or to oblige him to resign to thee any of his wives, or cattle, or substance. Say nothing that has such a tendency or with any such view, whether it seem right and just to you, or

-- 179 --

wrong, good, or evil. I leave not you to judge of the righteousness of what you shall say with this view, but charge thee to say nothing at all in the least to infringe on his liberty or his possessions.

Laban came out after Jacob with such intentions, and he was now meditating what he would say to this purpose. His head was exceeding full of matter; but God charges him to suppress all, and not say one word tending to the design on which he was pursuing Jacob, however right and reasonable it might appear to him. God knew the heart of Laban, and he speaks to his heart. He knew how ready he would be to plead that the design he was upon was just, and that what he had meditated to say to Jacob was good and just. But God prevents him by charging him to say nothing to the purpose he was pursuing, let it be good or bad.

Genesis 31:34–35.] When Rachel's idols were searched for by her father, she hides them most secretly. Thus persons are wont to hide their idols and their hearts, and cover them over when search is made for them by their spiritual fathers and their own consciences; they cover them over with the camel's furniture, and put 'em amongst those things that are necessary to carry 'em along in their journey through the world, and cloak their sinfulness and unlawfulness under a pretense of such necessity. Persons are commonly wont to put their idols in a secret place, and therefore this is strictly forbidden. Deuteronomy 27:15, "Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the Lord, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place." So Achan hid the accursed thing in his tent under ground [Joshua 7:21].

Genesis 32:10. "With my staff."] See Numbers 21:18.

Genesis 32:24. "Until the breaking of the day."] Jacob continued wrestling with God all night, or great part of the night, as Christ continued all night in prayer to God, which represents perseverance in prayer.

Genesis 32:24–30.] Jacob seems to have stayed behind alone on purpose, that he might earnestly seek to God for his mercy on the occasion of Esau's coming forth against him. And when this person came to him in the form of a man, he was doubtless immediately sensible by his appearance that it was some very extraordinary person, and probably took him to be a messenger from God sent to him on this occasion of his extraordinary danger by Esau. And probably he might soon make it known to him that he was so, by the conversation there was before they began to wrestle.

-- 180 --

This wrestling denotes the seeming opposition that God oftentimes makes to persons when seeking his blessing. When God has a design of bestowing the blessing on persons in answer to prayer, he stirs 'em up to be earnest in seeking, and oftentimes for a time seems not to hear and regard their requests, but on the contrary seems to oppose and resist them (as the angel seemed to strive against Jacob in the wrestle), which is for the trial of persons' resolution, constancy, and perseverance in seeking of it.

So Christ dealt with the woman of Canaan [Matthew 15:22–29]. Hence God is as it were overcome. The prayer he resists a while, and there is as it were a struggle or strife between God and the supplicant. And then God is conquered, as the unjust judge was conquered by the importunity of the widow [Luke 18:1–5]. There may be observed a fourfold trial of Jacob's perseverance in seeking the blessing that God exercised him with.This sentence and the following four paragraphs are incorporated directly into JE's sermon on Genesis 32:24–26, entitled Blessed Struggle, dated Aug. 1735, with the doctrine, "Tis frequently God's manner, when persons are seeking the blessing of him, to exercise them with tried of their resolution and steadfastness in seeking, before he bestows it upon them." See Works Jonathan Edwards, 19, The "Blank Bible", ed. M. X. Lesser (New Haven, Yale iv. Press, 2001), 423–24.

1. His opposing Jacob in wrestling. What Jacob sought by his wrestling was that the angel might stay with him longer, and might bless him. The angel, by striving and struggling against him, seemed to resist and oppose, and be very unwilling. Now this was a trial of Jacob's perseverance in seeking, that he should seem thus opposite. It looked discouraging on Jacob's design, but yet he held out.

2. It was more of a trial, that he seemed to deny and resist Jacob so long. It is said, "there wrestled a man with him till the dawning of the Jay." It probably would not have been so expressed had not great part of the night been spent in wrestling. It seems a wonder that Jacob was not weary, and that he did not give out when he saw the angel continued to resist and oppose him so long on what he sought. It looked as if he angel was very unwilling and determined against it.

3. Another trial was his putting Jacob's thigh out of joint. It is said that when he saw he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh" Genesis 32:25], etc. There had been long resisting and struggling before; and the angel seemed hereby as if he was resolved to conquer and get way from Jacob, and that rather than fail, he would disenable Jacob. But though Jacob was much disenabled by it, and it may be in great pain, yet

-- 181 --

he was so resolute that he went on still, like the woman of Canaan who would not give out though Christ gave her one response after another, and at last told her that "it was not meet to take the children's bread, and cast it to dogs" [Matthew 15:26].

It is said that "the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him" Genesis 32:25]. It seems to be expressed purposely to signify what disadvantage he was under for that exercise.

4. And lastly, another trial of his perseverance was his speaking to him to let him go because the day broke, as much as to say, Let me go, for it is high time that I was gone. You have detained me here a great while, even till the day is broke. But even then Jacob declares it to be his final resolution under all these discouragements and trials not to let him go except he blessed him. When he appeared thus as it were thoroughly obstinate and insuperable in his resolution, then God blessed him.

Wrestling was an exercise agreeable to Jacob's name,יַצֲקֹב which was by interpretation a "supplanter." He began it when he first came into the world; his hand got hold on Esau's heel [Genesis 25:26]. That and this wrestling with the angel are mentioned together (Hosea 12:3–4). As a prince he had power with God and with men. He showed that he had power with men in supplanting his brother Esau, and getting away the birthright and blessing from him. He had power with God in that he, in wrestling, overcame, and obtained the blessing of him. And he was hereby encouraged that he should have power with his brother Esau again, who was now coming forth against him, and should prevail and escape from him.

Wrestling is the employment that Christians must spend their lives in, wrestling with God in seeking of him, and wrestling with their enemies in resisting them.

It was in the night late, in the time that persons usually are asleep, that Jacob wrestled with the angel, which may denote the watching that ought to be used with prayer. It was in the night, in a time of darkness, as oftentimes persons' wrestling time, or the time wherein they are wrestling for the blessing before it is bestowed, is attended with a great deal of darkness, with many difficulties, temptations, and discouragements. But yet when the day broke, God bestowed the blessing. Though weeping may continue for a night, yet joy comes in the morning [Psalms 30:5]. When persons have held out and persevered through all darkness they meet with, the day will dawn at length; and the blessing will be obtained. The dawning

-- 182 --

of that day seems to typify the light that commonly arises to the soul when God bestows his blessing.The section of this entry that follows was written before the comments that precede this supernumeral.

"And Jacob was left alone, and there wrestled a man with him," etc.] Jacob did not know that it was God till the last, but immediately was sensible that it was some extraordinary person by his appearance,JE deleted "and conversation." though it was in the night. He might probably suppose him to be an angel, for it was no uncommon thing for angels to appear in those days. And Jacob himself had not been altogether unused to it before now, for he had a vision of angels at Bethel [Genesis 28:12]; and the angels of God met him again at Mahanaim [Genesis 32:1–2]. However, he doubtless perceived by his gesture and conversation that he was some person of very extraordinary excellency, wisdom, and holiness.

It seems to me probable that Jacob came to wrestle with him. Thus he had before been conversing with Jacob. And he appeared so excellent and amiable a person, and conversed with him in so sweet, condescending, and friendly a manner that Jacob was exceedingly delighted in his company, and could not bear to part with him. And therefore upon his making as though he would go away, he laid hold of him to stay him; and the person striving as though he would get away, and Jacob to stay him, hence ensued a wrestle. Jacob was emboldened to such freedom by the extraordinary meekness which he observed in him, and by the friendship and familiarity of his conversation with him. When the day broke, the person having not prevailed by wrestling, urges Jacob to let him go. Jacob replies, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" Genesis 32:26]. He was resolved if he would depart, and he could have no more of his company, yet he would if possible obtain his blessing before he went. The extraordinary excellency, wisdom, and holiness that appeared in him made him value and desire his blessing. But when upon this the person asked Jacob what his name was, and told him that his name should be no longer Jacob but Israel, because as a prince he had power with God, and had prevailed Genesis 32:28], then Jacob began to suspect that it was God, and prays him to tell him his name. And when he perceived that it was God, he expresses himself as one astonished to think that he had such familiar conversation with God. He "called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God, and my life is preserved" Genesis 32:30].

-- 183 --

Genesis 32:25.] So earnest and resolved was Jacob that he would not leave off wrestling, though his "thigh was out of joint," and he was under such a great disadvantage and discouragement, like the woman of Canaan who would not leave off importuning of Christ, though he had given her such a repulse by telling her it was not meet to take the children's bread and give it unto dogs [Matthew 15:26].

Genesis 32:29. "And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost inquire after my name?"] This compared with Judges 13:18, with other text there quoted, confirms that this person was the Son of God.

Genesis 32:31.] Jacob goes away with a blessing, but yet halting on his thigh. God commonly, when he bestows some extraordinary spiritual blessing and peculiar favor, he also at the same time brings some temporal affliction or difficulty, as Paul, when admitted to the third heaven, had "a thorn in the flesh" at the same time, lest he "should be exalted above measure" [2 Corinthians 12:7].The remainder of this entry is a later addition. Jacob's halting on his thigh represents the saints' getting along with difficulty, and trouble,JE deleted "in the world." and disappointment of their temporal aims, their failing in the steps they take of what nature aims at and desires. Jacob's lameness, after he had the blessing, made him lean more on his staff. So the saints' afflictions they meet with in the world make 'em live more by faith. See Genesis 32:10, and note on Numbers 21:18. Jacob himself, when he had the blessing, had with it that kind of lameness of which his halting on his thigh was a type, and so he had ever since he first stoleMS: "obtain'd ‹stole›." the blessing from Esau. He presently upon it suffered banishment, went away poor and solitary with nothing but his staff to Padan-Aram. There he met with crosses and disappointments. He was cheated with Leah instead of Rachel, for whom he served seven years, and was forced to serve another seven years. Rachel, his most beloved wife, was a great while barren. And after he had suffered twenty years exile from his father's house, and hard service and a great deal of trouble from his father-in-law, he was forced to steal away; and his journey was attended with great difficulty and peril. He was in great danger, first from Laban and then from Esau, and was forced to purchase safety from him with the loss of great part of his substance. He made him a present of 580 of his cattle, and was forced greatly to bow and cringe besides; and then his daughter Dinah

-- 184 --

was defiled, which doubtless was a very sorrowful thing to him. And then he had more sorrow by the cruelty and treachery of Simeon and Levi, two sons which made him to stink in the nostrils of the inhabitants of the country, so that he was in fear of his life from them. And then Rachel, his most beloved wife, died on bringing forth her second child. And then Reuben, his first-born son, was guilty of incest with one of his own concubines, which must needs be a great grief to him. And then he had most bitter affliction in the loss of his beloved son Joseph, and then doubtless had a great deal of sorrow from the great sins and calamities there were in Judah and his family. And then there was a sore famine, and Jacob and his family were put to a great deal of trouble to get provisions to support. And he had much exercise, perplexity, and distress in the affair managed between Joseph and his brethren. And then he and all his family as it were suffered a second banishment from the land of Canaan, the land promised to him, in Egypt, an idolatrous country, and never returned any more alive.

That Jacob, who was so often blessed of God, and to whom God so frequently manifested such abundant favor to, should yet meet with so much trouble and sorrow in this life, is a great evidence of a future state. The same may be observed concerning David.

Halting is put elsewhere for affliction or adversity. Psalms 35:15, "But in mine adversity they rejoiced." In the original,בְצַלְעִי "in my halting." Micah 4:6–7, "In that day, saith the Lord, I will assemble her that halteth, and will gather her that is driven out, and her that I have afflicted; and I will make her that halteth a remnant." Zephaniah 3:19, "Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee; and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out," etc.

Genesis 33:1–7.] See no. 417.Works, 15, 469–70.

Genesis 33:19. "And he bought a parcel of a field… at the hand of the children of Hamor," etc.] We read of no other land that either Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob possessed as their own but this that Jacob bought, and that which Abraham bought for a possession of a burying place. And this that Jacob bought never served him for any other purpose but to erect an altar to the Lord; and this also was used afterwards as a possession for a burying, for here they buried Joseph's bones that were brought out of Egypt. Both

-- 185 --

this altar, called El Elohe Israel,יִשְׂרָאֵל     אֳלהֵי     אֵל "God the God of Israel," and the sacrifices offered here, and also Joseph, whose bones were buried here, typified Christ, the great Immanuel, who ascended into heaven with his human nature after it has been subject unto death, there to be presented to God as a lamb that had been slain and offered to God, and his blood there presented before the throne of God. See note on Genesis 23.

Genesis 35:2.] Jacob, when he was going to Padan-Aram, vowed a vow that if God would be with him, and would provide for him, and return him again in safety, that the Lord alone should be his God (Genesis 28:20–21). And God, according to his request, had wonderfully blessed and prospered him when in Padan-Aram; and when he commanded him to return, he put him in mind of his vow. Genesis 31:13, "I am the God of Bethel," says he, "where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me. Now arise, get thee out from this land, and return unto the land of thy kindred." And God wonderfully preserved him in his return, first from Laban, and then from Esau. But Jacob seems too much to have forgotten his vow, and neglected to fulfill it. He still suffered them that belonged to his family to keep those household gods that they brought from Padan-Aram. And this seems to be the cause of those troubles in Jacob's family that we read of in the Genesis 30; and yet these troubles ben't sufficient to awaken him, till God again puts him in mind of his vow by directing him to go to Bethel, where he had made the vow, and build an altar there to him, which was a part of his vow. For he vowed that if God provided for him, and returned him, etc., that that place where he had set up that pillar that he anointed should be God's house. And God also put him in mind of his great mercy to him in delivering him from Esau, and appearing to him, and blessing him at that time, and that Jacob seems to be in good earnest about purging his house from idols, and so fulfilling his vow.

Genesis 35:4. "Earrings."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 239–40.

Genesis 35:5. "And they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob."] Though they had lately done so much to provoke them. See Genesis 34:30.

-- 186 --

Genesis 36:6–8.] Concerning the country where Esau and his descendants settled, and how the Red Sea was so called from "Edom," that signifies "red," see Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 14–15.Old and New Testament Connected.

Genesis 36:24. "Anah."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 244.

Genesis 37 ff.] See an explanation of the whole story of Joseph, in notes on Genesis 41:40–57, and more fully in sermons from Acts 7:9–14.No extant copy of these sermons has been located.

Genesis 37:2. "These are the generations of Jacob."] "Moses has no more to say of the Edomites, unless as they happen to fall in Israel's way, but now applies himself closely to the story of Jacob's family." These are the generations of Jacob. "His is not a barren genealogy as that of Esau (Genesis 36:1), but a memorable useful history." Henry, in loc.Exposition, I (1725), 118–19.

"And the lad was with the sons of Bilhah, and with the sons of Zilpah." Isaac was persecuted by him who was born of the bondwoman [Genesis 21:9], which, by what the Apostle says, seems to represent God's free people, true children, being persecuted by those that are of a legal spirit [Galatians 4:29–31]. And the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, Jacob's bondwomen, persecuting Joseph, the son of his beloved wife, seems to signify the same thing.

Genesis 37:4.] Thus early appeared the temper of that progeny of Israel, which was to envy their younger brother, as they did afterwards in the days of the new testament when they envied the Gentile church for the peculiar favor God showed them, which was represented in the parable of the prodigal son [Luke 15:11–32]. Thus as their fathers did, so did they. Stephen, rehearsing their history and mentioning this envy of their fathers towards Joseph among other things, accuses them with being as their fathers (Acts 7:51).

Genesis 37:7.] "Intimating upon what occasions they should be brought to do obeisance to him, viz. in seeking to him for corn, their empty sheaves should bow to his full one." Henry, in loc.Ibid., 119.

-- 187 --

Genesis 37:9.] Joseph's dreaming that the sun, moon, and stars made obeisance to him has respect to something beyond his father, and mother, and brethren bowing to him. It has respect to all things, not only in earth but in heaven, being put in subjection to Christ, and in him to the church, so that all shall be theirs, and they shall reign over all.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. And besides, this had a kind of literal fulfillment to one of Joseph's posterity, viz. Joshua, when he said, "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, moon, in the valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed" (Joshua 10:12–13).

Genesis 37:24. "The pit was empty; there was no water in it."] Joseph's brethren intended to famish him, or kill him with hunger and thirst. And it was so ordered afterwards that [they] would have died with famine, had not they come and bowed down to Joseph to the earth for relief.

Genesis 37:28.] See no. 126.Works, 15, 86.

Genesis 37:31.] Joseph's coat's being dipped in the blood of a kid was probably ordered in providence to point forth Jesus Christ, the antitype of Joseph, the Lamb that was slain, the great antitype of the paschal lamb, and of the lamb of the daily sacrifice, and all other lambs that were offered in sacrifice to God. The paschal lamb was either a lamb or a kid (Exodus 12:3, Exodus 12:5). Joseph was not actually slain, but he was like to [be] slain. He was designed for the slaughter; but it was so ordered in providence that his life was spared, and a kid slain in his room. Both together constitute a type of the death of Christ. In like manner, when Abraham offered his son Isaac, Isaac was not actually slain, but was like to be slain, and was intended to be killed and burnt on the altar; but God ordered the matter so that his life was spared, and a ram slain and sacrificed in his room [Genesis 22:1–14]. And both together constitute a type of the sacrifice of Christ.

Genesis 37:31–33.] "Jacob is deceived by the blood of a kid instead of his son Joseph's [blood], as he had deceived his own father with the flesh and skin of a kid," instead of his son Esau's skin and his venison [Genesis 27:6–29]. Bedford's Scripture Chronology, p. 354.JE marked this paragraph with a large "X."

-- 188 --

Joseph's brethren deceive Jacob their father by the blood of a kid instead of his son Joseph's, his best beloved son, as he, being Esau's brother, had deceived Isaac his father with the flesh and skin of a kid instead of his son Esau's skin and his venison, who was Isaac's best beloved son. Thus is Jacob punished by God's providence. See note on Genesis 29:25.This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 38:28–29.]JE deleted "See no. 127." Works, 15, 86. Zara put his hand out first, but Pharez, from whom came Christ, brake forth before him, which imports the same thing as Isaac's casting out Ishmael [Genesis 21:10]; Jacob's taking hold of Esau's heel [Genesis 25:26], from whence he was called "Supplanter," and afterwards getting the birthright of him; David's getting the kingdom from Saul, and being anointed before the elder brother that envied him in the camp [1 Samuel 16:13]. Zara represents the church of the Jews, and Pharez, the younger brother, the church of the Gentiles. As in the parable of the prodigal [Luke 15:11–32], the youngest, that was the prodigal, represents the church of the Gentiles, and his elder brother, that envied him, the church of the Jews. Ishmael represented the church of the Jews, and Isaac the Gentiles, as we know by the Apostle's explanation. The church of the Gentiles is called the "little sister," that is, younger sister, by a Hebraism.

This is agreeable to what Christ often says, viz. that the "first shall be last, and the last first" [Mark 10:31].This sentence is a later addition.

Genesis 39:4–6.] What we are informed of in these verses, of Joseph's being thus set over all that Potiphar his master had, seems to be typical of the same thing as Pharaoh's setting of him over all the land of Egypt, that we have an account of, Genesis 40:40–57, of which see notes on the place.

Genesis 39:14.] See no. 128.Works, 15, 86.

Genesis 41.] See how the Egyptian Apis and SerapisApis, a sacred Egyptian bull; Serapis, a Greco-Egyptian deity. are probably a symbol of Joseph (no. 407, and SSS on Genesis 41:57).Works, 15, 415; Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 265–66. [For] the traditions found among the heathen of this story of Joseph, see SSS on the Genesis 41:57.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 265–66.

-- 189 --

Genesis 41:40–57.] This typifies the Father's investing of Christ, the Mediator, with the government of the church and the world. Joseph was exalted out of the dungeon to be a prince and ruler over all the land. So Christ was exalted from being a prisoner of vindictive justice out of the grave, and as it were out of the pit of hell, to be a prince and to have all things put under him. Pharaoh set Joseph over his own house. So God exalted Christ and set him over his church, which is the house of God (Hebrews 3:6), and made him king of heaven itself, which is the palace of God. According to Joseph's word all Pharaoh's people were to be ruled; only in the throne, Pharaoh was to be greater than he. So Christ is made the head and ruler of angels and men; but yet God the Father is greater than Christ as Mediator, as Christ says, "My Father is greater than I" [John 14:28]. He is greater in his economical office than the Son, in that he is the person that sustains the dignity and maintains the rights of the deity. "Pharaoh took off his ring from off his hand, and put it upon Joseph's hand" Genesis 41:42]. So God the Father invested Christ with his own honor and dignity, "that all men should honor the Son as they honor the Father" [John 5:23]. "And they cried before him, Bow the knee" Genesis 41:43], as 'tis said concerning Christ, "Let all the angels of God worship him" [Hebrews 1:6]. And agreeable to this, it is said, Philippians 2:8–10, "He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." Joseph was thus exalted as a reward for his being the means of saving the people from famine and death. So Christ is exalted to God's right hand, and "put all things under his feet" [1 Corinthians 15:27], in reward for his working out the work of redemption. Pharaoh exalted Joseph, and made him head over Egypt, and put the people and all the land into his hand, that he himself might have the immediate disposal and ordering of that affair of saving the people from famine that he had laid the foundation for. So Christ is exalted to be a prince and a Savior, to dispose of the affair of the actual applying and accomplishing that redemption that he had purchased. All things were committed to him of the Father, that he might give eternal life to as many as God had given him. The food of the land, by which the people were to be saved from famine, was committed to Joseph's hands, that he might be the immediate dispenser of it. So the purchased blessings are committed to Christ; he has received gifts for men when he ascended on high. He had the purchased blessings given to him, that he himself might bestow them on them that he purchased them for. He received the promise of the Father, even the Holy Ghost

-- 190 --

without measure, to shed down on believers, as Joseph had corn brought into him in immense quantities (Genesis 41:49). Joseph had a vast stock in his hand; this typifies the sufficiency of Christ for the supply of the wants of his people. Joseph was advanced thus to be a savior to his brethren and kindred; so Christ was exalted to be the Savior of men, whom he became related to by his incarnation, becoming the brother of believers. The saints are Christ's near relations. He that hears the word of God, and keeps it, the same is his mother, and sister, and brother [Matthew 12:50]. Joseph, by his exaltation in Egypt, made way for his brethren's reception there; he there prepared a place for them in Goshen, and made way for their reception there by taking his brethren and presenting them to the king, and interceding with him for them (Genesis 47). Pharaoh gave 'em "the best of the land," by giving it to Joseph for them (Genesis 47:6). And Joseph nourished his brethren in Egypt. So Christ, by his exaltation in heaven, made way there, coming there, prepared a place, etc. Joseph saved his brethren, though they had been enemies, yea, though they had been his mortal enemies, though they would have put him to death, though they sold him. He saved them by that banishment, those very sufferings which their sin, their enmity, brought upon him. As it was with Christ, he saved 'em from famine. He first humbled them before he made himself known to them. He exercised them with variety of dispensations, hopes, fears, disappointments, confusions, perplexities, to humble 'em before he made himself known to them. They bring their money with them to buy corn, whereas that was not their way to obtain it of Joseph. He would not accept of their money. So we must come to Christ for spiritual food, without our own righteousness, without money, and without price. Joseph at first made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly to them, charges them with not coming as friends, but as enemies; and thereby he makes 'em sensible of their guilt in their former treatment of him. So when the elect are under convictions, and are first stirred up to seek to God for salvation, God is wont as it were to frown upon them, to express his anger as though he looked upon them as enemies, thereby to bring their sins to remembrance and make 'em sensible of their guilt in their former treatment of him. Joseph insists on it that he should look upon them as enemies till they deliver up their younger brother, that one brother that they kept back, that they were tender of as a child, that they pitied and spared and looked upon it that it would be too hard for him to be brought out of the family, and rent from the arms of his father, and delivered up to another lord. So oftentimes sinners, when they begin to seek salvation, keep back something

-- 191 --

that is dear and tender in their eyes, and flatter themselves that they ben't obliged to deliver it up. They think it is too hard and cruel for 'em so to expose such an enjoyment or possession, but God will surely look upon 'em as enemies till all is delivered up, and nothing kept back. Joseph put 'em all together in ward three days. So God for a while holds sinners prisoners under conviction; they are shut up as condemned creatures, exposed to the execution of God's wrath. Joseph pities them, and weeps with compassion for them, at the same time that he treats them thus roughly. So God oftentimes pities sinners under conviction at the same time that he seems terribly to frown on them. While they were backward to deliver up Benjamin, Joseph "took from [them] Simeon, and bound him before their eyes" [Genesis 42:24]; so while persons keep back some dear lusts, God takes away some of their enjoyments from 'em. Before Joseph made known himself unto them, they don't understand his language, for he spake to 'em by an interpreter. So sinners before their conversion don't understand God's language, and they therefore need the help and advice of ministers under that conviction as interpreters for them. For a while they seem to have obtained their end, to have obtained food for their money; but this food lasts 'em but a little while before it was spent. So the false comfort that sinners obtain under conviction by their own righteousness lasts 'em but a little while before it is all spent. For a while they hoped their money was accepted, but they soon find it rejected, to their great disappointment and confusion. They came back to their father in the land of Canaan, who in this case represents the first Adam, or nature which men have from him by their parents, the father whose tenderest and dearest child Benjamin was that was kept back. They consult with their father under this difficulty, as men in their difficulties are wont to consult nature. Their father blames them for yielding to the lord of the land so far as they had done, and greatly objects against delivering up Benjamin. He cries out all these things are against me, as persons under convictions often do in a kind of discouragement. But, however, he at length is forced to it by sore famine. So men are as it were forced to deliver up their dearest lusts, that it grieves 'em to part with, by sore famine, by a sense of the extreme necessity of their case. He is brought to it by the persuasions of Reuben and Judah. Reuben here represents the faculty of reason, which is the eldest child of men's nature. Jacob in his blessing calls Reuben "the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power" [Genesis 49:3]. The standard of the camp of Reuben bore the image of a man. Reuben never consented to the selling of Joseph. Man's reason never consents to his sin. Judah, the progenitor of

-- 192 --

Christ, the Word of God, the other brother that persuaded Jacob to deliver up Benjamin, signifies the word of God; or Judah represents the ministers of the word, who preach the word of Christ to souls under conviction. And therefore he rehearses the word of Joseph, and particularly declares his threatenings and solemn declarations, to persuade Jacob to deliver up Benjamin. Jacob, after disputing with Judah, delivers up Benjamin, the "right hand son,"בִּנְיָמִין as the name signifies. So nature, after it has long hung back, and much disputing with the word of God, and objecting against it, by the word being earnestly set home, at last yields to cut off and deliver up the beloved lust and right-hand sin.

Jacob, being at length forced to the extreme necessity of the case, delivers up that one son that he was most fond of ("If it must be so now," says he [Genesis 43:11].).
