Judges

The BOOK OF JUDGES. Concerning the ancient government by judges, see SSS, at the beginning of this book.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1061–62.

Judges 1:12–15.] No. 352.Works, 15, 338–39.

Judges 2:1.] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1069–71.

Judges 2:6.] Concerning the connection of this verse with what went before, see SSS.Ibid., col. 1072.

Judges 2:7.] Agreeable to this are some traditions preserved concerning the Jews among the heathen, mentioned by Grotius, de verit., Bk. 1, Sect. 16. As he observes in his notes, "Strabo, in his fourteenth Bk., after the history of Moses, says, 'That his followers for a considerable time kept his precepts, and were truly righteous and godly.' And a little after he says, those who believed in Moses worshipped God, and were lovers of equity."Truth of Christian Religion, 63.

Judges 2:11–12.] See the reason why the children of Israel were so prone to idolatry, in SSS, on Judges 10:6.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1139.

Judges 2:13.] Of this Ashtaroth, see Bedford's Scripture Chronology, p. 234.Bedford links Naamah, identified as the wife of Ham, who survived on the ark, called Ashtaroth (in Hebrew) or Astarte (in Greek), with Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, identified as Venus by the Romans.

Dr. Winder in his History of Knowledge, pp. 192 ff., observes that Ashtaroth is a wordעַשְׁתָּרוֹת that in the Hebrew signifies "flocks," and is so from time

-- 330 --

to time translated, and supposes that the moon was the deity that was called "Ashtaroth, a name of office with regard to some particular expectations, which they had from that luminary, with regard to their flocks, they having a notion, that the moon especially presided over the night and governed its affairs. And that, in that season wolves and other beasts of prey range about, and robbers and spoilers often march forth to plunder and destroy, so in this time of danger their flocks will be especially exposed. And as a principal part of the wealth of those early ages consisted in their flocks, for these reasons they might particularly address themselves to the moon, who ruled the night, for protection, and worship this luminary under the name of Ashtaroth, or the guardian, των Ashtaroth, of their flocks."This paragraph is a later addition. Critical and Chronological History (2nd ed.), I, 192–94.

Judges 4:2. "Of the Gentiles."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1082–83.

Judges 5:4. "And the heavens dropped."] See note on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210.Works, 15, 135–40.

Judges 5:10. "White asses."] The wordאֲתֹנוֹת signifies white "she-asses." "The judges in Israel were types of Christ," who came with great labor and doing a hard service, of which an ass was the hieroglyphic. They rode on she-asses, it being "the nature of those creatures to bring forth their young only in the dark, as Christ, by lying in darkness and the grave for a while, was to bring us forth to light and glory, viz. at his resurrection. And so we are called, Luke 20:36, 'the children of the resurrection.' And God is said 'to have begotten us again to a lively hope, by the resurrection of Christ from the dead' [1 Peter 1:3]; who, according to the promise, was to 'see of the travail of his soul, and be satisfied' [Isaiah 53:11]. And therefore he exults in spirit, and says, 'Behold I and the children, which God hath given me' [Hebrews 2:13]." (See Merrick's sermon on Christ the True Vine, p. 14.)Merrick, Parable of the Vineyard and Christ. Marshal Montagu Merrick (1719–82), an Anglican divine. The church also, who may be represented by the she-ass, brings forth when subject of much toil and labor, and when brought into great darkness.

-- 331 --

Judges 5:11. "Righteous acts."] We find God's goodness often in Scripture called his "righteousness," the true reason of which seems to be that righteousness is a word of extensive meaning in Scripture, including all moral perfection. This is confirmed by Psalms 25:8, "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore will he teach sinners the way." See also Psalms 30:4.

Judges 5:14. "They that handle the pen of the writer."] This shadows forth the great hand that authors shall have in the great and last battle that the church shall have with her enemies, of which that, about which is this song, was a type.

Judges 5:15. "He was sent on foot into the valley."] Without chariots or horses, in which his enemies abounded.

Judges 5:15–16. "For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart."] I.e. for their division from the rest of Israel in this affair, that they did not come and join themselves with the rest of God's people in fighting against their enemies, it was much wondered. And therefore 'tis said of Reuben in the Judges 5:16, "Why abodest thou among the sheep-folds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks?" Ephraim, and Issachar, and Zebulun, and Naphtali are here commended for the hand that they had in this matter, but 'tis complained of Reuben, Gilead, and Dan, and Asher, that they stayed at home.

Judges 5:20.] When God is doing some great thing for his church on earth, the hosts of heaven are engaged with the church on earth; and hence God's army is a company of two armies. So when Jacob was going against Esau with his host, the host of heaven appeared with him at Mahanaim [Genesis 32:2]. Thus heaven is concerned in what is done for the church on earth. So when Christ goes forth to battle against Antichrist (of which this battle is a type), it is said the armies of heaven "followed him on white horses" [Revelation 19:14].

"They fought from heaven." See no. 211.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 140–42.

Judges 5:21. "That ancient river."] The river Kishon was probably so called because it was designed of old in the council of God to serve his purpose against Sisera at this time, and did so as if it had been made on purpose.

-- 332 --

Thus the water of the old pool God is said to have fashioned long ago for that use to which it was put (Isaiah 22:11).

Judges 5:22. "The pransings of their mighty ones."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1098–99.

Judges 5:24. "Women in the tent."] SSS.Ibid., col. 1099.

Judges 6:3. "Children of the east."] See Genesis 25:6 note.

Judges 6:8–11 ff.] Here was a prophet raised up to convince the people of sin before Christ comes, giving comfort and with the glad tidings of salvation, which we have account of in the Judges 6:11 and following verses. Very much as it was when Christ came into the world by his incarnation, John the Baptist, a prophet, comes first as his forerunner to convince of sin and to preach repentance, to prepare the way before him.

Judges 6:25.] Gideon was ordered to offer two bullocks: "his father's young bullock, and the second bullock of seven years old." So it should be read. Henry.Exposition, 2 (1725), 95.

Judges 6:26. "In the ordered place."] I.e. in the place where I ordered thee to put the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and where I caused a miraculous flame to consume them, as Judges 6:20. This seems to be the same altar with that spoken of, Judges 6:24.

Judges 6:32.] Concerning Sanchoniathon's acquaintance with Jerubbaal, see "Miscellanies," nos. 959 and 962.Works, 20, 239–40 and 242–46.

Judges 6:37–40.] No. 364.Ibid., 2, 350.

Judges 7:5. "Him shalt thou set by himself."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1111–12.

Judges 7:20.] Gideon and his company represents the church, and the army of the Midianites represents the host of the enemies of the church. The

-- 333 --

earthen pitchers represent two things, viz. the frail human nature of Christ and also the ministers of Christ. The lamps that were in the pitchers representMS: "Represents." gospel truth and grace. Christ had this treasure in him when on earth, and the ministers of the gospel have this treasure in earthen vessels. By the breaking of the frail nature of Christ, the light of the gospel shone forth in the world; and the grace of God appeared to the salvation of his people, and the confusion of Satan and the enemies of his church. And the martyrdom of the ministers and saints of Christ has been made a means of propagating the gospel and confounding the enemies of the church. The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.This saying in various translations is identified with the African church father Tertullian (c. 160–c. 225 C.E.). See Tertullians Apologie or, Defence of the Christians, against the Accusations of the Gentiles. Now made English by H. B. Esq. (London, 1657), 178; and Apology, in The Ante-Nicene Fathers: Translations of The Writings of the Fathers down to A.D. 325, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (10 vols. Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 1980), III, 55. The blowing with trumpets signifies the preaching the gospel.

Judges 7:24. "Unto Bethbarah and Jordan."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1117.

Judges 9:5.] One lust harbored kills all at last. Gideon had seventy sons and one bastard, but that one bastard was the death of all his seventy sons. Some men have many excellent gifts, and perform multitudes of duties; but one secret sin indulged and allowed will destroy all at last.

Judges 9:6. "And all the house of Millo."] "I.e. the common council, the full house, the house of fulness, as the wordמִלּוֹא signifies, those that met in their guildhall. We read often of the house of Millo, or the state house in Jerusalem, or the city of David (2 Samuel 5:9, 2 Kings 12:20)." Henry.Exposition, 2 (1725), 105.

Judges 9:28. "Serve the men of Hamor."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1134.

Judges 9:45. "Sowed it with salt."] The end of sowing the place with salt was not to make it barren, for it was a city, not a field, that is spoken. But this action seems to have been used in those days as a symbolical to signify the curse of being perpetually desolate. It was an open, solemn declaration

-- 334 --

that they devoted the place thus sowed with salt to everlasting desolation and emptiness. Probably it came to [be] thus used from what was observed of the providence of God with respect to Sodom, and the cities and country round about, that was effectually devoted to perpetual desolation by being covered with the salt sea. See SSS.Ibid., col. 1136.

Judges 10:4. "Called Havoth-jair."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1138–39.

Judges 10:6.] Concerning the reason why the children of Israel were so prone to idolatry, see SSS.Ibid., col. 1139.

Judges 11:12. "My land."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1145–46.

Judges 11:24. "Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess?"] The land which the Ammonites now possessed was a land that they had taken from others, viz. from the Zamzummims (Deuteronomy 2:20–21). They had been extraordinarily assisted to prevail against and drive out this people, though a very mighty and gigantic [people]. This they ascribed to Chemosh their god, and they therefore thought they had a good title to the land, seeing their god had given it to them. See SSS.Ibid., col. 1147.

Judges 11:30–40.] Concerning Jephthah's vow and offering his daughter, see no. 223.Works, 15, 160–69.

Judges 11:39. "Who did unto her according to his vow."] See fables of the heathen from hence, in SSS, at the end of this chapter.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1153.

See no. 223.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 160–69.

Judges 12:1–4.] "The Ephraimites had the same quarrel with Gideon (Judges 8:1), who was of Manasseh, on their side Jordan, as Jephthah was of Manasseh, on the other side Jordan. Ephraim and Manasseh were nearer akin than any of the other tribes, being both the sons of Joseph; and yet

-- 335 --

they were more jealous one of another than any of the other tribes, Jacob having crossed hands, and given Ephraim the preference, looking as far forward as the kingdom of the Ten Tribes, which Ephraim was the head of, after the revolt from the house of David" (and that tribe having been preferred in the wilderness as the standard-bearing tribe, and Joshua being of that tribe). [Ephraim], "not content with that honor in the promise, was displeased, if Manasseh had any honor done it in the meantime. It is pity that kindred and relation, which should be an inducement to love and peace, should be ever an occasion (as often it proves) of strife and discord. A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and their contentions are as the bars of a castle." Henry.Exposition, 2 (1725), 116.

Judges 12:4–6.] "Let us observe the righteousness of God in the punishment of these proud, passionate Ephraimites, which in several instances answered their sin. 1. They were proud of the honor of their tribe, gloried in this, that they were Ephraimites; but how soon are they brought to be ashamed or afraid to own their country. 'Art thou an Ephraimite?' No, now rather any tribe than that. 2. They had gone in a rage over Jordan to burn Jephthah's house with fire; but now they come back to Jordan as sneakingly as they had passed it furiously, and were cut off from ever returning to their own houses. 3. They had upbraided the Gileadites with the infelicity of their country, lying at such a distance, and now they suffer by an infirmity peculiar to their own country in not being able to pronounce 'Shibboleth.' 4. They had called the Gileadites unjustly 'fugitives,' and now they are really and in good earnest become fugitives themselves. And in the Hebrew, it is the same wordפְּלִיטֵי (Judges 12:5) that is used of the Ephraimites that escaped, or that fled, which they had used in scorn of the Gileadites, calling them 'fugitives.' He that rolleth the stone, or reproach unjustly upon another, let him expect that it will justly return upon himself." Henry.Exposition, 2 (1725), 117.

Judges 12:6. "Say now Shibboleth."] No. 367.Works, 15, 357–58.

Judges 13:2.] See no. 138b.Ibid., 89–90.

-- 336 --

Judges 13:8. "Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?"] This argues that this is the same person spoken of in the Isaiah 9:6, "To us a child is born," etc., "and his name shall be called Wonderful," which is the same word in the originalפֶּלֶא that is here rendered "secret." And what is said in the Judges 13:20 further argues it. See note on Isaiah 9:6. What is here said about the name of this person, compared with Proverbs 30:4, argues that it was the Son of God. See also Revelation 19:12.

Judges 13:19. "And offered it upon a rock."] That rock doubtless represented Christ, who is the rock of Israel, and is so often called a rock. Hence we may infer that the altars on which the legal sacrifices were offered were doubtless typical of Christ, especially the divine nature of Christ that sanctifies the gift and renders it satisfactory and meritorious, so that Christ is both priest, sacrifice, and altar. See note on Genesis 28:11–12. See Judges 6:20.

Judges 13:20. "For it came to pass, when the flame went up toward heaven."] See no. 139.Works, 15, 90.

Judges 13:25. "Camp of Dan."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1162.

Judges 14-16.] The history of Sampson, see no. 377.Works, 15, 361–62. Concerning his cleaving to the daughters of the Philistines and their proving his ruin.

Judges 14:5–6. "And, behold, a young lion roared against him. And the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would a kid."] Thus it was to the lion's cost that he roared upon Sampson, though [he] roared upon him as his prey, and thought to have a sweet repast of him, and to satisfy his appetite on him; but when he expected to have rent Sampson, Sampson "rent him as [he] would a kid." Herein Sampson was a type of Christ who most effectually destroyed Satan in his last sufferings, when Satan did so dreadfully roar upon him as his prey. And Christ, by thus destroying him, caused that out of the eater should come forth meat, and sweetness out of the strong [Judges 14:14], agreeable to

-- 337 --

the riddle Sampson put forth on occasion of his finding honey in the carcass of the lion that before roared upon him and that he had slain.

Judges 14:9.] Sampson's father and mother here seems to represent the old testament church that is often called hisI.e. Christ's. mother. The patriarchs, kings, prophets, and elders of the church were as it were his father. Many of these were his progenitors, as Adam, Seth, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, etc.; these were his fathers. Christ imparted to the people of God under the old testament the benefits of his conflict with the roaring lion and conquest of him in his death and resurrection, but did not particularly and clearly reveal to 'em the manner how these benefits were procured, as Sampson gave his father and mother the honey he took out of the carcass of the lion, but told 'em not that he took the honey out of the carcass of the lion. See note on Judges 14:17–18.

Judges 14:14. "Out of the strong came forth sweetness."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1165–66.

Judges 14:17–18.] Sampson's wife in this case represents the church, the spouse of Christ. Sampson, after a long time of his wife's weeping and sorrowing and earnest supplication to him, explained to her his riddle, which he had never explained to his father or his mother. So Christ revealed to his church in the gospel day the mystery of the gospel, which had been kept hid from ages and generations, after his church had long sorrowed and wept under her legal dispensation that bringsMS: "bring." sorrow and conviction of conscience. The law also stirs up earnest desires after the gospel, and moves to seek to Christ for his salvation.

On the seventh day Sampson told his wife the riddle. So Christ revealed the mystery of the glorious gospel to his church in the fullness of time in the latter day, and will most fully reveal it in the seventh thousand year of the world. The people learned the riddle by plowing with Sampson's heifer, or conversing with his wife. So it is in the church of Christ, by the teachings given in the church and by conversing with the saints, that persons come to a saving acquaintance with the mystery of gospel salvation. Sampson's companions won change of raiment by explaining the riddle. So do believers obtain spiritual change of raiment—by a saving knowledge of the mystery of the gospel.

-- 338 --

Judges 14:20. "But Sampson's wife was given to his companion, whom he had used as his friend."] Sampson was a type of his wife. By nature a Philistine, of that people that were his great enemies, signifies Christ's church, naturally sinful, an alien and an enemy. Sampson's wife forsook him, and became an whore, and committed adultery with him who had stood in the place of groomsman, or the friend of the bridegroom at the wedding, this typifying the apostasy under Antichrist, the church of Christ forsaking him, yielding to the usurpation ofJE deleted "the man of sin, or the Romish clergy who." the clergy, and especially the bishop of Rome, and committing adultery with him, and so becoming the great whore. Ministers of Christ are, with respect to him as the bridegroom of his church, expressly compared to the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29). This may also refer to the apostasy of the Jewish church, and her forsaking Christ, and yielding to the usurpations of her false teacher, the scribes and Pharisees.

Judges 15:4–5.] Foxes represent heretics and heretical doctrines (See note on Canticles 2:15, and also Mr. Hellenbroek's sermon on that text, pp. 4 ff.).Abraham Hellenbroek, A Sermon. From Canticks, 4–12. Hellenbroek (1658–1731), a minister at Rotterdam, provided an extended comparison between foxes and heretics. In his sermon, preached in 1717 and translated in this edition, he sounded the theme that "if ever there was a time since the Creation, in which it might be said the Church crawls with all Kinds of Foxes, we must confess it is even in our Day" (p. 25). The sermon was translated and published in 1742. See Works, II, 43, 102. Christ will destroy the food and support of the enemies of his church by showing the inconsistency of false doctrines, by bringing them and comparing one with another to show that they can have no union, but have as it were a firebrand between. Then the great number of foxes represents the multitude of heresies that infect the church. Foxes also represent the crafty enemies of the church in general. Christ will destroy the food of the Philistines by setting the enemies of the church at variance one with another by causing them, against their wills, to counterwork each other, as he set the builders of Babel at variance, and as he often made the enemies of his people to kill one another, and so delivered Israel, as the Midianites before Gideon and other instances.

See SSS on the verse, and also see ibid., concerning the fables of the heathen derived from hence, this double mark || in the margin.This reference is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1169–72.

-- 339 --

Judges 15:8. "And thigh."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1173.

Judges 15:15.] Sampson slays the Philistines with a jawbone, a despicable instrument. He triumphs over them in this, which typifies Christ's victory over Satan and his enemies by despicable means. He triumphed over principalities and powers in the cross (See note on Colossians 2:15.), and chooses "the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world to confound the things that are mighty, and the base things of the world, and things that are despised, and things that are not, to bring to naught the things that are" [1 Corinthians 1:27–28].The remainder of this paragraph is a later entry. But especially by the "jawbone of an ass" here is meant the mouth or preaching of ministers, who are often compared to oxen, and here to the ass for its foolishness, ministers being in themselves weak, insufficient, blind, and foolish. And their preaching, which is the main instrument by which Christ destroys his enemies, is called "the foolishness of preaching" [1 Corinthians 1:21].

Judges 15:18. "And called on the Lord, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant; and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?"] As Sampson in most of his wonderful acts was certainly intended as a type of Christ, and his miraculous conflicts with and victories over his enemies shadows of Christ's great conflict with the powers of darkness and victory over them, so this that we have here an account of is probably a representation of Christ's intercession, by which he obtained the Holy Spirit after his sufferings, pleading those sufferings, that great battle and victory, and also the prayer of believers who are the members of Christ, or the church, which is as it were Christ, using that argument with God, that seeing God hath wrought that great redemption for us by that conflict and victory of Christ, may they not well think his mercy sufficient to give them the Holy Spirit, that living water, that they may not die for thirst and fall into the hands of the mortal enemies of their souls, which is the same argument which is mentioned, Romans 5:6–10 and Romans 8:32. Christ pleads this argument in heaven, for if his elect people perish with thirst, 'tis all one in his view and God's view, as if he perished with thirst. And he pleads this argument by his spirit (the spirit of faith and prayer in his saints). The Israelites'

-- 340 --

binding and delivering up Sampson (as we have account in the foregoing part of the chapter) into the hands of the Philistines represents the Jews' binding, delivering up, Christ unto the heathen, and as it were to Satan and to death, in the time of his last sufferings. His bursting their bonds represents Christ's bursting the bonds of death when he rose from the dead. The victory he obtained afterwards represents the glorious victory of Christ by the preaching of the gospel consequent on his resurrection (see note on Judges 15:15). The great thirst that followed represents the exceeding low state of the church after that first victory whereby Christ conquered the Roman Empire, in the great withdrawings of the Spirit, especially in the times of Antichrist and in the present time. Sampson's crying to God for relief from his thirst represents the prayers and cries of the church of God for the outpourings of the Spirit with Christ's intercession. The abundance of waters from the jawbone represents the glorious and abundant outpouring of the Spirit with the foolishness of preaching that shall be in the latter days.

Judges 15:19. God's causing water to flow out of the jawbone of the ass to refresh and revive Sampson when thirsty.] The jawbone, I have observed (note on Judges 15:15), signifies the mouth of ministers. The water flowing thence is the word of God, and the blessed spirit of and grace of God which accompanies the word preached, which things are very often in Scripture compared to water. And particularly the words of wisdom in a man's mouth are compared to a flowing brook. Proverbs 18:4, "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook." Proverbs 10:11, "The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life." And Proverbs 13:14, "The law of the wise is a fountain of life." This flowing stream of the word of God is that which refreshesJE deleted "the heart." the church of Christ, and satisfies the thirst of the people of Christ, which is Christ mystical, and also refreshes the soul of Christ, as hereby he reaps his fruit and obtainsMS: "obtain." the success of his great labors. The success of the gospel in the salvation of souls is the joy that was set before Christ [Hebrews 12:2]. Jesus rejoiced in spirit when the disciples returned and told him the success of their preaching.

Judges 16.] Delilah in this chapter seems to represent beloved sin, or lust, or sinful pleasure. Sampson's love to her and cleaving to her became his

-- 341 --

ruin. Sampson resists her awhile, but he was wedded to her, and had such a love to her that by her continual solicitations she at length overcame him. Much so it is oftentimes with men with respect to their lusts. If they ben't divorced in their hearts from them, they may resist them a while, but their importunate solicitations will at length overcome them. Such men's righteousness is but short-lived; they can't hold out always against the enticements of their lusts. "It happens to them according to the true proverb: The dog is returned to his vomit again, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" [2 Peter 2:22]. The mighty power of sin in the hearts of those that harbor it is well represented by her overcoming Sampson whoJE deleted "was so backward and." resisted her so much; and in that she overcame and weakened him that was of such mighty strength, it was because God was departed from him. Sin will overcome the strongest man in the world when God leaves him, and he stands only in his own strength.JE deleted "Sampson disobeyed God in suffering." Delilah robbed Sampson of his strength, and betrayed and ruined him when she had lulled him asleep. So men's lusts stupefy them, and lull them asleep, and then have fair opportunity to rob them of their strength, of all that is good in them, and utterly to ruin them. Delilah, under a show and pretense ofJE deleted "great." love, and with enticing, bewitching behavior of a lover, became his traitor; while she lulled him asleep in her bosom, she betrayed and ruined him. So men's lusts, under a show of friendship, of entertaining and delighting 'em, do indeed destroy them.

Judges 16:17.] The Nazarite's hair represented the contemplation, consideration, sense, and watchfulness of the mind. When these things are gone, men's strength is soon gone; and they are an easy prey to their enemies. See, of the hair of the Nazarite, Numbers 6:5. See fables of the heathen from hence, SSS.This sentence is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1181, 1183.

Judges 16:21.] Which is a very lively image of the miserable bondage and slavery that men are brought into by the spiritual Delilah, their lusts and sinful pleasures. These betray men into the hands of devils while they are lulled asleep in their lap, as Delilah betrayed Sampson into the hands of the Philistines; and they serve them as the Philistines did him. They keep them close prisoners, as it were shut up in prison and bound with fetters

-- 342 --

of brass, so that they can by no means deliver themselves. And not only so, but they make them do their drudgery in the prison. They grind in the prison house their bread to feed them, and satiate their pride and cruelty. And besides that, they put out their eyes, and make 'em serve blindfold. And more than that, all the wages they intend for them is to kill them when they have done, and all to make themselves sport in their calamity.

1 Samuel 2:1–10.] THE SONG OF HANNAH. This song of Hannah (as 'tis with some parts of the song of Moses at the Red Sea, and the song of Deborah) is not so much accommodated to the event that is the immediate occasion of the song as that much greater event of which it was a type. Hannah's having a child, who had been barren, especially her having a child that was so great a prophet, and so her being exalted above her adversary Peninnah, was an undoubted type of [the] event foretold, Isaiah 54, and events of that kind. And therefore Hannah's song is a kind of prophecy of these great events with their circumstances. This observation is much confirmed by Psalms 113:7–9.

Psalms 2:2. "There is none holy as the Lord."] God's holiness here, as in many other places, is to be understood in the most extensive sense for all his moral perfection, and including his goodness and grace. See Psalms 97:12.

1 Samuel 5:2.] So the Papists set the ark of God and Dagon together in the house of Dagon. They mingle heathenism and Christianity together. The beast has horns like a lamb, and speaks as a dragon [Revelation 13:11].

1 Samuel 5:3. "And they took Dagon, and set him in his place again."] So when Dagon was fallen in the overthrow of the heathen empire, they took him, and set him in his place again by setting up the popish hierarchy and idolatry.

1 Samuel 5:4.] The Bible and other remains of the true religion that were kept in the Church of Rome, the antichristian church, will at length be the occasion of the fall of their Dagon, and of breaking off his head and hands. When Antichrist falls, there will be a remainder of him yet, but he shall be utterly despoiled of strength and glory. He will be like a stump without head or hands.

This is a type of the same thing as Sampson's overthrowing Dagon's temple and killing the Philistines at his death, and of Jonah's being vomited out after swallowed by the whale. The ark of God being taken captive by its enemies represents the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, who therein was taken captive by his enemies. The ark of God was brought by Dagon's people into Dagon's temple, was by the Philistines presented to Dagon as his captive. So Christ for a time was as it were Satan's prisoner and captive. It was to Dagon's cost that he had such a captive, for

-- 348 --

he fell and lost his head and hands before it. The bringing this captive into Dagon's temple proved the ruin of Dagon; the ark ruined him in his own temple. So when Satan had taken Christ captive, and had procured his death, and held him his prisoner, it was to his cost. This very thing was what ruined him; Christ in dying bruised Satan's head. Dagon and the Philistines were sick of their captive, and were forced to send it back, as the whale was sick of Jonah that he had swallowed, and was forced to vomit him up again on the dry land. The ark's entering into Dagon's temple, and the effects of it in Dagon's falling and losing his head and hands, and nothing being left but the stump of Dagon, represents Christ's entering into the soul in conversion, which before was the temple of sin and Satan, and making it his own temple, and the mortification of sin that attends it.

1 Samuel 15:32–33.] When Samuel was about to kill Agag, the king of the Amalekites, Agag came to him delicately; he came in his best hue, put on the most taking and pleasing appearance that he could, that he might appear innocent, and desirable, and as one that was worthy to be saved alive, and that it was a thousand pities to kill. Thus do those lusts that are most beloved, and are chief in our affection, and are among our lusts as the king among the Amalekites, when we go about to slay them or do anything in order to it. Thus do they plead for their lives. They represent themselves to us in their most innocent and taking hue, and come to us delicately, pleading that they are not worthy to be slain, but worthy to be well entertained. "Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal," in the place where the congregation of Israel was circumcised, and their reproach rolled away. Thus our most beloved lusts must be served. They must be utterly destroyed without mercy in order to our being delivered from the bondage of sin, and the rolling away our reproach; and thus do men treat their beloved lusts before the Lord in true circumcision of heart. They serve sin as Saul did Agag, and as the children of Israel did Achan. See notes on the story of Achan."Scripture," no. 360, Works, 15, 344–47.

Samuel declared to Agag that he would make his mother childless. Many in their pretended repentance and conversion slay some of the children of original corruption, but save some one of the children alive, that which is dearest and chief in their esteem, or has the highest place in their hearts. Samuel gave that reason why his mother should be made childless, that his "sword had made women childless." So the beloved lust, the sin that is chief in affection and esteem, has destroyed multitudes of souls, and made many women childless. This work was done by Samuel, the prophet of the Lord. So when such a mortification is wrought in the heart, it is by the word of the Lord.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Samuel 16.] Warburton, vol. 2, p. 318.Warburton writes a long footnote about the difficulties in the history of David as related in 1 Samuel 16-17. He notes that 1 Samuel 16:14–23 is out of historical order, being an anticipation of a later account, an episode that correctly follows David's defeat of Goliath. Warburton adds that such literary anticipation is common in sacred history (Divine Legation of Moses Demonstrated [2nd ed. London, 1742], pp. 313–17). The principal text on these same pages contrasts the character of Saul the king and the youthful David as well as their "different Acceptation with the God of Israel." David's successes came when he was armed "with no other Power but of Miracles… and with no other Wisdom but of Truth," which is characteristic of all of God's dispensations (p. 318).

Therefore 'the elders of the town trembled at his coming' 1 Samuel 16:4], fearing it was an indication of God's displeasure against them, and that he was come to denounce some judgment for the iniquities of the place. The Anakims who fled to Gath (Joshua 11:22–23) were a race of giants (Numbers 13:28, Numbers 13:32–33; Deuteronomy 9:1–2), and this Goliath of Gath exceeded them all in stature. And as the common size of men is but half so high" (i.e. 5 feet, 10 inches, and an half), "so if every part was proportionable to his height, as probably it was, the weight of his whole body, or of each limb, must be to others, as the cube of two to the cube of one, or eight times as much; and consequently his head was a sufficient burden for a man to carry. The weight of his armor seems proportionable to his bulk. The weight of his coat of mail, 1 Samuel 17:5, 'was 5000 shekels of brass,' so that as a shekel weighed about half an ounce of our common weights, sixteen of which goes to the pound, it weighed about 156 pound and a quarter. 'The staff of his spear (1 Samuel 17:7) was like a weaver's beam.' The 'spear's head' (ibid.) 'weighed 600 shekels,' or eighteen pound and three quarters. Hence the weight of his whole armor hath been thus computed. The spear's head 18 lb. ¾, the staff of

the spear 18 lb. ¾, the helmet 15 lb., the shield 30 lb., the coat of mail 156 lb. ¼, the sword 4 lb. ¼, total 243 lb. 1 Samuel 17:40. "And he took his staff in his hand" (See Numbers 21:18), "and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook."] This brook and the stones that he chose out of it were doubtless typical of something. The brook seems to be a type of the Spirit of God, the same with Ezekiel's waters of the sanctuary [Ezekiel 47], and the "pure river of water of life that proceeded out of the throne of God and of the Lamb" [Revelation 22:1]; and the same with those "rivers of living water" spoken of, John 7:38–39, which we are there told is meant of the Holy Spirit; and the same with the brook that descended out of Mt. Sinai, spoken of, Deuteronomy 9:21 (See notes on the place.); and the same with the well spoken of, Numbers 21:18. As the princes of Israel obtained the water of that well by their staves, so David comes to gather those stones out of the brook with his staff. The stones that David chose out of the brook seem to denote words of the Lord, or passages of his word, which weapon is from the Spirit of God, and therefore is called "the sword of the Spirit" [Ephesians 6:17]. WithMS: "which." such weapons, Christ the true David, fought with Satan, the spiritual Goliath, as in the account of his temptation in the wilderness. This, viz. the word of God, is the great and only offensive weapon of the Christian that the Apostle mentions in his description of the Christian armor (Ephesians 6:13–16), but these stones are David's offensive weapons by which Goliath was to be slain. As the word is called there "the sword of the Spirit," so those stones are out of the brook, which represents the Spirit of God. The stone with which Goliath was slain signifies the same with Daniel's stone "cut out of the mountains without hands" [Daniel 2:45], which smote the great image

-- 356 --

and destroyed [it], which signifies the word of God. David chose smooth stones, a variety of them, as a Christian may find a variety of apt passages in the Holy Scripture wherewith to resist and fight against Satan in all his temptations and against all his spiritual enemies.

1 Samuel 17:50.] The stone with which Goliath was slain typifies the word of God, the same that was typified by the stone that smote Nebuchadnezzar's image [Daniel 2:35]. The stone is taken out of the brook, which brook is the Holy Ghost. See Psalms 110:7. The sling is the gospel ministry. Ministers are instruments in the hand of Christ. They are but slings in his hand wherewith the stone of his word is cast.

1 Samuel 17:55–58.] Concerning Saul's not knowing David, and Abner's not being able to tell who he was. 'Tis probable that Saul never had seen him but once before. He once was sent to him by his father Jesse to try the experiment of relieving Saul by his music, and then returned again to his father's house. And what is said in the 1 Samuel 16:21–23's standing before Saul, or continuing in his presence, and his loving him greatly, and his becoming his armor-bearer, and Saul's sending to Jesse to let him continue with him because he had favor in his sight, is evidently anticipated. 'Tis an account of what came to pass after David's killing Goliath, as is evident by the 1 Samuel 18:2. "And Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father's house." 'Tis very common that when the Scripture begins the history of any affair, some things that are most remarkable in the affair are first generally and briefly mentioned, and then a more particular account is begun. So here when David's being sent for to relieve Saul by his music is mentioned, the historian then generally mentions the consequences of it, though they happened some considerable time after his being first sent for, and after some particulars that are related afterwards. It was after David's killing the Philistine that Saul loved David. He set his heart on him at the same time that his son Jonathan did. And it was after that that he became his armor-bearer, as is evident by 1 Samuel 18:5; he "set him over the men of war," for he appeared only a musician, and not a military man, before that. If he had been his armor-bearer before, he would have been then in the army with Saul.

And it was after that that Saul sent to Jesse to let David stand before him, as is evident by 1 Samuel 18:2. There was some time, after David came from the slaughter of the Philistine, that David was in great favor with

-- 357 --

Saul, before his falling out with him on occasion of the songs of the women ascribing to Saul but thousands and to David ten thousands, as is evident by the beginning of the 1 Samuel 18. David had gained the love of Israel by his discreet behavior before that, as 1 Samuel 18:5.

And therefore 'tis not much to be wondered at that Saul did not know David, seeing he had never seen him but once before. In such a multitude of business as kings have, and among so many new faces which they see every day, it was easy to forget a man. David also now came in another kind of habit than when he was sent to wait on Saul at court, for he was clothed as a shepherd in a rustic dress. He appeared then in the soft airs of a musician, and therefore was the less suspected to come now as a champion. And as for Abner, he, being a military man and much abroad, might not have seen David when he was at court, or perhaps knowing that his three eldest brethren were in the army, and that David was not among the number, though they might both know his face, yet they could not call him to mind as not expecting to see him at that time.Conjecture for illegible word. Here compare Ruth 3:16.This sentence is a later addition.

1 Samuel 23:26–28.] It seems as though this mountain that divided between Saul and David was a very steep rocky mountain, and at or near that place impassable, and so was a defense to David, kept Saul from coming at him. And therefore, in remembrance of the great benefit David had by it, it was thenceforward called by a name taken from the benefit, "the rock of divisions." This mountain or rock, as it is called, was a type of Christ, the Rock of Israel and the Rock of Ages, who is the rock of their defense. Christ is the true Sela-Hammah-Lekoth.הַמַּחְלְקְוֹת סֶלַע He is between his people and their enemies as an impassable mountain. He was so all along between Saul and David. David often calls God his "rock of defense" in the Psalms. And probably the defense that he had by this mountain led him to the consideration of the defense he had by God; and that it [was], with a pious and grateful respect to God, and that he might keep the remembrance of his mercy in defending him, that he thus named the mountain.

2 Samuel 7:10.] God's ceasing to walk in a tent and tabernacle, and dwelling in a temple, was a great token of mercy to the children of Israel, for while God dwelt in a movable tabernacle he dwelt as a wayfaring man, as one that was not fixed in his abode, was ready to depart, that is to stay but a little while, or that is undetermined whether to stay or no. But when he came to dwell in a temple, that [was] a fixed habitation, it was a token for good several ways. It was a token that God would dwell among them, and make his settled abode among them, and that he would not lead them forth out of the land, but continue them in the possession of it. For they were to go where the tabernacle went before them, but now God dwelled in an immovable temple. It was a token that they should no more be removed. It was a token that God would not cast them off from being his people, for if he should so do, he would remove 'em out of that land, for that land was his land, a land that he had chosen to be a holy land.

2 Samuel 10:18. "David slew the men of seven hundred chariots."] Which amounted to seven thousand men, ten men to a chariot. So this place is reconciled with 1 Chronicles 19:18. See SSS on 1 Chronicles 19:18.Ibid., col. 774. "And forty thousand horsemen." See note on 1 Chronicles 19:18.

2 Samuel 11:4. "For she was purified from her uncleanness."] When David saw her washing herself, she was then washing herself at the end of the seven days of her uncleanness (Leviticus 15:19). The time being come that she should be clean, she was, as usual at the time of her cleansing, washing her body from all remaining stain or pollution from her issue of blood. And therefore we are told that David saw her washing herself "in an eveningtide" (2 Samuel 11:2). It was probably just about sun setting", which was the time of day when those that were legally unclean were cleansed. The case being thus, it greatly increased David's temptation, for when a woman was thus cleansed from her uncleanness, then it was lawful for her husband to lie with her, so that it put David in mind of that act, and stirred his lust.

2 Samuel 15-18.] ABSALOM seems to be a type of Antichrist. He was a son of David, as the man of sin was originally a Christian bishop, one of the ministers of the gospel who in a peculiar manner are as it were Christ's sons. Absalom was David's son by Maachah, the daughter of the king of Geshur, the only wife he had that was a Gentile. So popery is a mixture of Christianity with heathenism. Absalom was the son of a heathen mother, or one that had been a heathen; so the Church of Rome is the daughter of old heathen Rome. Absalom usurped his father's authority over his kingdom, and his city Jerusalem, and over his house, as the pope usurps the authority of Christ, sets himself up to be king in his kingdom, and takes possession of the church, the spiritual Jerusalem, and sits in the house of Christ as lord of that. Sitting in the temple of God, he showeth himself that he is God. Absalom was a person of great beauty, and was exceedingly admired and praised by the people for his beauty. So it has been with the pope, whereas Christ himself appeared in a mean and low condition, without form or comeliness, without any external

-- 366 --

magnificence; and when the people saw him, there was no beauty wherefore they should desire him [Isaiah 53:2]. On the contrary, Antichrist appears in exceeding external pomp and glory, decked with gold, and silver, and precious stones,MS: "Stone." fine linen, and scarlet, which all the world has admired, and all wondered after the beast, saying, "Who is like unto the beast?" [Revelation 13:4]. Absalom's head was exceeding fruitful in hair, representing the exceeding policy and subtilty of Antichrist. See note on Numbers 6:5. Absalom cloaked his rebellion and usurpation with a pretense of religion and the service of God, like Antichrist. He said to his father, 2 Samuel 15:7–8, "Let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed. For thy servant vowed a vow while I abode at Geshur in Syria, saying, If the Lord will bring me again indeed to Jerusalem, then will I serve the Lord." Absalom drove David and those that adhered to him out of Jerusalem; so Antichrist casts out of the church all the true and faithful followers of Christ. David went away into the wilderness, and his faithful subjects went with him wherever he went (1 Samuel 15 ff.). "And David said unto all his servants that were with him at Jerusalem, Arise let us flee.… And the king's servants said unto the king, Behold, thy servants are ready to do whatsoever my Lord the king shall appoint. And the king went forth, and all his household after him" 2 Samuel 14:14–16]. 2 Samuel 14:17, "And the king went forth, and all the people after him, and tarried in a place that was far off." Ittai the Gittite expressed the spirit of his true followers on this occasion. 2 Samuel 15:21, "As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be," which is agreeable to what is described to be the spirit of the true followers of Christ in the time of Antichrist. Revelation 14:4, "These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth." Revelation 17:14, "They that are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful."

Jerusalem was left, and as it were given up to Absalom and his multitude; and it was as it were trodden down by them, which is agreeable to the description of the time of the reign of Antichrist. Revelation 11:2, "It is given to the Gentiles, and the holy city shall they tread under foot."

Absalom committed whoredom with his father's concubines, and that openly in the sight of the sun. Thus Antichrist defiles the church that by profession is bound to be faithful to Christ as his spouse. He claims the peculiar prerogatives of the husband and lord of the church, and usurps these prerogatives in the most open manner.

But they that were defiled by Absalom were not any of hisI.e. David's. true wives

-- 367 --

who went with David, but only his concubines. So Christ's true followers during the reign of Antichrist are not defiled when other women are defiled. Revelation 14:4, "These are they which were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth."

The place where David and his men went was the wilderness (2 Samuel 15:28). So David in the Psalms 42, which probably was penned on this occasion, speaks of himself as an exile in the wilderness of Mt. Hermon, a place noted for beasts of prey. (See Canticles 4:8, "Look from Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards.") So the church is represented as flying away into the wilderness to reside there during the reign of Antichrist (Revelation 12:14).

The time of Absalom's usurpation is represented as a time of great affliction with David and his followers. 'Tis said, 2 Samuel 15:23, "And all the country wept with a loud voice." And 2 Samuel 15:30, "And David went up by the ascent of Mt. Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and went barefoot. "And all the people that was with him covered every man his head; and they went up, weeping as they went up." And David, in the book of Psalms, speaks of himself as then in great affliction (Psalms 3 and Psalms 42). So the time of the reign of Antichrist is represented as a time of great affliction and sorrow to the church of God, wherein the witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, etc. [Revelation 11:3].

The time of Absalom's usurpation was a time wherein David was greatly reproached and persecuted, as when Shimei cursed him [2 Samuel 16:7–8], aptly representing the great blasphemies of Antichrist that we read of, Daniel 7:8, Daniel 7:11, Daniel 7:25; Revelation 13:1, Revelation 13:5–6, and the cruel persecutions of Antichrist.

David, when bitterly reviled and persecuted by Shimei, reviled not again, nor took any revenge, but bore all with great patience and meekness, representing the spirit and practice of God's true saints under antichristian persecutions, as that is represented in Revelation 13:10 and Revelation 14:12.

Ahithophel well represents the Jesuits and other subtile, crafty counselors of Antichrist. God's defeating the counsels of Ahithophel to his own exceeding and intolerable vexation livelily represents the same thing that is prophesied of, Revelation 16:10. "And his kingdom was full of darkness, and they gnawed their tongues for pain."

The battle that was fought in Gilead between David's men and the great multitude that followed Absalom, wherein the latter were overthrown, represents that great battle between Christ and his true church, and Antichrist and his adherents, which we read of, Revelation 16:14 ff. and Revelation 19.

-- 368 --

This battle was fought when David and his friends were come to Mahanaim, which wordמַהֲנַיִם signifies two armies, and was the place where the army or host of angels met himI.e. not David, but Jacob. to encourage and defend when the host of Esau, his false, persecuting, and murderous brother was coming against him, thirsting for his blood. David's company was truly the company of Mahanaim, as the church of Christ is called, Canticles 6:13. And that battle, which this company had with Absalom and his followers, was the more fit representation of the great and last battle of Christ and his church with Antichrist and his followers, in which "the armies which were in heaven" are represented as following Christ (Revelation 19:14), and which is said to be fought at Armageddon, or at the mountain of Megiddo, where the battle of Deborah and Barak with Sisera and his host was fought, wherein it is said that "the stars in their courses," or the glorious angels and hosts of heaven, "fought against Sisera" [Judges 5:20].

In the end, Absalom's hair, that he so much gloried in, proved his destruction, representing that Antichrist, though so exceeding subtile and crafty, shall finally be ruined by his own craftiness, shall be taken in his own snare. The same thing is also represented by Ahithophel's hanging himself [2 Samuel 17:23].

Absalom was "cast into a great pit in the wood" [2 Samuel 18:17]. This "great pit" represents that bottomless pit into which it is said the beast and false prophet were cast (Revelation 19:20 and Revelation 20:10). Absalom had a "great heap of stones" raised upon [him], a most conspicuous and lasting monument of his wickedness and ruin, representing the same thing as that smoke of Babylon's torment which is said to rise up forever and ever (Revelation 19:3 and Revelation 14:11). Soon after this was that joyful triumphant song of praise which we are told, 2 Samuel 22:1, he "spake unto the Lord in the day that he had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies," which song agrees much better with the description of the great things God did for his church in and upon the destruction of Antichrist than to anything David himself was the immediate subject of. As that in the 2 Samuel 22:8 ff., "Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook because he was wroth," which agrees with the account of the great earthquake that accompanied Antichrist's destruction. "There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it." 2 Samuel 22:13–15, "Through the brightness before him were coals of fire kindled. The Lord thundered from heaven; the Most

-- 369 --

High uttered his voice. He sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them. And the channels of the sea appeared; the foundations of the world were discovered" 2 Samuel 22:16]. In the same song, as we have it, Psalms 18, we have these words, Psalms 18:12–13, "At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hailstones, and coals of fire. The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice, hailstones and coals of fire." These things agree with Revelation 11:19. "And there were lightnings, and voices, and thunderings, and an earthquake, and great hail." And Revelation 16:18, "And there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great. "Revelation 16:20–21, " And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found. "And there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent." There are also other passages in that song of David that agree much better with the time of Antichrist's destruction than the times wherein David sang it, as 2 Samuel 22:28. "And the afflicted people thou wilt save; but thine eyes are upon the haughty, that thou mayst bring them down." And 2 Samuel 22:44–46, "Thou hast kept me to be the head of the heathen; a people which I knew not shall serve me. As soon as they hear, they shall be obedient unto me. Strangers shall fade away, and they shall be afraid out of their close places." Thus Christ will lead the way in the joyful songs of the church after Antichrist's destruction (Revelation 19:1–7). Soon after this great victory of David and his company, and this joyful song, succeeds the peaceable, joyful, and glorious reign of Solomon, which undoubtedly was a type of the glorious day of the church after the fall of Antichrist.

2 Samuel 15:21.] Ittai is a type of a true convert and follower of Jesus Christ, the true David. He was originally a Philistine of Gath, but became an Israelite. He was far off, but is made nigh. He left his own country for

-- 370 --

David's sake. He cleaves to his master David in the time of his affliction and adversity, when his affairs ran very low, and it looked dark on his side, and it seemed very doubtful what would be the issue, and David's party seemed to be the underling party, and were fleeing before their enemies. Yet Ittai resolves to cleave to him whether in life or death, as true Christians "follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth" [Revelation 14:4].

2 Samuel 20:15–22.] It is probably the design of the Holy Ghost to represent something spiritual in this story. The city of Abel of Beth-maachah may here

-- 372 --

fitly represent a people or the heart of a particular person. Sheba, the son of Bichri, the rebel against the lawful rightful sovereign that that city harbored, represents sin. Joab, the captain of the king's host that besieged the city with all his army, and battered the wall to throw it down, represents the wrath of God. Joab requires that the head of Sheba be thrown over the wall in order to his leaving the city. So the wrath of God will stand against us with all its army, and seek our destruction, till we destroy and give up sin. The wise woman in the city represents either the church or God's saints among a people, or a principle of true wisdom and grace in the heart of a particular person. She makes the city willing to cut off the head of Sheba, and throws it to Joab over the wall, whereupon Joab blew a trumpet, and his army retired from the city. So when once we have given up sin, God proclaims liberty and peace to us. Repentance is the condition of the remission of sins.

2 Samuel 23:39. "Thirty and seven in all."] The Historian first gives an account of the first and the second three, which makes six, and then reckons up after

-- 374 --

them the thirty, which makes thirty-six. And in order to make the number thirty-seven, we must reckon in Joab, who had always the chief place of dignity and office among all David's men of war, but yet seems to [be] mentioned here in this catalogue only occasionally, in the 2 Samuel 23:37 on occasion of the mention of his armorbearer, and again in the 2 Samuel 23:18 on occasion of the mention of his brother Abishai. The reason why he is not inserted in this catalogue seems to be either that the design of the catalogue was only to mention those that were then called of the first and second three, and of the thirty, for David's mighty men were wont, it seems, so to be reckoned by parcels in Israel. But Joab, though a very mighty man, yet was not wont to be reckoned to any of these parcels, for he did not stand as mate with any of them, but was one by himself alone, distinguished from all as the captain general of the whole host. And there was not that occasion to mention him now, or relate what he had done in this catalogue, he and his acts having been so particularly enlarged on in the foregoing history. But yet the Historian shows that he was not forgotten, he being twice occasionally mentioned in this catalogue. The reason why he is not mentioned can't be because he was not one of David's mighty men, for by all the history 'tis evident he was one of the greatest warriors. Asahel is here mentioned among the mighty men [2 Samuel 23:24], who is represented in the history as a child to Abner, when he was killed by him by the hinder end of his spear. But Abner don't appear to be more than Joab's match; and here the armor-bearer of Joab is mentioned, who can't be supposed to be a greater warrior than Joab himself. Or secondly, it might be because of Joab's infamous carriage in murdering Abner and Amasa. He therefore deserved that his name should be blotted out of the roll of David's worthies, noble warriors. That seems to be typical of the book of the Lamb, or the true David, wherein are enrolled the names of his faithful valiant soldiers, or those that overcome, to whom 'tis promised that they shall not be blotted out of the book of life, and that his name shall be confessed before his Father, and before his angels (Revelation 3:5). 'Tis unreasonable to suppose that its being said that David's mighty men were "thirty and seven in all" was a blunder in the Historian, for it cannot be supposed that the Historian should mistake so as to mention over thirty-six names, and expressly divide them into the lesser sums of thirty and twice three, and then not know that these three sums added together made thirty-six, and that such a mistake should stand in the public records of the Jews from age to age. The Historian mentions those mighty men that were wont to [be] reckoned by parcels amongst their fellows, mentioning

-- 375 --

first the two threes, and then the thirty, not mentioning Joab, he belonging to none of these parcels, and supposing the reader would not want to have him mentioned,MS: "mention." so great a part of the foregoing history being about him. Yet when at the end he goes to tell how many David's mighty men are in all, Joab, the one by himself, must not be left out of the sum; and therefore the Historian declares it to be thirty-seven. This being so plain a case, it may ease us with respect to other difficulties of the Scripture of this nature that look like blunders, and may well make us think they are not so, but that there is some good reason for the seeming inconsistence, though we don't know what it is. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 402.

1 Kings 10:1–14. Concerning the story of the queen of Sheba who came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. She (as well as Pharaoh's daughter that Solomon married) was a remarkable type of the Gentile church and of the church of Christ in general, for she was a Gentile queen. Bedford in his Scripture Chronology, p. 608, says that, "She lived in the southern parts of Arabia near the Red Sea, which was therefore called 'the uttermost parts of the earth' [Matthew 12:42], because there was no traveling any further that way by land"; and observes that, "'Tis probable that she came to hear of Solomon's character by the ships that went to Ophir. For they sailed by her coast, and spread his fame there, as they did in all other places where they touched, proclaiming his magnificence, and especially his wisdom, and the glorious temple which he had built for the worship of God"; and says that, "The questions that she asked seemed to be about things pertaining to piety and the service of God. For our Savior saith, that she came 'to hear the wisdom of Solomon,' and should therefore 'rise up in judgment' [Matthew 12:42] against that generation, who would not learn of him. And it is said (1 Kings 10:1 of this

-- 380 --

ch.) that the particular fame, that she heard of Solomon, was 'concerning the name of the Lord,' and this most probably was the occasion of her journey." Herein she is a type of the church of Christ, which is made up of those that are naturally far off, that have as it were wandered from God to the ends of the earth, and are aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and have their souls black with sin, as the people of Sheba, who were Ethiopians, were black, and could not change their skin, or wash off their dark color. The queen of Sheba comes to hear the wisdom of Solomon, as those that are of the church of Christ come to hear his wisdom, and learn of him who is the wisdom of God and the light of the world. She came with spices and precious things to present to Solomon, which are a type of the graces of the church and her good works. Solomon instructed her and told her all her questions, which is a type of Christ's instructing and enlightening the souls of believers, and satisfying their doubts, and extricating them out of their difficulties by his divine teaching.

She says, "It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it. And, behold, the half was not told me. Thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard" 1 Kings 10:6–7]. So when persons come to Christ, they are never disappointed in him by finding less in him than ministers told them of while they were in a natural condition.

But the queen of Sheba is especially a type of the Gentile church, for she was a Gentile, and as she came from the uttermost parts of the earth. So in the calling of the Gentiles, they that "were far off were made nigh," as in Ephesians 2:13, Ephesians 2:17. 'Tis said that "she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones" 1 Kings 10:2], which is very agreeable to the prophecies of the Gentiles coming to the spiritual Jerusalem. Isaiah 60:5–6, "The forces of the Gentiles shall come unto thee. The multitude of camels shall cover thee, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from SHEBA shall come. They shall bring gold and incense; and they shall show forth the praises of the Lord." And Isaiah 60:9, "Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the Lord thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee." Isaiah 66:20, "And they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the Lord out of all nations upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift

-- 381 --

beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem," saith the Lord, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.

1 Kings 11:3.] David is a type of Christ in his suffering state, and of the church in that militant state it is in before the glorious times. Solomon is a type of Christ in his exalted state, and especially in his glorious dominion in the latter days, the days of the church's peace and prosperity. And the multitude of his wives is probably typical of the largeness of Christ's church, the multitude of souls and multitude of nations espoused to him at that time, the multitude of national churches.

"And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines." See no. 249.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 200–201.

1 Kings 11:4.] 'Tis very observable that when persons are old, they are more yieldable, and more easily prevailed upon by those that they have long had a fondness for, and persuaded to this or that.

1 Kings 11:5–7.] It does not appear that Solomon did himself worship these strange gods, but what his wives persuaded him to was to build high places for them to worship their gods in. He probably went after other gods, only as he honored them so far as to build places for their public worship in the land of Israel, wherein his wives and their attendants might worship them. For 'tis said in the 1 Kings 11:8, that he did this "for his wives, which sacrificed and burnt incense unto their gods" in them. He might possibly think it but reasonable that his wives should be allowed the exercise of their own religion, and the worship of their own gods, and might think it hard, seeing he had brought 'em out of their own country, to deny 'em high places and altars at which they might worship them in his country.

1 Kings 14:14–15.] 'Tis God's manner in Scripture, when threatening the wicked for their sins, to pass from those judgments that are soon to be inflicted and are the more immediateJE deleted "fruits of the punishment of their sins." occasion of God's sending a messenger to threaten them, to some great remote judgments, of which perhaps the judgments more immediately threatened are images or forerunners. Thus when God first sent Moses to Pharaoh, he sent him with a threatening of the last and greatest plague; and the other foregoing plagues are all omitted. Exodus 4:22–23, "And thou shalt say unto Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord. Israel is my son, even my first-born. And I say unto thee, Let my son go, that he may serve me. And if thou refuse to let him go, behold, I will slay thy son, even thy first-born." So in the Exodus 9:15, God again threatens the last plague, and Pharaoh's own destruction that was accomplished in the Red Sea: "For now I will stretch out mine hand, and I will smite thee and thy people with pestilence; and thou shalt be cut off from the earth," though there was the plague of hail, and locusts, and darkness afterwards before the plague of pestilence. So when the wife of Jeroboam comes to the prophet to inquire whether her son shall live, the prophet passes from a threatening of his

-- 383 --

death and judgments suddenly to be inflicted on his family to the captivity of the Ten Tribes, though it was to be long after Jeroboam's death.JE deleted "So also it is God's manner when promising blessings to his people." So also it is the manner of the prophets, when sent on some particular occasion to promise some mercy to God's people, to insist on some greater mercy that is remote, and that is to be bestowed on God's people in after generations. Thus when Isaiah was sent to Ahaz, when Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, were combined against him, to comfort him by foretellingJE deleted "the frustration of his design." the disappointment of their enemies and deliverance of Judah, he comes to Ahaz with Shearjashubיָשׁוּב שְׁאֶר his son, that signifies "the remnant shall return," to foretell the return from the captivity to Babylon, as in the Isaiah 7. And it is very frequent with the prophets, when foretelling lesser mercies that God has to bestow on his people, to pass to and insist upon that greatest of all mercies, the coming of Christ. So did Isaiah when he came to Ahaz on the forementioned occasion (Isaiah 7:14). So the prophets, when foretelling the return from the Babylonish captivity, often insist on the redemption of Christ, of which this is a type. So do the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, when sent to encourage the people to build the temple with promises of success therein, insist chiefly on the prosperity that God will give the church in times of the gospel.

1 Kings 18:30. "Repaired," etc.] Not that this was the same individual altar that had before been used in the service of God, which was now built up again of the same materials. But it was as it were a repairing the altar of the Lord, as it was a restoring the worship of God, in this way of offering sacrifices to him according to his own appointment.

1 Kings 18:33–35.] Elijah's sacrifice, in the time wherein it was offered, was attended with the greatest obstacles to its being consumed by fire. God, who has more ends than one in what he does, probably did not only intend by this to show his power beyond that of Baal, but to represent what came to pass with respect to the sacrifice of Christ, the great antitype of all the ancient sacrifices, whose last suffering were attended with such circumstances as seemed to tend in the highest degree to hinder his going on to offer himself in the heavenly flames of divine charity, and voluntarily presenting himself to suffer the flames of divine wrath. Such was God's hiding his face from him, and dealing with him in some respect as if he had been an enemy, which was a great trial of his love to the Father, and tending like floods of water to quench the fire of divine love in his soul, and to prevent that great degree of it which was necessary to carry him through the extreme sufferings that were before him. And also the extraordinary view which Christ had then given him of the unworthiness

-- 385 --

of mankind for whom he died, the hateful nature of their sin that he was about to expiate by his extreme sufferings, and their great enmity against him, which was then set before him and exercised towards him in the contempt and cruelty of his enemies, and some of them the very persons that he was about to die for, and the ingratitude of his own disciples that had already received saving benefits of his death, in their coldness toward him in the time of his agony, their being unwilling to watch with him one hour, their all forsaking him when he was apprehended, Peter's denying him with oaths and curses—these were like floods of great waters that were then thrown upon him to quench his love and to prevent his going on to endure those extreme torments in the fire of God's wrath, as was also that extraordinary view he had given him beforehand of the cup he was to drink, which made his soul exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. But many waters could not quench his love, neither could the floods drown it.

1 Kings 18:42. "He cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees."] The posture of most humble and earnest prayer, agreeable to what the apostle James says, James 5:18, "Elias… prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit."

1 Kings 18:44 ff.] The rain, after the great drought, came on Israel from a little cloud that came out of the west from beyond the sea. So probably that great outpouring of the Spirit that shall be in the latter days, so often compared to plentiful showers of rain on the dry [land], will arise in and from America.

That drought continued three years and six months, or a time, times, and an half [Revelation 12:14], answerable to the time of the continuance of the church's trouble and spiritual drought before the glorious times. See Luke 4:25 and James 5:17. The king of Israel also at that time came in his chariot from Carmel to Jezreel, which was from the west to the east. See note on 1 Kings 18:46. So the materials of which the temple was built were brought by sea (1 Kings 5:9). See note on Psalms 19:3.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Kings 18:46.] Elijah here, in this case of the approach of this plentiful shower, is the forerunner of the king of Israel in his speedy and swift entrance in Jezreel, as John the Baptist, the New Testament Elijah, was the forerunner of Christ, the great king of Israel.

-- 386 --

The church of God is called by the name of Jezreel in a prophecy of the glorious gospel days (Hosea 1:11 and Hosea 2:22).

1 Kings 19:19–21.] See notes on Matthew 24:17–18.

The truth with respect to what is related in these verses probably was thus. Elijah was directed by the Spirit of God to cast his mantle on Elisha. But Elijah had not the design of God in it fully made known to him, supposing it to be intended as a sign that Elisha should be prophet after him, agreeable to what God had said to him at Mt. Sinai. But God [had] a further meaning in it, which was intimated by his spirit which went with Elijah's mantle to Elisha, viz. that he should immediately forsake all, and follow him, and devote himself to the work of the ministry in the business of a prophet. Elisha, supposing Elijah had this design of God made known to him, and had been directed to cast his mantle on him with this view, and finding at first a reluctance, desires of Elijah that he by his prayers would obtain leave of God that he should first kiss his father and mother. Elijah, surprised at this request, as is natural, supposing him thus ignorant, says, "Go back; for what have I done" 1 Kings 19:20] that should hinder it? However, Elisha, who understood the mind of God, soon recovered from his reluctance, and went no further back than to his oxen, and took them and the instruments, and offered up all to God, signifying by this action his full consent to forsake all, and make a sacrifice of all this world's possessions and concerns to the great and infinitely important designs of his ministry.This paragraph is a later addition.
