II Kings

2 Kings 2:1–6.] Elisha obtained the great blessing of such a measure of the spirit of God as he inherited from Elijah in a way of constant seeking of it. He constantly and resolutely followed and clove to Elijah. His constancy was tried three times, and three times he declared his resolution, that as the Lord lived, and as his soul lived, he would not leave him. "As soon as Elijah had prophesied against Ahaziah, king of Israel, and sent the letter to Jehoram, king of Judah, he departed from Samaria, and went with Elisha to Gilgal, a place near Jordan about five and twenty miles from Samaria. And to try Elisha's constancy, he proposes to go back again to Bethel, a journey of about twenty miles, not far from the road to Samaria." And then further to try his constancy, he goes back again to Jericho, which was near Gilgal, and to try him further goes again to Jordan by Gilgal. And Elijah had thoroughly proved the constancy of Elisha's resolution. He ceased to speak to him any more. Bedford, Scripture Chronology, p. 626.

Elisha's following Elijah so closely hither and thither, and following him to and through Jordan, and after that seeing him ascend, and receiving his blessing and a double portion of his spirit, signifies that the way to pass safely through death, and to receive the portion of the firstborn is to "follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth" [Revelation 14:4], and to follow him even unto death, and to be "made conformable to his death" [Philippians 3:10].This paragraph is a later addition.

2 Kings 2:3. "Hold you your peace."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 593.

2 Kings 2:7.] SSS.Ibid.

2 Kings 2:8.] Elijah's passing through Jordan, when going out of the world, on dry ground without passing through water, represented his passing out of the world without dying. Jordan's being divided by his mantle signifies

-- 390 --

that believers in general pass through death without being overwhelmed or hurt by death, so that Christ says, They die not [John 11:25–26]. Jordan's being divided by Elijah's mantle signifies believers' having this privilege by the righteousness of Christ, and it signifies Christ not being overwhelmed and destroyed in death through his own righteousness.

2 Kings 2:9.] Elijah was now about to leave the world; and as parents, when they are leaving the world, are wont to bequeath portions to their children, so Elijah asks Elisha what he shall bequeath to him. Elisha was as it were his child, and Elisha calls him his father (2 Kings 2:12). That portion that he desires to inherit from his father is his spirit; and he desires a double portion of it, i.e. a much larger portion than the rest of his children, as it was ordained that the eldest son should inherit a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). It was his birthright to have the best share of his father's estate.JE deleted "So Elisha desires that his father Elijah would now in his last will and testament bequ." Elijah had many other children besides Elisha. There were many sons of the prophets that were under Elijah's care and instruction, so that he was as it were a father among them, as afterwards Elisha was, as is evident by 2 Kings 4:38 ff. and 2 Kings 6:1–2. Now what Elisha desires is that he may be distinguished from all the rest of the children by having a double portion of his spirit bequeathed to him, for Elijah's estate did not consist in silver and gold, but in those gifts of the spirit which he possessed. So that he was about to give something he might say as Peter, Acts 3:6, "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have, give I unto thee." Elisha desires that he might inheritJE deleted "the principal part." a double portion of this, and beGrosart inserted this word and deleted the following two words on the MS. made therein the main heir of those blessed spiritual gifts which he had, which was accordingly granted him.

2 Kings 2:9–13.] How Elijah's ascension [was] a type of Christ's, see no. 283.Works, 15, 240.

2 Kings 2:11.] Note on Genesis 5:24.

2 Kings 2:12. "Chariot of Israel, and horsemen thereof."] See Hervey's Dialogues, vol. 3, p. 365, margin.Hervey writes, "There is a peculiar Beauty, and most apposite Significance in this proverbial Saying, as used by the antient Israelites. Horses and Chariots were deemed, in those Ages, the principal Strength of the Battle, the most formidable Apparatus of War. Of these the Israelites were intirely destitute. Their GOD had expressly forbidden them to multiply Horses; and We never read of their bringing any considerable Number of Cavalry into the Field.—But, so long as they enjoyed the Presence of their Prophets, they wanted not this Arm of Flesh. They had more than an Equivalent for Chariots and Horses, in the fervent, the effectual Prayers of those holy Men of GOD (Dialogues, 3, 365–66, note).

Isaiah 43:2, "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee."

2 Kings 2:23–24.] Bethel was the place where one of Jeroboam's golden calves was set, and it was the chief seat of Israel's idolatry. And therefore instead of Bethel, the house of God is called Beth-aven,אָוֶן בֵּית "the house of iniquity," by the prophet Hosea [Hosea 10:5]. The inhabitants were probably chiefly idolaters. Hence their very children manifested such contempt of the prophet of the Lord. They seem "to mock both at him as an imposter, and at the miracle of Elijah's ascension as a fiction. They laughed at him, and called him 'baldhead' as a term of reproach (Jeremiah 16:6, and Jeremiah 48:37; Ezekiel 27:31, and Ezekiel 29:18; Micah 1:16; 2 Samuel 10:3–6; Isaiah 3:24), and bad him, Go up to heaven, as Elijah was reported to do, that they might see it, and believe it, and be troubled with him no longer." Bedford, Scripture Chronology, p. 626.

2 Kings 3:15. "But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the Lord came upon him."] The prophet composed himself to receive instructions from God. His mind was somewhat ruffled and disturbed at the sight of Jehoram, though he was not put into a sinful heat or passion, nor had spoke unadvisedly. Yet to be in the fittest frame for divine contemplation and the operations of his spirit, he needed the greatest calmness, and sedateness of spirit, and a mind more disengaged from temporal objects than that fervor of zeal against

-- 392 --

Jehoram's sin did well admit of. He therefore called for a devout musician, one that used to play upon his harp and sing psalms to it. Probably it was some hours after his conversation with the kings, possibly in the evening. To hear God's praises sweetly sung, as DavidJE deleted "used to do it." had appointed, would settle and compose his mind, and help to put him into a right frame, both to speak to God and to hear from him. We find a company of prophets prophesying "with a psaltery and a tabret before them" (1 Samuel 10:5). See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, cols. 601–2.

2 Kings 3:16–26.] They were now in the deserts of Arabia, a dry country, where were no fountains nor streams of water; and it was a time of drought. "The Moabites knew that they were in those difficulties, which they expected before that they would be in, and therefore advanced with their whole army to take the advantage, resolving to attack them early in the morning. Their enemies, being in a valley, as 2 Kings 3:16–17, and themselves on an advanced ground, when the sun was risen in the east, on which side their enemies were, the angle of incidence with the rays upon the water coming directly into their faces, made it look red like blood. They, knowing that there was no water in those parts, and that there had been no rain, concluded that it was blood indeed, and that their enemies had quarreled among themselves, and destroyed one another, so that there was nothing to do but to take the plunder. This made them run thither without any military order, expecting that they who came first should enrich themselves most, and so they tired themselves before they came to the camp." So that the Israelites, when they came up, "gained an easy and entire victory over them, and pursued them into their own country, and there made a greater havoc of them, plundering their cities, destroying their fields, stopping up their wells, and cutting down their trees." Bedford, Scripture Chronology, pp. 629–30.

2 Kings 4:34. "And put his mouth upon his mouth," etc.] Elisha's doing thus is doubtless typical. The prophet here represents Christ, and the raising of the child to life represents the regeneration of a sinner. And by its being done in such a manner, several things are signified.

First. Hereby is signified the universality of the change in conversion. They are renewed in the whole man, sanctified throughout in every part and member. They put off the old man, and put on the new man. They have new eyes, new tongues, new hands, and new feet. Every part was before dead, but every part has new life put into it.

Secondly. Hereby is signified the universal conformity of the new man to Christ. As the parts of the body of the child corresponded with the parts of the body of the prophet, so doth every member of the new man to Christ. There, grace for grace, part for part, the new man is created after God. 'Tis after the image of him that created it. A man, when he is converted, he puts on Christ. Every feature, every part of the body, corresponds exactly with theJE deleted "answerable." parts of Christ's body.

Thirdly. Hereby is signified that the life of every part of the new man is by communication of Christ's life to us. Christ unites himself to us. He

-- 394 --

stretcheth himself upon the dead child to impart of his warmth and his life to it. Christ doth as it were put his hands upon our dead hands to impart the life and virtue of his hands to ours, that our hands may be disposed and fitted to the same work that his hands doth. He puts his eyes to our blind eyes to impart the life and powers of his eyes to ours, that we may see the same spiritual objects that his eyes see, and so of the other parts.

2 Kings 4:41.] This meal that healed the poisoned pottage, and took death away from the pot,JE deleted "was a type of the same." signified the same with the tree that healed the bitter waters (Exodus 15:25). Wheat and other corn is often made use as a type of Christ. It was so in the sheaf of the first fruits, and in the first fruits of wheat harvest, in the wave loaves offered at Pentecost, and in all their meat offerings. Christ compares himself to a corn of wheat which,JE deleted "is not quickened." except it die, abideth alone [John 12:24]. And how often is Christ compared to bread. This meal was corn ground to powder; so Christ, before we can be healed by him, must suffer to the greatest extremity. See no. 217.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15 150–51.

2 Kings 18:5. "So that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that was before him."] The same is said of Josiah (2 Kings 23:25). And yet we observe the words annexed and the manner of expression in each place; there is no inconsistence. Hezekiah exceeded all before and after in the manifestation and exercises of piety, fortitude, resolution, and steadfastness, with which he carried on the work of reformation, "trusting in the Lord God of Israel, departing not from him, but keeping his commandments," as is here said 2 Kings 23:5–6], manifesting this confidence

-- 398 --

in God and steadfastness under very great temptation. Having taken the kingdom under the power of that great king of Assyria, he ventured to rebel against him, and continued steadfast under the great trial he had when his kingdom was, most of it, subdued, and he was besieged, and so proudly and terribly threatened in his royal city by Sennacherib's great army. But Josiah exceeded him in the degree to which he carried his reformation, his care and earnest endeavor that everything should be brought up exactly to the law of Moses. 2 Kings 20:12.] The special reasons of the king of Babylon's putting so much respect upon Hezekiah on this occasion were probably these. First, God gave Hezekiah exceeding great temporal prosperity in reward for his piety, as he had David and Solomon before. This appears by the next verse and 2 Chronicles 32:27 ff. These messengers probably showed this by applauding his prosperity, which probably was Hezekiah's temptation. 2. Hezekiah had been raised high in his reputation with the Babylonians by God's so wonderfully weakening the kingdom of Assyria (with whom the Babylonians were at war, as Mr. Henry observes) for Hezekiah's sake, as he did by the destruction of Sennacherib's army by the angel. See 2 Chronicles 32:21-23:3. By reason of that wonderful sign that God had given Hezekiah of the sun's going back ten degrees (2 Chronicles 32:31). This was the more taken notice of because the sun (as says Mr. Henry) was the Babylonian god, so that on their apprehension their god did very greatly favor, or was a great friend of Hezekiah's, which the more induced them to show themselves friendly to him.Exposition, 2 (1725), 464–65.

2 Kings 20:13.] It is an hard matter, says Mr. Henry on the place, to keep the spirit low in the midst of great advancements. God had given Hezekiah great outward wealth and prosperity, and had wrought one great miracle after another for him: first, overthrew the mighty army of Sennacherib, that great and proud potentate, by an angel; and now even caused the sun to go back ten degrees. And he saw him greatly famed and honored in distant lands by these things, and now was receiving the compliments of a great prince on this occasion.Ibid., 465–66.

2 Kings 21:10–15.] 'Tis evident by this and many other passages of Scripture that the first destruction of Jerusalem was principally for the sins of Manasseh and the wickedness that the people were guilty of in his reign (2 Kings 23:26–27, and 2 Kings 24:3–4, and Jeremiah 15:4). And yet the first captivity in Jehoiachin's time was not till about forty-four years after Manasseh's death, and the total destruction of Jerusalem in Zedekiah's time not till about fifty-five years after his death. Hence I would observe that 'tis no argument against the dreadful destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, its being an evident token of God's wrath against the people for their rejecting and crucifying Christ, that that destruction happened about forty years after Christ's crucifixion.

1 Chronicles 4:9–10.] Jabez's mother was probably a type of the church, and Jabez a type of that man-child which the church brings forth with the sorrow and travail of persecution, that we read of John 16:19–22, Revelation 12:2, Revelation 12:5, which shall be born especially at the commencement of the promised glory and enlargement of the church, which shall be given in answer to the prayers of the saints and especially of godly ministers, when God shall "bless his people indeed, and enlarge their coast, and his hand shall be with them, and when God shall keep 'em from evil, that it may not grieve 'em" (as is here said of God for Jabez, in answer to his prayer). See Ezekiel 36:33–38; Isaiah 40:1–2; Isaiah 54:1–4, and Isaiah 54:9, Isaiah 54:11–17; Psalms 102:13–22; Isaiah 26:15–17. 'Tis probable that it is for this very reason that these things concerning Jabez are inserted in this place.

One thing more may be worthy to be noted concerning Jabez, viz. that he was probably a scribe or divine, and that he "was more honorable than his brethren" 1 Chronicles 4:9], especially in "learning and piety," because we find "that the families of the scribes dwelt at Jabez (1 Chronicles 2:55), a city which it is likely took its name from his name," as Mr. Henry observes.Ibid., 486. So that

-- 404 --

he is especially a type of the Christian ministry, and what is here said of him represents God's comforting and enlarging the church in answer to the prayers of gospel ministers.

The whole forty thousand are here called footmen because they did not ride in chariots, and they are all called horsemen in Samuel because the bulk of the army were horsemen. 1 Chronicles 21:18-22:2.] Though there was so much land possessed by the children of Israel, yet God chose the land of Ornan the Jebusite, a Gentile proselyte, for the place where his temple should be built, which seems to be to signify two things, viz. 1. the calling of the Gentiles, and that when the gospel church should be erected by Christ, the true Solomon, of which this temple was a type, it should be erected on Gentile ground; and 2. his being a Jebusite, one of the accursed nations of Canaan, which seems to be to signify that Christ's church in all ages is made up of those that are naturally sinners and under the curse, and Christ's kingdom erected in the hearts of such. The church of Christ, in being set up here in this fallen sinful world, is set up on accursed ground, on the possession of those that were as it were Amorites, Hittites, and Jebusites. The corruption of nature that derive by natural generation is compared to our father's being an Amorite, and our mother an Hittite, and our births' being of the land of Canaan (Ezekiel 16:3). The children of Israel's settling in the land of those accursed nations seems to signify the same thing, for the children of Israel were the visible and typical church of God. And both these things seem also to be signified in the 1 Chronicles 22:2. They were strangers that were improved to hew stones for the temple, and this temple was therein the more fit type of the Christian church that was built up by the Gentiles. Isaiah 60:10, "And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls." Zechariah 6:12–13, Zechariah 6:15, "Behold the man whose name is the Branch, and he shall grow up out of his place. And he shall build the temple of the Lord. Even he shall build the temple of the Lord, and he shall bear the glory," etc. "And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord." And 'tis herein a more fit type of the church or spiritual temple in all ages, that is built up of those that are naturally strangers and aliens from the commonwealth of Israel.

Oman's giving freely the possession he had there for a place for God's altar, and the oxen for a burnt offering, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for a meat offering—his thus freely and readily giving everything that he had there, signifies to us how the true convert consecrates all to God, is ready to sacrifice all to the interest of religion, and is ready to part with all for Christ. See no. 217.Works, 15, 150–51.

1 Chronicles 22:13. "Dread not, nor be dismayed."] Persons need a great deal of courage that undertake any great enterprise for the church of God and the advancement of Christ's kingdom. Not only did Joshua need courage to conquer the land of Canaan, but Solomon to build the temple when all was in peace.

1 Chronicles 22:18–19.] So when persons are converted and have got through the great opposition that stood in the way of their safety, and God has given 'em rest, and given them the possession of the good, it is so far from being a just reason for slothfulness that it should, on the contrary, be improved as a reason why now they should set their heart and soul to seek the Lord their God, and to build the house of God.

1 Chronicles 23:26. "They shall no more carry the tabernacle," etc.] Thus the ceremonial law was in part altered before Christ's time. The service of the Levites, by the law of Moses, consisted much in carrying the tabernacle, and vessels, and instruments of it (Numbers 3-4). But when the temple was built, this service ceased, and was abrogated by David, there then ceasing to be occasion any longer for that work. And therefore David gave 'em new ordinances, and appointed them new work, which shows that the ceremonial law was alterable. If it may be altered in part, it may be altered in the whole. If David might abrogate some ordinances, Christ, the true David, might abrogate all. See note on Jeremiah 3:16–17 and Isaiah 56:3–4. InMS: "in the." 2 Chronicles 23:18, the ordinances of David are mentioned as of parallel validity with those of Moses as a rule for their public worship. See note on Isaiah 51:4. See "Miscellanies," no. 1027.This reference is a later addition. Works, 20, 358–65.

1 Chronicles 25:9–31.] The company of singers in the temple, in their several ranks and exact number and order, were a lively type of the triumphant church. And therefore there is, undoubtedly, something mystical and significant in this number and order that we have here an account of: twenty-four wards with twelve persons in each ward, so that the whole number was twice twelve times twelve, which is agreeable to the numbers by which things are reckoned that appertain to the church of God and the New

-- 410 --

Jerusalem in the Revelation, where we find the number twelve in these things are always made use of. And the leaders or heads of these twenty-four wards do probably represent or typify the same thing that is signified by twenty-four elders in Revelation.

1 Chronicles 28:19.] The Spirit of God acted and guided the prophets "as to the very organs of their bodies, whereby they expressed the revelation which they had received by inspiration from him. They spake as they were acted by the Holy Ghost.… So when David had received the pattern of the temple, and the manner of the whole worship of God therein by the Spirit, he says, 'All this the Lord made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the work of this pattern.' The Spirit of God not only revealed it unto him, but so guided him in writing of it down, as that he might understand the mind of God out of what himself had written; or he gave it him so plainly and evidently, as if every particular had been expressed in writing by the finger of God." Owen, On the Spirit, Bk. 2, ch. 1, §10.ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΟΛΟΓΙΑ, p. 105.

1 Chronicles 29:2 ff.] David did not lay up those vast treasures he obtained in his wars for the enriching his family, and to leave to his son that should be the heir of his sin, but gave it to God. But God rewarded him in the exceeding great wealth of his son. He had not less then, but doubtless much more than if David had laid up all that he had gotten for him. So the princes of Israel and the people in general gave most liberally to the house of God, and how was the whole land enriched soon after. There appeared a wonderfully liberal, bountiful spirit amongst the people, and what riches soon ensued throughout the whole land.

1 Chronicles 29:8–9.] God greatly rewarded this extraordinary liberality of the people by exceedingly enriching them afterwards in the days of Solomon, as well as rewarded David's liberality, in giving that which he might have laid up for his son and successor, by bestowing such vast riches and honor on Solomon.

1 Chronicles 29:15. "For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers."] These words are exegetical of the last words in the foregoing verse: "of thine own have we given thee." They that only sojourn with another, the habitation they live in and the things they use are not their

-- 411 --

own, but their landlord's. They are but lent to them. And this is added, "as were all our fathers," perhaps as a further evidence that what we have is not our own, for though we have it from our fathers, come by it by inheritance, yet our fathers themselves had it not of their own, but only lent to them by God.

2 Chronicles 5:12–14.] When the priests and Levites "were as one, to make one sound" in praising God with trumpets, singing, and instruments of music, praising "the Lord, saying, He is good, for his mercy endureth forever," then the glory of the Lord came and filled the house. So when it shall come to that in the latter days, that the ministers of the gospel shall generally be united in preaching the true doctrine of the gospel of God's glorious grace, those doctrines especially that are in a peculiar manner evangelical, by which especially is manifested the glory of God's eternal mercy, and free and sovereign immutable grace through Christ Jesus, by which especially the preached gospel is like a song of praise to the Most High: I say, when once it comes to this, and when, withal, ministers shall be united in affection and act in union as fellow laborers and fellow helpers to the grace of God, then shall the glory of God remarkably appear in his church and fill the world. When ministers are thus of one mind and live in peace, then shall the God of love and peace be with them (2 Corinthians 13:11). Then shall the Spirit of God, as a spirit of light, holiness, and joy, descend from heaven in a very new and glorious manner; and remarkable success shall attend the preaching of the gospel everywhere; and then shall be the proper commencement of the day of the church'sJE deleted "letter glory." rest, glory, and triumph on earth.

The peaceful reign of Solomon in his wisdom, wealth, and glory, after the militant troublesome reign of David, is evidently typical of the peaceful, joyful, and glorious reign of Christ in the latter days; and God's dwelling in the magnificent temple as the settled place of his rest, after removing to and froMS: "from." in a tent and tabernacle, is typical of the glorious manner of his dwelling with his church in the latter days, as compared with preceding times.

The magnitude of the temple, vastly exceeding the tabernacle in dimensions,

-- 413 --

represents the vast increase of the church in its extent; and the cloud of glory filling the temple represents the filling the whole earth with God's glory. See Isaiah 6:1, Isaiah 6:3.

He is the angel of God's presence who is entered into the holy of holies, into the heavenly temple, that is always full of the glory of the Lord, and is set down on the throne of God, the very seat of the cloud of glory.

Then God will make stones to live, and of stones will "raise up children unto Abraham" [Luke 3:8].

Nehemiah 8:16–17.] It was so ordered in providence, and particularly noted in Scripture, that the children of Israel should keep the greatest feast of tabernacles, on occasion of the restoration of the Jewish church after the Babylonish captivity, that ever was kept since the first settlement in Canaan, because that restoration was a remarkable type of that glorious restoration of the church and time of the church's happiness on earth, that was the antitype of the feast of tabernacles. It is often spoken of as suchJE deleted "especially." by the prophets.

Nehemiah 8:17.] This is a remarkable instance how some of God's institutions are sometimes long neglected in his church, even in the church's flourishing times, and how God winks at such a neglect. 'Tis remarkable that this ordinance had been neglected in David's, and Solomon's, and Hezekiah's, and Josiah's times; and we have no account of the people's being particularly reproved for it by any of the prophets. This ordinance never

-- 421 --

was observed in the Israelitish church from about the time of its being first settled in Joshua's time till after the captivity when it was drawing to an end. So the due keeping the Passover seems to have been neglected from the days of the judges till Josiah's time (2 Kings 23:22, 2 Chronicles 35:1). So the law against polygamy, Leviticus 18:18, seems even to have been neglected and not understood, nor the contrary practice reproved, till Malachi's time. So in the Christian church, some Christian institutions have been perverted, and others neglected, almost from the days of the apostles till these latter ages since the Reformation. So the right order of the minister, Christ's institution of the two orders of bishops and deacons, and the purity of ministers, seems to have been set aside from near the apostolic age till the Reformation, which well answers to the Jewish return from the captivity into Babylon, for the Reformation is the church's return out of the spiritual Babylon. So how long has that very great and essential part of the stated public service of the Christian church been neglected, viz. charity.JE deleted "which is an essential part of the public service of the Christian churches."

Corol. 1. The Scripture only is our rule to direct us in matters of faith and worship, and not fathers, or councils, or ecclesiastical history, or the practice of the church in former times or in its flourishing times.

Corol. 2. Hence no argument can be drawn against infant baptism from the practice of the Waldenses, if it should really appear that they did not baptize infants.

Nehemiah 9:8. "For thou art righteous."] Hereby it is evident that sometimes by the righteousness of God is sometimes only intended his truth and faithfulness to his promises. And so it is always to be understood when rewarding the saints is spoken of as an act of righteousness.

Esther

THE BOOK OF ESTHER. See no. 46; Works, 15, 60–63. and "Miscellanies," no. 702, third last paragraph in Corol. 3.This reference is a later addition. Works, 18, 305–6.

Esther 1:8. "None did compel."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, cols. 992–93.

Esther 1:14.] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, p. 255.The seven princes were seven privileged counselors to the king of Persia (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 255).

Esther 3:2.] The probable reason why Mordecai refused to bow to Haman was because he was an Amalekite, as he is called an Agagite (Esther 3:1), that is, of the posterity of Agag, or of the royal race of Amalek. The kings of Amalek used to be called Agag, as the kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh (Numbers 24:7), so that he was probably, before his advancement in Ahasuerus's court, looked upon as the head of the remains of that nation. As Mordecai was the chief [of] the Jews in those parts, his bowing to HamanMS: "Mordecai." would therefore look like the Jewish nation's bowing and submitting to the nation of Amalek, which MordecaiMS: "Haman." refused out of a conscientious regard to what God had declared and commanded Israel concerning that nation, in Exodus 17:8, Exodus 17:13–14, Exodus 17:16, and 1 Samuel 15:2–3, God probably by his Spirit influencing him,MS: "of him." and giving him some intimations of his being supported in his resolution of refusing to bow to him. For the extraordinary and prophetical influences of God's Spirit had not as yet ceased on Israel, and probably Mordecai himself was inspired and divinely directed in writing this history. God, in Exodus 17:16, had declared that he would "have war with Amalek from generation to generation," i.e. that his people should have war with them, which was an implicit command never to be at peace with them. But submitting or bowing to them would

-- 424 --

have been inconsistent with upholding a state of war with them. Those would have been manifestations of peace.

Esther 3:7.] "Haman consults the soothsayers to find out a lucky day for the designed massacre. The resolve was taken up 'in the first month, in the twelfth year' of the king, when Esther had been his wife about five years. Some day or other in that year must be pitched upon. As if he doubted not, but that heaven would favor his design, he refers it to a lot." (So the lot was cast for each month, and for the days of the month that the lot fell upon from day to day, till they came to the day that the lot favored.) "And the lot fell upon the twelfth day of that month, so that Mordecai and Esther [had eleven months] to turn them in, for the defeating the design." Henry.Exposition, 2 (1725), 651. Henry reads "for the Lot fell upon the twelfth Month, so that Mordecai and Esther had eleven Months to turn them in, for the defeating of the Design." See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 1005.

"So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the scepter."] Favor was offered by the king by holding out to her the golden scepter; but it was expected that she, in order to a title and interest in the offered favor, should draw near and touch the top of the scepter as an expression of her joyful acceptance of the favor, submission to the royal dominion and power of which the scepter was the ensign, and her dependence on the king's free, sovereign, but offered, favor. The act and benefit of saving faith in Christ may be compared to this act of Esther towards Ahasuerus her king, her husband, and in this affair and in what followed, her savior.

Esther 8:11. "Little ones and women."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 1022.

Esther 8:15. "And the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad."] See Proverbs 11:10.

Esther 9:5–16.] Probably at this time the Jews slew, with Haman and his ten sons, all that were found anywhere of the nation of Amalek that they belonged to; and this seems to have been the last that was done by the nation of Israel in fulfillment of God's curse and command in Exodus 17:14, Exodus 17:16. There were three remarkable destructions that Israel made of that nation. There were several remarkable destructions that Israel made of that nation in fulfillment of what God had said to 'em in the wilderness: one by Saul (1 Samuel 14), and [an]other by David (1 Samuel 27:8, and 1 Samuel 30), and the last before this was that which we have account of in 1 Chronicles 4:43.

Esther 9:13.] The reason why Esther desired that Haman's ten sons might be hanged probably was not from a revengeful spirit, desiring to revenge Hanan's injury on his sons, but that she might fulfill the will of God concerning the Amalekitish nation declared in Exodus 17:14, Exodus 17:16. And probably she did it by Mordecai's direction, that he gave by the direction of the Spirit of God. See note on Esther 3:2.

Esther 9:30. "With words of peace and truth."] I.e. wishing them "peace and truth," saying, Peace and truth be with you, or the like, as the Apostle in his epistles, "Grace, mercy, and peace" [Titus 1:2] be with you, and the like.

Job

The Book of Job.] See no. 145, concerning the manner of wise men's discoursing in those times by taking up their parable.Works, 15, 91. Job 2:4.] Or "skin even unto skin." Job 2:9. "Curse God, and die."] "Some of the heathens used to reproach their gods when any great adversity befell them. The Idumeans, it is probable, did so, among whom Job's wife might have her education. The ancient Persians, who are said to have worshipped fire as a god, used to threaten to extinguish it by water, when enraged by any grievous calamity. And it may be, to some such irreligious temper, the Prophet at least alludes, Isaiah 8:21. 'They shall fret themselves, and curse their king, and their God, and look upward.' Job's wife, if she had not the principles of these enemies of true religion, it seems, on this occasion, falls into their disposition and language." Bennet, Christian Oratory, vol. 2, p. 207.Second Part of the Christian Oratory. This selection is from a sermon on Job 2:10 by Benjamin Bennet (1674–1726), a Nonconforming divine of evangelical orientation, entitled "Of Receiving Evil, as well as Good at the Hand of God" (pp. 204–32). This volume is not a "second volume." Edwards apparently designated it as such because it is titled "Second Part." It is a posthumous publication edited by Latham.

-- 427 --

Job 2:9–10. "Dost thou still retain thine integrity," etc.?] Job did not only retain his integrity just now for a little while while his calamity was new, but he held it to the end. And theJE deleted "long." continuance of his affliction did wear out his integrity, but he persevered and held out to the end; and so Satan was confounded. Though his weakness appeared under the strength and continuance of his temptations and sufferings, so that he spoke many things very wrong, and God rebuked him sharply, yet he did not curse God and cast him off, as Satan supposed he would, but all along resolves to cleave to him, as appears by Job 13:15 and Job 27:2–10.

Job 3:6. "Let it not be joined to the days of the year," etc.] It seems to have been the opinion of the church of God of old, even in the most ancient times and all nations, that it was proper that those days wherein anything remarkably sorrowful happened should periodically be looked upon and observed as sorrowful days, and that those wherein anything very remarkably joyful [happened] should periodically be observed as joyful days. But if Job thought his birth so sorrowful an event that it was worthy that that day should periodically be distinguished as a day of sorrow and mourning, how much more may the day of Christ's resurrection, the birth day of the whole church of God to eternal glory, be periodically kept as a joyful day.

Job 3:8. "Who are ready to raise up their mourning."] In the original,לִוְיָתָן עֹרֵר "raise up leviathan," i.e. the devil, alluding probably to some custom of the heathen who in their cursings used to raise the devil.

Balaam was a magician of those eastern parts. And by what we are told concerning him, it seems to have long been a custom for such magicians, by their enchantments or concern with the devil, to curse and bring evil upon persons and people. And so probably they might from malice curse particular seasons and days on which certain affairs were to be managed. The word "leviathan" is never used for mourning. See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. Poole, Synapsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 21–23.

Job 3:23. "Whose way is hid."] I.e. from him, that he knows not where to go, what to do, or which way to turn himself for relief or rest, etc.

Job 4:8. "Reap the same."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 4:9. "Blast of God."] In this figure, whereby the curse of God is called the "blast of God," allusion is had to some sorts of winds in those countries that caused the fruits of the earth to fade and wither away, especially east winds.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. Or else in allusion to those pestilential blasts of wind that sometimes there were in those parts. See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, p. 35.Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 35.

Job 4:18. "Behold, he put no trust in his servants," etc.] The love and faithfulness of the saints, or of innocent men, or angels, is not at all to be depended on if God should leave them. Job 4:21. "Die without wisdom."] See "Old Testament Intimations of a Future State," p. 21e.The extant portion of JE's "Intimations" manuscript contains only ten pages. The section referred to here has not been located.

Job 5:5.] Here it seems to beJE deleted "supposed." implied that they sow among thorns, as in Job 8:17 it is implied that the wicked sow in stony places. The prosperity and substance of oppressors is an harvest among the thorns of worldliness, and envy, and malice, etc. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 41–42.

Job 5:7.] In the Hebrewעְוּף יַגְבִּיהוּ וּבְנֵ־רֶשֶׁף it is, "as the sons of the burning coal lift up to fly." No wonder that coals that are full of fire send forth sparks. No more is it any wonder that trouble proceeds from that fountain of sin that is in man. Sinful man is like a burning coal, full of sin, as fuel that is full of fire, from which affliction proceeds as necessarily as sparks proceed from a fire.

-- 429 --

Or the meaning may be that man, that is born of corrupt fallen man, does as naturally and necessarily live a life of sorrow as the sparks that are sons of the burning coal fly upward. As soon as these sons of the coal are born of the burning coal, they begin to fly upward, and continue to do so till they go out, which is very soon. So man, as soon as born, begins to suffer affliction, and so goes on as long as he lives, hastening to his end till his life quickly goes out, like the light of a spark. This seems the more probable meaning. The sparks are driven upwards by a hot blast of wind. A being followed with affliction isJE deleted "often." compared to a being lifted up and made to ride on the wind (Job 30:22). So the wind is put for trouble (Proverbs 11:29); so Ecclesiastes 5:16, Isaiah 27:8 and Isaiah 32:2, Hosea 8:7. See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. This reference was added even later. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 42–43.

Job 5:10–11.] See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 44.

Job 5:12–16.] By these and many other parallel passages in this book it seems that it was a thing noted and commonly observed in the church of God of old, before Moses' time in the age of the patriarchs, that the wicked of the world used to persecute God's saints.

Job 5:24.] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 6:3. "Heavier than the sand of the sea."] The word rendered "heavier," יִכְכָּד, signifies not only heavy, but great. Job therefore has respect not only to the weight, but the abundance of the sand of the sea. See SSS.This and the following reference are a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 50. "Swallowed up." See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 50–51.

Job 6:5.] Job was become so poor that he had nothing to eat, and that made him complain. See the two next verses.

Job 6:6.] Job was reduced to such necessity that he was forced to content himself with such insipid unsavory morsels. This is the meaning, as appears by the next verse.

-- 430 --

Job 6:10. "For I have not concealed the words of the Holy One."] As a teacher, ruler, and judge, the things which I have spoken, the instructions, and counsels, and commands I have given, and the sentence I have pronounced, has been right agreeable to God's mind, agreeable to his revealed will.

Job 6:11. "What is my strength, that I should have hope? What is my end, that I should prolong my life?"] I.e. "what is my end," or what good issue or event of things, and end of these troubles, is there that I can reasonably hope for, that I should desire to prolong my life? See note on Ecclesiastes 4:15–16. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 55–56.

Job 6:13. "Is wisdom driven quite from me?"] I.e. is my grace? God, have I utterly lost that principle? This is often the language of the hearts of saints in trying times.

Job 6:16. "Blackish by reason of the ice."] Or as the wordsמִנִּי־קַדַח הַקֹּדְרִים are literally, "before the frost," i.e. under the ice they appear black, as though there was much water there.

"Wherein the snow is hid." I.e. the snow water. SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 58.

Job 6:19. "The troops of Tema looked."] In the winter when they did not want water, then there was enough. But in summer when they needed, there was none. So Job would intimate it was with his friends. They were friendly in time of his prosperity, but failed in adversity.

Job 6:24–25.] Eliphaz had charged him with being a wicked man, but had not told him wherein. He had mentioned no crime or wicked practice of his. Job challenges him to show on particular instances wherein he had been wicked. He charged and reproved, but what was the thing that he reproved? It was in general his supposed wickedness, but he could fix upon nothing.

Job 6:26.] I.e. do ye imagineJE deleted "to force." by your rebukes to oblige me to hold my peace and not utter my complaint, as though it were causeless? Do you think

-- 431 --

toJE deleted "prevent." deny me even the small relief of venting my sorrow, whose desperate case forces me to complain? You had as good think to hinder the wind from blowing, as to hinder me in my extreme sorrow from complaining (Job 10:1, and Job 13:13, and 2:19).

Job 6:28.] This refers to what Job had said in the Job 6:26. (See note.) As much as to say,MS: "See." Look upon me, and behold my case. Consider it in its circumstances, and see if you can think any other than that the extremity of my case is not enough to extort these complaints. The Job 6:27 comes in as a parenthesis. The Job 29:11 confirms this explanation of these two verses, and Job 10:1.This sentence is a later addition.

Job 7:7. "My life is wind."] Alluding to the breath. See note on Psalms 78:39, and James 4:14, and "Images of Divine Things," no. 141.Works, 11, 100.

Job 7:15. "Rather than my life."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 71–72.

Job 7:17. "That thou shouldst magnify him?"] As if he were a whale, or sea, or some powerful and terrible creature. See Job 7:12.

Job 7:20. "O thou preserver of men."] The wordsהָאָדָם נֹצַר might more exactly be rendered, "O thou keeper of men." Mr. Hervey says, "Not preserver, but observer, the phrase expressing the strict and incessant inspection of the divine eye; as it intimates the absolute impossibility, that any transgression should escape the divine notice." Hervey's Meditations, vol. 2, p. 138.Meditations and Contemplations, II, 138 note. See also SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 73–75.

"To myself." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 74–75.

Job 8:8.] See no. 111.Works, 15, 81–82.

-- 432 --

Job 8:9. "For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow."] Bildad here has respect to the much longer lives of preceding generations, whereby they had much greater opportunity to gain wisdom and experience. In Job's time the age of men was shortened very much from what it was a few generations before.

Job 8:11. "Can the rush grow up without mire," etc.?] It seems that there was a sort of weeds in those parts of Arabia, that used to spring up in the spring in the puddles and places moistened with snow water, that died when the sun advanced, and the weather grew hotter and dried up the moisture. To these Bildad here compares Job'sMS: "Bildads." hope and prosperity.

Job 8:14.] See Spencer's Similies and Sentences, p. 99.Under the heading, "The Vanity of heaping up Riches," John Spencer (d. 1680) writes, "It is a great deal of care and pains that the Spider takes in weaving her web, she runneth much, and often up and down, she fetcheth a compass this way and that way, and returneth often to the same point, she spendeth her self in multitudes of fine threads, to make her self a round Cabinet, she exenterateth her self, and worketh out her own bowels, to make an artificial and curious piece of work; which when it is made, is apt to be blown away with every puffe of wind; she hangeth it up aloft, she fastneth it to the roof of the house, she strengthneth it with many a thread, wheeling often round about, not sparing her own bowels, but spending them willingly upon her work; And when she hath done all this, spun her fine threads, weaved them one within another, wrought her self a fine Canopy, hanged it aloft, and thinks all's sure; on a sudden, in the twinckling of an eye, with a little sweep of a Beesom, all falls to the ground, and so her labour perisheth: But here is not all; a Poor Spider, she is killed either in her own web, or else she is taken in her own snare, haled to death, and trodden under foot; Thus the silly Animal may be truly said either to weave her own winding sheet, or to make a snare to hang her self. Just so do many Men wast and consume themselves to get preferment, to enjoy pleasures, to heap up riches, and encrease them; and to that end they spend all their wit, and oftentimes the health of their bodies, running up and down, labouring and sweating, carking and caring; And when they have done all this, they have but weaved the Spiders web to catch flyes, yes, oftentimes are caught in their own nets, are made instruments of their own destruction, they take a great deal of pains with little success, to no end or purpose" (ΚΑΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ ΠΑΔΑΙΑ. Things New and Old. Or, a Store-house of Similies, Sentences, Allegories, Apophthegms, Adagies, Apologues, Divine, Morall, Politicall, &c. With their several Applications. Collected and observed from the Writings and Sayings of the Learned in all Ages to this present [London, 1658]).

Job 8:17.] This verse implies that they grow in stony places where they have no deepness of earth. Their "roots are wrapped about the heap," but don't penetrate into the ground, and so are withered before the scorching sun. See Matthew 13 concerning them that grew in stony places.

Job 8:18.] "His place will deny him, saying, I have not seen thee."] I.e. he shall be totally destroyed from his place; neither root nor branch shall

-- 433 --

be found there. There shall be no remnant. The place shall be as though he had never stood there.

Job 9:7.] See note on Job 34:20.

Job 9:8. "And treadeth upon the waves of the sea."] See note on Matthew 14:24–25.

Job 9:24. "He covereth the faces of the judges thereof."] I.e. covers their eyes, blindfolds them so that they cannot see to [do] justice, so that the wicked are justified, and the righteous suffer.

Job 9:26. "They are passed away as the swift ships, as the eagle that hasteth to the prey."] A most lively and beautiful comparison. When we stand upon the brink of an harbor as a ship sets sail under a full gale, and we look after, or see an eagle aloft in the air upon the wing, swiftly hasting to some distant prey, how fast do they lessen and grow dim, and how soon do they totally disappear and appear no more. We can see nothing of them.

Job 9:29.] I.e. if I am wicked after I have used such care to avoid sin, and taken so much pains to wash myself, if still thou holdest me as a wicked man and treatest me as such, it is not worth the while to strive to be clean and pure, for I have done my utmost. See the two next verses. See also Job 9:1–2, and Job 9:15, and Job 9:20–21, and Job 9:23.

Job 9:31. "And mine own clothes should abhor me."] The marginal readingI.e. margin of the KJV. seems preferable: "make me to be abhorred," i.e. my clothes, which hide my deformity and be my ornaments to recommend me, shall instead of that make me appear the more deformed and loathsome, being as filthy rags, as a man's garment would be if he were plunged in a ditch and rolled in mire and filth.

Job 10:1. "My complaint upon myself."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 98–99.

Job 10:17. "Changes and war are against me."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 104–5.

-- 434 --

Job 10:22. "Without any order."] Where high and low, superiors and inferiors, princes and subjects, masters and servants, are all confounded, and on a level without any of the order and distinction that is kept up in the land of the living. Job 3:19, "The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master."

See another more probable sense in SSS. "Where the light is as darkness." Or "as the darkness," i.e. where the day, or the time when it is day in this world, is as the night, i.e. equally dark without any distinction. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 106–7. Light and darkness in Scripture are often put for day and night, and particularly in this book, as in Job 26:10, in the Hebrew.This paragraph is a later addition. עִם־חְשָׁךְ אוּר

"Without any order." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 106.

"The light is as darkness." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 106–107.

Job 11:2.] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 107.

Job 11:12. "For vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt."] It would be better without the word "like" that is supplied, and as it is [in] the original,יִוָּלֵד אָדָם פֶּרֶא וְעַיִר "though man is born a wild ass's colt," i.e. ignorant, perverse, untractable, going astray as soon as he is born. See Jeremiah 2:24. See SSS on Job 24:5.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 247.

Job 11:17. "Thine age."] I.e. "thine old age," as the wordחֶלֶד in the original may well be so interpreted.

Job 11:18.] This verse may probably be explained by Hebrews 6:19, "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast."The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. "Thou shalt dig about thee." I.e. thy virtue shall secure thee as if it made an entrenchment around thee.

Job 11:20. "As the giving up of the ghost."] Or as the breath of a dying [man], his breath goeth forth and can't be recovered. It never shall return again. So the hope of the wicked shall be lost in despair.

-- 435 --

Job 12:7–25.] The discourse that is begun in this verse and continued to the end of the chapter is connected with Job 12:3, "But I have understanding as well as you: I am not inferior to you; yea, who knoweth not such things as these?" as is confirmed by the conclusion of this discourse in the Job 13:1–2, where the same thing in sense is repeated that was said in that Job 12:3. And it appears that what Job has special reference to in the preceding discourses of his three friends, when he thus asserts that he knows as much as they, is what they had said of the greatness, perfections, works, and dominion of God, as Eliphaz (Job 5:9–18) and Zophar, in the Job 11:7–10.

Job 12:18. "The bond of kings."] I.e. the bond that kings bind with, as Psalms 68:6, "He bringeth out those which were bound with chains"; Psalms 146:7, "Which executeth judgment for the oppressed, which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners." "And girdeth their loins with a girdle." I.e. he girdeth those with strength and beauty that before were bound by the strength of others, as 1 Samuel 2:4. "The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girt with strength." So a girdle was an ornament. Isaiah 3:24, "Instead of a girdle a rent."

Job 13:8. "Will ye accept his person? Will ye contend for God?"] A true respect to God, which primarily consists in a love to his moral perfections, don't tend to any immorality, for surely a true love to moral virtue and excellency don't tend to a regard to moral evil and deformity. A love to God for his justice don't incline to injustice. A love to God for the mercifulness of his nature don't incline to harshness and cruelty. But a false respect to God is very commonly exercised in the vilest and most unrighteous actions. So a false zeal for God commonly is shown in hating men and in the greatest injustice, persecution, and cruelty. This is accepting God's person, which the righteous God will thank no man for, but infinitely abhors and is greatly provoked by, as it follows in the Job 13:10. "He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons."

Job 13:9. "Is it good?"] Would it prove well for you?

"As one man mocketh another, do ye so mock him?" I.e. do ye think to impose upon God and cheat him with your hypocritical pretenses of zeal for him by speaking wickedly for him? Do you think you can deceive him as one man deceives another?This paragraph is a separate entry.

-- 436 --

Job 13:14.] I.e. though I say, I will speak, let come on me what will, yet I run no dreadful venture. There is no reason for you to imagine that in so expressing myself and solemnly appealing to God, I am devouring my own flesh with my own teeth, or destroying my life with my own hand, for though I boldly refer myself to God's judgment, yet I shall be justified. Yet I am safe; I know I shall be justified. The wordsבְשִׁנּי בְשָׂרִי אֶשֶּׂא עַל־מָה might have been translated most properly, "Wherefore should I take my flesh in my teeth," etc., signifying that he should do so in thus solemnly appealing to God, if his own conscience did testify to his integrity. Job expresses himself thus to confirm his friends that he did not speak against his conscience, as much as to say, Why should I be so foolish as to appeal thus to God, and to go to "take my flesh in my teeth," etc., as I should do if I made such an appeal, and was not conscious to my integrity?

Job 14:4. "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?"] No. 334.Works, 15, 318–19.

Job 14:13–15.] See Dr. Sherlock's Use and Intent of Prophecy, pp. 240 ff.In Dissertation II, "The Sense of the Antients before Christ upon the Circumstances and Consequences of the Fall," Thomas Sherlock declares that Job, despite his present distress, expected "another Time for Justice" from God based on his hope and expectation "to be called from the Grave." His friends did not share that expectation (Use and Intent of Prophecy, 5th ed., pp. 240–41).

Job 14:18–20.] See Sherlock's Use and Intent of Prophecy, p. 241.Sherlock describes the responses of Job's friends to his declaration that "all Things were drawing to an End, the Earth, and the Inhabitants thereof" (5th ed., pp. 241–42).

Job 14:22.] 'Tis not unlikely that the Spirit of God in this has some respect to the misery of wicked men inJE deleted "another world." a future state, when both soul and body shall be cast into hell. See Ecclesiastes 11:10.

Job 15:20. "The number of years is hidden to the oppressor."] That is the wicked man spoken of who is an oppressor (Job 15:28, Job 15:34–35). The number of the years of his prosperity and life is hidden to him. The continuance of it is exceeding uncertain, which causes him to be full of fears and suspicions, and have "a dreadful sound in his ears." Oftentimes in the midst of his prosperity, when he seems to be most safe, destruction

-- 437 --

comes upon him, as it follows in the next verse. He is in constant fear of sudden destruction, and this makes him travail in pain.

Probably Eliphaz here has reference to what Job had said before concerning himself in his prosperity. Job 3:25–26, "The thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came." And when Eliphaz in the next verse speaks of the destroyer's coming upon him, he probably [has] reference to the Sabeans and Chaldeans, which came suddenly and destroyed Job's substance. And when he says, Job 15:22, "He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness," he seems to have respect to the desponding thoughts which Job had expressed. Job 9:21, "Though I were perfect, yet would I not know my soul. I would despise my life." And Job 9:16, "If I had called, and he had answered me, yet would I not believe that he had hearkened to my voice." And when in the Job 15:23 he speaks of the wicked's wandering "abroad for bread," he probably has reference to Job's poverty.

Job 15:22. "The sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Job 15:26.] "He runneth" boldly on God, even when clad in dreadful armor.

Job 15:32. "His branch shall not be green."] While the branch is only in the bud, before it is leaved out.

Job 15:35. "Bring forth vanity."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 16:11.] Thus these good men censured one another as ungodly.

Job 16:18.] I.e. if I have shed any blood wrongfully, sitting an judge, let not the earth cover the blood that I have shed; and if I have done so, let my prayer not be accepted.

Job 17:5.] His friends, he supposed, had flattered before his calamity; and that now it was evident that in times past, when he was "as a tabret" (as he says in the next verse), when they appeared so fair and friendly when he was in his prosperity, it was all nothing but flattery, and that now it evidently proved so when he was come to be in adversity, he being now their byword.

-- 438 --

-- 439 --

Job 17:12. They change the night into day; the light is short because of darkness."] The words seem evidently to be wrong translated. Most literally rendered, the wordsיָשִׂימוּ לְיוֹם לַיְלָה are thus: "They put the nightJE mistakenly writes "light." into the day," i.e. they bring the night or darkness into the time that, according to the ordinary course of things,MS: "thing." is the time of day, and so shorten the day, make it much shorter than its natural period. Thus the former part of the verse agrees with the latter part, and with the content, and with Job's plain drift and design, which is to represent how his day of prosperity and life is shortened, and suddenly cut off, and all his purposes and hopes broken.

As for that manner of speaking, "They put the night into the day," see note on Lamentations 4:15.

Job 17:13–14.] The grave is the house that is my home; and corruption and worms are the rest of the family that is of the same house, and [that] I am to dwell with in the house of my near relatives of the same family. I desire the grave as a child desires to go home, and desire worms and corruption as the child desires to dwell with its father, mother, etc.

Job 17:15–16. "Where is now my hope? As for my hope, who shall see it? They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust."] The more literal translation of the last of these versesנָחַת עַל־עָפָר אִם־נַחַד תֵּרַדְנָה שְׁאֹל בַּדֵּי is thus: "The bars of the pit descend, when our rest together is in the dust," which seems to be a better translation. The expression signifies as much as that when Job was gone to the grave as his house, and had there took up his settled abode with corruption as his father and with worms as his mother and sister, and was dwelling together in that house with such a family, the door of the pit should be everlastingly shut and barred upon him so that he never should come out again. This he gives as a reason why death would be an end to all his hope. A phrase for a door's being open is its being "lifted up," as in the end of the Psalms 24: "Lift up, ye gates; and be ye lift, ye everlasting door." See SSS on Psalms 24:7.This reference is a later addition. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 703–4. So a door's descending seems to be a phrase for its being fast shut, and the bars' descending, their being thrust down or thrust in for the fastening of the door.

-- 440 --

Job 18:2. "Mark, and afterwards," etc.] I.e. mark out some limits to your talk. Set some bounds to your words. Let us know when you have done, and then we will speak.

Job 18:4. "Shall the earth be forsaken?"] I.e. shall God forsake the earth, and cease to take care of mankind, and to exercise his moral government over them, that you may escape punishment? In this sense the phrase of God's "forsaking the earth" is used, Ezekiel 8:12. "The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth." "Shall the rock be removed out of its place?" Must the fixed order of the divine government be changed for thee?

Job 18:13–14.] By the "first-born of death" here is probably meant the devil, or the prince of the devils. One that is subject to death, or liable to death or destruction, is called a son of death or destruction, as 1 Samuel 26:16 and Proverbs 31:8. And therefore the devil, that was the first being that ever became subject to death, or the leader of the devils, who first became liable to death, may be called the "first-born of death." The same is probably meant by the "king of terrors," in the Job 18:14.

Job 18:14. "His confidence shall be rooted out of his tabernacle."] I.e. that which he set his heart upon, and placed his happiness [in], and depended upon for safety, comfort, honor, or any good that his heart had dependence upon.

Job 19:4. "Mine error remaineth with myself."] It hurts me, and not you. I must bear the punishment alone. I am punished enough by God, and you need not add to my affliction lest I should not suffer enough. This agrees best withMS: "which." what follows.

Job 19:25. "For I know that my redeemer lives."] Job mentions this because he is about to express his hope of what would be after he was dead. He should die, and the worms should destroy his body, but his redeemer lived. And hence he hoped that he would redeem his body from the power of the grave. The resurrection of the body, and that glorification of the whole person that will then be, is especially called "redemption" in the New Testament. And because his redeemer lived, he hoped that though he died, he should live again by his redemption, for in that he lives, we shall live also.

-- 441 --

"I know that my redeemer liveth." Though I shall die, and my flesh shall be destroyed with worms. "And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." In the original, it is, "he shall stand over the dust," עָפָר עַל. The word "earth" is very often used in the book of Job, and the word is everywhere eretz,אֶרֶץ and nowhere this word that properly signifies "dust." And it is not true that at the day of judgment Christ will properly stand on the earth. The meaning is that Christ will stand over the dust of the dead saints.This and the following paragraph are a separate entry.

"My redeemer," גֹּאֲלִי. The word also, as it was used among the Hebrews, signified near kinsman, as in Ruth 3:12. "And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman, goeēl; howbeit there is a kinsman, goeēl, nearer than I." Ruth 3:13, "Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, or if he will redeem thee, יִגְאָלֵךְ, well; let him do the kinsman's part, יִגְאָֹל. But if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, לְגָאֳלֵךְ, then I will do the part of a kinsman to thee, וגְאַלְתִּיךְ." So the word is the same, 1 Kings 16:11. "As soon as he began to reign, he slew all the house of Baasha; he left none of his kinsfolks, וְגֹּאֲֹלָיו.

There were four things the goeēl was to do for his kinsman unable to act for himself. 1. He was to marry the widow of the deceased kinsman to raise up seed to his brother, as Christ marries the elect church that was left a widow by the first Adam, the first surety, and by the law or first covenant, the first husband having no seed (Romans 7:3–4). 2. He was [to] redeem the inheritance of his poor kinsman (Leviticus 25:25). So Christ redeems the inheritance which we sold. 3. He was to ransom his poor kinsman in bondage, paying the price of his redemption. Leviticus 25:47, "If thy brother wax poor, and sell himself," Leviticus 25:48, "after that he is sold, he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him." Leviticus 25:52, "According unto his years shall he give him again the price of his redemption." Thus does Christ redeem us from bondage after we have sold ourselves. 4. He was to avenge the blood of his slain kinsman on the slayer. Thus does Christ avenge our blood on Satan.This paragraph is a later addition.

See Dr. Sherlock's Use and Intent of Prophecy, pp. 225 ff.This reference is a later addition. Sherlock argues that Job's declaration in this verse contains "a degree of Knowledge" of the "great Mystery" of the future resurrection "beyond the Proportion of Light communicated to the Age in which he lived." Neither Moses nor Jewish interpreters had such knowledge, which was not available until the time of the New Testament (5th ed., pp. 225–28).

"And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." In the original,יָקְוּם עַל־עָפָר וְאַחֲרֹוֹן

-- 442 --

it is, "And that at last he shall stand over (or rise above) the dust," concerning which, see SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 191–94.

Job 19:26. "And though after my skin."] Job says thus because his skin was destroyed already by the sore boils that he was smitten with from head to foot, and the worms had destroyed that, as he says, Job 7:5. "My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome." The literal translationנִקְּפוּ־זאֹת עעוֹרִי וְאַחַר is, "Though after my skin, they shall destroy this," probably putting his hand on his flesh and bones. The expression is such a kind of impersonal phrase as is used, as Job 18:19, and Daniel 2:30, and many other places.

The proper meaning of the expression, according to the idiom of the language, is no more than this: "Though after my skin, this is destroyed." See SSS.This paragraph is a later entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 194–95.

Job 19:27. "Be consumed within me."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 196–97.

Job 19:28.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 197–99.

Job 19:29.] A being slain by the sword is a phrase often used in this book for a being destroyed by God's vindictive wrath. So Job 15:22, 17:18, and Job 33:18, and Job 36:12.There is no Job 17:18, but also no obvious other passage intended by this erroneous citation. In the same context JE inserted a second "Job 35:8, " duplicating the Ezekiel reference in the following sentence. So Ezekiel 31:17, and Ezekiel 32:28, Ezekiel 32:32, and Ezekiel 35:8; Psalms 63:10–11. See "Old Testament Intimations of a Future State," pp. 22–23.This sentence is a later addition. See footnote on Job 4:21 entry. The remainder of this paragraph is another later addition. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 199–200. The "flaming sword" (Genesis 3:24), and the sword of the angel that opposed Balaam [Numbers 22:31], signified vindictive wrath.

Job 20:11. "His bones are full of the sins of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust."] Both these expressions impart the same thing,

-- 443 --

and are as much as to say, The sins of his youth remain with him after he is dead;MS: "death." his sin shall lie down with him in his grave, and shall remain on his dead corpse there. When his flesh is putrefied and turned to dust, then his iniquity shall still remain on his bones. His bones shall be full of them, which signifies that his sin shall forever remain with him after he is dead. He shall never get rid of them, but they shall to all eternity lie upon him. See Ezekiel 32:27.

Job 20:16. "He shall suck."] See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 206.

Job 20:17. "He shall not see the rivers."] Which there are in the heavenly Canaan, which is a land flowing with milk and honey.

Job 21:2. "Let this be your consolations."] I.e. if you have no other comforts to administer to me, deny me not this, of suffering me to speak, and hearing me diligently.

Job 21:29. "Have ye not asked them that go by the way? Do ye not know their tokens?"] By "them that go by the way" seems to be meant the angels that were wont often to appear to godly persons before there was any written revelation. Job probably refers to what Eliphaz had said of the vision he had of an angel, and what they had said to 'em (Job 4:12–21). Elihu speaks of such things as common (Job 33:14 ff.). The angels may fitly be called these "that go by the way," being constantly employed as God's messengers and posts as it were, sent forth by the great king into the various parts of his kingdom, and constantly ascending and descending in the way between heaven and earth (Genesis 28:12), and are also continually going to and fro on the earth on messages on which God sends 'em. As evil angels are continually walking about, seeking whom they may devour, and "going to and fro in the earth, and walking up and down in it" (Job 1:7 and Job 2:2), so the good angels walk "to and fro through the earth" (Zechariah 1:10). And the angels frequently appeared to holy men of old before Moses' time as wayfaring men. So they appeared to Abraham as "he sat in the tent door" (Genesis 18:1). So they appeared to Lot, who found 'em "in the street" [Genesis 19:2]. So 'tis probable the angel of God appeared to Jacob that night that he wrestled with him [Genesis 32:24]; so to Hagar (Genesis 16:7). So the angels appeared to Jacob (Genesis 32:2).

-- 444 --

Job 21:30.] I.e. that this present life is not the time of their punishment. Here they often prosper, but they are reserved to a future state, which is the proper state of retribution.

Job 21:32–33. "Yet shall he be brought to the grave. He shall remain in the tomb. The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him; and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him."] The proper translation of these wordsיִשְׁקְוֹד וְעַל־גָדִישׁ יוּבֶל לִקְבָרוֹת וְהוּא Job 21:32
מִסְפָּר אֵין וּלְפָנָיו יִמְשׁוֹךְ כָּל־אָדָם וְאַחֲרָיו נָחַל רִגְבֵי מָתְקוּ־לֹוֹ Job 21:33 seems to be thus. "And he shall be brought to the grave; and he that is over the heap" (i.e. the heap of dust over the grave, meaning the devil, who has the power of death) "shall watch" (for him), or "he shall watch for him at the heap or grave. The clods of the grave shall sweetly devour him, and shall draw every man after him. And there is no number of those that are before its face," that is before the face of death or the grave, whom it is about to devour and swallow down as its sweet morsels. So the last expression is but an amplificationOr: "ampliation." MS: "amplication." of what is said in the foregoing words, that "the grave shall draw every man into it." The same verb in the same conjugation, which is here rendered by our translators neutrally, "shall be sweet unto him," is rendered actively in Job 24:20, "The worm shall feed sweetly on him." Here it is לוֹ מָתְקוּ; there it is מְתָקוֹ. The true sense is undoubtedly much the same in both places; and this rendering well agrees with the context, and makes the sense plain, which otherwise is exceeding intricate and wholly unintelligible. And this not only makes the words plain, but in this sense they are exceeding significant, and elegant, and agreeable to figures of speech used elsewhere in Scripture, which elsewhere represent death, the grave, and hell as waiting for the wicked, making them welcome when they come, very gladly receiving them as proper inhabitants, as those that are most suitable for it. So in Job 24:20 and Isaiah 14:9. The saints are not the proper food of death; and therefore, though they are devoured by it, yet it shall vomit 'em up again as not suiting its stomach, as the whale vomited up Jonah. When it is said, "He that is over the grave shall watch for him," or "He shall watch for him over the grave," it may well be understood of him who is called, in Job 18:13–14, the "first-born of death" and the "king of terrors," whether by the "king of terrors" we understand the devil or death itself. That this should be understood and not expressed is not strange; such kind of ellipses,JE deleted "a relative without an antecedent." a verb without a nominative case

-- 445 --

expressed, is very common in Scripture and in this book.JE deleted "Then the pronoun 'he' is in this book often used." A verb of the third person singular without a nominative case expressed is often used in this book when sometimes theJE deleted "antecedent." nominative case understood is God, sometimes Job.JE deleted "and yet the antecedent is not expressed." (Here see my note on Lamentations 4:15.)This is a later interlineation. See Job 35:15. Or the words might be well rendered thus. "He is watched for at the grave." For as Bp. Kidder observes (Demonstration of the Messiah, Pt. II, pp. 28–29), "It is common among the sacred writers, that an active verb, that hath no person going before it, is to be understood as a passive or impersonal," as Luke 12:20, "This night do they require thy soul."Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 28–29.

Job 22:2.] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 231–32.

Job 22:4. "Will he enter with thee into judgment?"] SSS.Ibid., col. 233.

Job 22:12.] This verse shows that the heaven of the blessed, the heaven that is the dwelling place, or house, or temple of God, is the highest of the heavens. God is "in the height of heaven," i.e. according to the idiom of the language, in the highest part of heaven, and that this heaven is above the stars, and yet in the upper parts of our atmosphere, as some have supposed.

Job 22:16.] Their foundation is mentioned because they were in great outward prosperity, as Job once had been (See Job 22:18.), and they trusted that their foundation stood strong. They blessed themselves in their hearts that they should never be in adversity, but the destruction God brought upon them showed the foundation of their prosperity to be sandy. And what then happened to them was a representation of that which is spoken of, Matthew 7:26–27.

"Foundation." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 238–39.

Job 22:19.] See Revelation 18:20.

-- 446 --

Job 22:20. "The remnant of them the fire consumeth."] Here may probably be some reference to the destruction of Sodom and the neighbor cities, the next remarkable judgment that followed the flood, destroying the ungodly.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 240–41.

Job 22:24. "Ophir."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 243.

Job 23:8–9.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 249–50.

Job 23:12.] By this it appears that the people of God had the word of God, or the mind and will of God, made known by revelation for their rule before the church enjoyed a written revelation for their standing rule.

Job 23:14. "And many such things."] SSS.Ibid., col. 252.

Job 24:1. "Times are not hidden."] I.e. seeing he knows the state of things. So the phrase, "knowing the times," is used (Daniel 2:21, and Daniel 7:25; 1 Chronicles 12:32; and Esther 1:13; Psalms 31:15). "Not see his days." I.e. days wherein God shall manifest himself in behalf of his people, days of the divine favor, or days wherein God shall interpose in a visible manner as ruler and judge, days of his kingdom wherein the state of things shall visibly be under him and ordered for him. Psalms 77:10, "I will remember the years of the right hand of the Most High."

Job 24:2–8.] Job here has respect to two sorts of unrighteous ones. 1. Tyrants, or those that do wrong under pretense of authority (Job 24:1–4). 2. He speaks of robbers, and rapparees, and those that do wrong by downright force, as the bands of the Sabeans and Chaldeans which had lately plundered him. Among the Arabians, children of the East, Job's country, there were those that lived by spoil and rapine, making incursions upon their neighbors, and robbing travelers. "Behold, as the wild asses in the desert" Job 24:5]. These robbers were like wild asses, untamed, untractable, unreasonable—Ishmael's character. Genesis 16:12, "He shall be a wild man." The word properly signifies a wild ass-man. They choose the desert that

-- 447 --

they may be lawless and unsociable, and that they may have opportunity of doing the more mischief. "They go forth to their work, rising betimes for a prey." Robbing is their trade which they follow, as the husbandman does his labor; and therefore they get up early, and go forth to it as their work. "The wilderness yieldeth food for them and their children." Not the fields, but the wilderness, i.e. the roads through the wilderness. "They reap every one his corn," etc. Job 24:6]. They not only rob travelers, but make incursions upon their neighbors' fields and vineyards, and rob them. "They cause the naked" Job 24:7], travelers whom they have stripped, to lodge without clothing, etc.

Or perhaps in these words, Job 24:5, "The wilderness yieldeth food for them and their children," the relative may belong to the remote antecedent, viz. the poor and needy, spoken of in the foregoing verse, who, being robbed of their food, are forced to seek it in the wilderness, to live on herbs, roots, etc. See Job 30:3–4.

Job 24:5.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 256–57.

Job 24:14.
