"The murderer rising with the light killeth the poor and needy."] The poor, who are obliged to get up and go about their business very early to get a livelihood, the murderer watches and kills 'em as soon as they come abroad, that he may do with the greater secrecy, being concealed in the twilight.

Job 24:18. "He is swift as the waters."] I.e. as the waters swiftly hasten to the sea, so he is making haste to destruction. "He beholdeth not the way of the vineyards." I.e. the way to life, comfort, and joy. Here the broad way that leads to destruction is fitly compared to the course of the waters which is descending to the great abyss, and the narrow way that leads to life to the way of the vineyards which were wont to be upon hills, and where were their pleasantest and most reviving fruits which made glad the heart. Spiritual blessings are often compared to wine, andJE deleted "clusters of grapes." God's church to a vineyard, in Canticles and elsewhere. Compare Job 20:17, Proverbs 2:18–19, and Proverbs 5:5–6.

"He is swift as the waters." The instability of this present life, and of all earthly enjoyments, and of all the welfare of wicked men is fitly and elegantly compared to running waters that pass away, and particularly to the

-- 448 --

waters of the streams of Arabia (which Job and his friends were well acquainted with), that soon all run off, having no steady fountain to supply them, and therefore quickly left their channels dry. The instability and short continuance of this life is compared to this very thing in Job 14:10–12. "But man lieth down, and wasteth away. Yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? As the waters fail from the sea, and as the flood decayeth and drieth up, so man lieth down," etc. So Zophar, speaking how soon Job's misery would be at an end if he would turn from his sin, represents it thus. Job 11:16, "Thou shalt forget thy misery, and remember it as waters that pass away." This interpretation is greatly confirmed by the next verse. "Drought and heat consume the snow waters; so doth the grave them that have sinned" Job 24:19]. Those brooks of Arabia that so soon run off and dried up were mostly streams of snow water that flowed in the spring, but when the sun rose higher and shone with greater heat, they dried up, as is particularly observed in Job 6:15–18. Therefore when it is said, They are swifter than the waters, the meaning is their life and prosperity is more fleeting than the water, i.e. the waters of the brooks of Arabia, which is also confirmed by the last part of the same sentence, "their portion is cursed in the earth."This paragraph is a later addition.

Job 24:19. "Drought and heat," etc.] There is a like difference between the life and happiness of the wicked and the godly, as there is between the streams and puddles of snow water when the spring approaches and those streams that are maintained by living springs.

Job 24:20. "The worm shall feed sweetly on him."] The wicked are the proper food of death, which is well represented by death's feeding sweetly on them. See note on Job 21:32–33. See Psalms 49:14.

"The womb shall forget him." I.e. his nearest relations, his mother and brethren who were from the same womb. And his destruction shall be so total and perfect that it shall be as though he never had been brought forth or conceived in the womb. (See note on Job 8:18.) It is said in the latter part of the verse, "He shall be no more remembered." The womb shall forget him, from whence he had his life. It shall as it were reject him after it has given him life, as one to whom life don't belong, being unworthy of life. "The worm, or death, shall feed sweetly on him," as its proper food; or death shall embrace him as one that properly belongs to death.This paragraph is a separate entry.

-- 449 --

Job 24:23.] The wordsעַל־דַּרְכֵיהֶם וְעֵינֵיהוּ וְישָּׁעֵן לָבֶטַח יִתֶּן־לוֹ more literally translated are, "Though it be given him to be in safety, and he depends upon it, yet his eyes are upon their ways." I.e. though God gives these wicked [ones] that are so unjust to be in safety, and they, because God protects and preserves 'em for the present, depend on future safety, as though God took no notice of their wickedness, and would never punish it, yet God's eyes are upon their ways.

Job 25:1.] Concerning Bildad's aim in what he says in this short speech of his, see SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 267.

Job 25:2. "He maketh peace in his high places."] I.e. in heavenly places where he dwells in the midst of those numberless armies spoken of in the next verse. He causeth and maintaineth perfect peace there, and thither shall he gather together in perfect unity all things in Christ. And thence he commands peace for his people here below. He is the author of that perfect peace and happy love that is in that glorious numerous society above, and from thence he sends peace on earth.This sentence is a later addition.

Job 25:3. "Upon whom doth not his light arise?"] His providenceJE deleted "extends." and influence, his knowledge and his goodness, are universal; and the light of his gospel, the light of the Sun of righteousness, shall be upon all nations. (See Psalms 19.) And the light of his glory and love arises on all his heavenly armies. These things are shadowed forth by the universal shining of the sun.

Job 25:4. "Or how can he be clean that is born of a woman?"] No. 334.Works, 15, 318–19.

Job 25:5–6. "The stars are not pure in his sight. How much less man, that is a worm, and the son of man that is a worm?"] Which is not only small, weak, and impotent, but a filthy creature, bred in putrefaction, and fed by putrefaction.

Job 26:2–3. "How hast thou helped him that is without power," etc.?] As much as to say, You and your friends have been abundantly insisting in

-- 450 --

your speeches on the duty of pitying and relieving the poor and afflicted, and the great sin and dreadful punishment of those that oppress them, but is this your way of relieving the indigent and helpless? See note on Job 27:12.

Job 26:5. "Dead things."] Or the rephaim, which seems to [be] a word by which they signified the inhabitants of the infernal world, which, indeed, only are dead; and especially devils are meant. Giants in the Hebrew tongue are called rephaim,רְפֶאִים from rephau,רָפה which signifies to make weak, or to cause to faint or fail, because they were so terrible that they caused the hearts and hands of those that saw them to fail. For the same reason, the inhabitants of the infernal world are called by the same name because when men see apparitions of them, they are very frightful and terrifying. These are the same that are called "the destroyers" (Job 33:22). The place of their abode is called "destruction," here in the next verse Job 26:6]. They had this notion of old, that down in the lower parts of the earth was the place of these rephaim. To this abode, they supposed, descended the uncircumcised heathen and the wicked when they died, as Ezekiel 32:17 ff. And this is the place that is frequently meant by "hell" in the Old Testament as well as New. It may be special reference is had to the sinners of the old world that were drowned by the flood, the leaders of which were giants, whose spirits are now in prison. The same word is used Proverbs 2:18, and Proverbs 9:18, Proverbs 21:16.

There may be respect to whales, and crocodiles, and other water monsters which God forms from under the waters, which were, according to the signification of the word rephaim, terrible huge monsters.This paragraph is a later addition.

"Dead things are formed from under the waters, and the inhabitants thereof." Mr. Henry observes that "some ancient versions" render the word thus." Behold, the giants groan under the waters, and those that dwell with them."Exposition, 3 (1725), 85. Or the words might have been rendered, "Raphaim are wounded or pierced through under the waters," agreeable to the original.וְשֹׁכְנֵיהֶם מַיִם מִתַּחַת יְחוֹלָלוּ הָרְפָאִים (See Buxtorf.)Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum (6th ed. London, 1646), 712–13. "From under the waters" seems to allude to the waters of the flood under which the giants were destroyed in God's terrible wrath, which deluge of waters was a remarkable type of the deluge

-- 451 --

of God's wrath which comes on the ungodly in another world. The observing this is to Job's purpose, for as Mr. Henry says, "Is there anything in which the majesty of God appears more dreadful than in the eternal ruin of the ungodly, and the groans of the inhabitants of the land of darkness?"Exposition, 2 (1725), 85. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 270–72. The Job 26:12 confirms this interpretation, and also Job 26:13. See note on that v.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 26:7.] See no. 101.Works, 15, 79. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. For Job 26:12–13, see Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 275–76.

Job 26:12. "By his understanding he smiteth through the proud."] That is the way that God chooses for the baffling, bringing down, his proud enemies, to do it by his wisdom, foiling them, and confounding them in their own devices, etc., rather than a mere exercise of his omnipotent power by which he could, if he please, immediately and in a moment, destroy Satan and all the powers of hell without lengthening out the war against them any further.

Note on Job 34:20.This reference is a separate entry.

Job 26:13.] "By the 'crooked serpent,' the Hebrews understand the Galaxy or Milky Way." Dr. Owen, On the Spirit, Bk. 1, ch. 4, §7.ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΟΛΟΓΙΑ, p. 72. Owen's observation follows his declaration, "Now the Forming and Perfecting of this Host of Heaven and Earth, is that which is assigned peculiarly to the Spirit of God." The Spirit "garnishes" the heavens, making them "glorious and beautiful" (p. 71). See Sherlock's Use and Intent of Prophecy, pp. 213 ff.This reference is a later addition. Fifth ed., pp. 213–17.

"His hands have formed the crooked serpent." Itבּרִיחַ נָחָשׁ יָדוֹ חלֲלָה might have been translated, "His hands have wounded or tormented the crooked serpent," that is, the devil. The wordחָלַל translated "formed" is the same that is used Job 26:5. "Dead things are 'formed' from under the waters." (See notes on that v.) That the devil, that old serpent, that great leviathan, should be meant agrees with the foregoing verse. "He divideth the sea with his power; by his understanding he smiteth through the proud," which was remarkably fulfilled in dividing the sea, and destroying Pharaoh, compared

-- 452 --

to leviathan, the water monsters that are especially to be found in the waters of Egypt. Psalms 74:13–14, "Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength; thou breakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou breakest the heads of leviathan in pieces," where he is spoken of as the image of the devil. And this leviathanJE deleted "as compared to the water monsters of Egypt." is called the "crooked serpent" in Isaiah 27:1. "In that day [the Lord] with his sore, and great, and strong sword shall punish leviathan, the piercing serpent" (or "the serpent lying across like a bar," nahash bariach,בָּרְחַ נָחָשׁ the very same name used here) "even leviathan, that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea."

This is fitly subjoined to the former part of the verse, "By his spirit he hath garnished, or beautified, the heavens." For at the same time that God cast Satan down to hell, he purged and also beautified heaven, increasing the holiness and happiness of his elect angels, and at every time of Christ's remarkably overcoming Satan, and bruising his head, and beautifying heaven, and advancing his holiness and happiness, as when [he] rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, and when he shall destroy Antichrist, and at the end of the world. And 'tis not incredible that Job should here speak of such mysteries, for 'tis evident he now spake under the influence of the spirit of prophecy by what he says in the preceding verse concerning the dividing of the sea, etc., fulfilled afterwards. This interpretation is confirmed by Job 26:5. See note on that verse.This and the preceding paragraph are separate entries. This paragraph is a later addition.

Job 26:14. "Lo, these are parts of his ways."] "Or, as the original word more literally signifies; and may, I think, be more elegantly rendered; These are only 'the skirts,' the 'very outermost borders,' of his works. No more than a small preface, to the immense volume of the creation. From the Hebrew mar;?—extremitates. I cannot forbear thinking, on the extreme and very attenuated fibers of the root, when compared with the whole substance of the trunk; or on the exquisitely small size of the capillary vessels, when compared with the whole structure of the body." Hervey's Meditations, p. 129.Hervey, Meditations and Contemplations (4th ed.), II, 129, note. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 276–77.

"But how little a portion." Literally translated, it is, "how very very small a word."This sentence is a separate entry.

-- 453 --

"But how little a portion is heard of him? But the thunder of his power, who can understand?" The former wordsנִשְׁמַע־בּוֹ דָּבָר וּמַה־שֵמֶץ are literally translated, "How very small a word is heard of him?", as it were a small whisper. "But the thunder of his power, who [can] understand?" Itיִתְבּוֹנָן מִי גְּבוּרֹתָו וְרַעַם might have been translated, the "thunder of his greatness," or "glory," or "sufficiency." The word sometimes seems to signify as much as "glory," as Judges 5:31. "Let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his strength." But especially "greatness" and "glory," as appearing in a sufficiency for great and glorious "effects," as 'tis these that Job is here speaking [of], called God's "ways." In this sense we often read of the might of princes, as 1 Kings 15:23; 2 Kings 10:34, and 2 Kings 13:12, and 2 Kings 14:15, 2 Kings 14:28; and 1 Kings 16:5, 1 Kings 16:27; and 2 Kings 20:20; and 1 Kings 22:45; 1 Chronicles 29:30; Esther 10:2. What we hear of God's greatness is but a very little word, as a small whisper. Whereas if all God's greatness, power, and glory as appearing in all his works should be fully declared, it would be in comparison of what we actually hear as a mighty incomprehensible thunder to the smallest whisper. We are not able to understand the language of that thunder. See SSS.This paragraph is a later entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 276–77.

Job 27:5. "God forbid that I should justify you."] I.e. by doing as you do, that I should this way manifest my approbation of such evil ways, by speaking wickedness and uttering falsehood as you do.

Job 27:7. "Let mine enemy be as the wicked," etc.] Hereby Job expresses his sense of the miserableness of the state of an ungodly man, however he may seem to prosper, so that he could desire no worse misery to his worst enemy than to be as they. He don't mean that he wished his enemy such misery, for that is contrary to what he solemnly and expressly professes and swears in the same discourse (Job 31:29).This sentence is a later addition.

Job 27:12. "Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it. Why then are ye thus altogether vain?"] "Ye all have seen it," i.e. the things which I am about to declare of the punishment of wicked men and oppressors." You have all you in your speeches much insisted on this very thing as what you have clearly seen and been fully assured. Why therefore are you so very wicked,

-- 454 --

and why are you yourselves guilty of so great a degree of oppression of the poor and afflicted as you now see me to be? See in the beginning of this speech of Job in Job 26:2–3, and the note on Job 26:2–3.

Job 27:14–15.] Here is mention of three calamities which shall come on the posterity of the wicked: sword, famine, and death, i.e. pestilence. Buried in death, buried privately, and in haste, and without any solemnity, without being attended by their friends, as is common in the time of the pestilence and other great calamities. See Ezekiel 24:16, Ezekiel 24:23.

Job 27:19. "Gathered."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 282.

Job 27:20.] 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Job 34:20, Job 34:25; Matthew 25:6.

Job 28.] In the Job 27:11, Job had said, "I will teach you by the hand of God: that which is with the Almighty will I not conceal," which was an introduction to what he intended to speak on two things. First, the dreadful nature of sin, and the misery of the wicked, of this he spoke in that chapter, Job 27:12–23. Secondly, the preciousness of wisdom or true godliness, he proceeds to treat of this in this chapter.

See note on Ecclesiastes 7:24.This reference is a separate entry.

Job 28:4. "The flood breaketh out from the inhabitant." (In the Hebrew,מֵעִם־גָּד "from with the inhabitant.") "They are dried up. They are gone away from men."] Here seems to be reference to some of the brooks of Arabia, which at some time of the year brake out in some parts of that vast wilderness, where none dwelt to make any use of the water, and were "forgotten by the foot," that is, were neglected by the foot. Men came not to them, sought not after the water; and this were neglected and never made use of by men till that time of year came when they dried up. And if any came to the place where their channels were, they would find them dry, and the waters gone away. He mentions this as a mysterious work of God whose wisdom in his works is unsearchable, to the like purpose with Job 38:25–26. "Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of the waters, and a way for the lightning of the thunder; to cause it to rain

-- 455 --

on the earth where no man is, on the wilderness wherein there is no man?" This place is illustrated by Job 6:15–20.

Job 28:5. "Under it is turned up as it were fire."] I.e. that which shines like fire, as in Deuteronomy 33:2. The law of God, because it as it were shines and gives light, is called "a fiery law." See note in loc.

Job 29:25. "And dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners."] A king in army has very great power. A captain over soldiers says to one, Go, and he goes; to another, Come, and he comes; to another, Do this, and he doth it. They are all near him and about him, constantly attending on him, drawn up in order to be in constant preparation to observe his words of command without dispute or delay; and disobedience is attended with immediate execution. And a king in an army is peculiarly terrible, terrible to his enemies, and terrible to the disobedient soldiers. "As he that comforteth the mourners." By this contrast Job would set forth how great a terror he was to evildoers, to those that needed [terror], and at the same time how great a comfort he was to such as needed comfort. The literal translationיְנַחֵם אֲבֵלִים כַּאֲשֶׁר is, "As he comforteth them when mourning," or when sorrowful, i.e. as the king comforting his sorrowful soldiers. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 306.

Job 30:1. "I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock."] I.e. to have taken among the lowest of my servants, to have attended the sheep as the servants of my shepherds with the dogs. They were so vile, and barbarous, and immoral that they were not fit to be seen among my servants, nor fit to be trusted with any, even the meanest service, so lazy, awkward, raw, and brutish that they had not sense enough to do anything to purpose.

Job 30:2. "Old age was perished."] I.e. their old age was lost, had gained no knowledge or experience by living long in the world, were as raw and ignorant as children, and had now got past the age of learning. See SSS.Ibid., col. 307.

Job 30:4. "Mallows."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 308–9.

-- 456 --

Job 30:9–10 ff.] Vagabonds and others of the worst and vilest of men that infested human society now insulted Job, because as a good governor he had put the laws in execution against such.

Job 30:11.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 310–11.

Job 30:12. "They push away my feet."] I.e. they push me away as I go. They roughly turn me aside out of my way to make me give place to them. See Isaiah 32:20. That expression, "Turn our feet into the way of peace," is parallel.See Luke 1:79. This sentence and the preceding reference are a later interlineation. "They raise up against me the ways of their destruction." I.e. they rise up again and come against me in a way of malignancy and enmity, seeking mischief or destruction.

Job 30:13. "They mar my path."] I.e. by laying snares or stumbling blocks in my way, or something that entangle or incommode me as I go, and bring me into difficulty, that from thence they may take occasion to ridicule and insult me.

"They have no helper." I.e. I am so contemptible and so helpless, and little able to defend myself from them, that they are not afraid, any of them singly, to assault me that before was so much feared by a multitude. I am an easy prey to 'em. Nor are they ashamed to abuse me openly without anyone to appear to lead or defend them in it. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 312.

Job 30:14. "The desolation they rolled themselves upon me."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 312–13.

Job 30:15. "Terrors are turned upon me."] SSS.Ibid., col. 313.

Job 30:18. "By the great force of my disease is my garment changed; it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat."] The first part in the Hebrewלְבוּשִׁי יִתְחַפֵּשׂ בְרָב־כֹּחַ is thus: "By the greatness of power is my garment changed," i.e. God by his great power has stripped me of my glory and of my garments of joy, and has clothed me with grief, sorrow, and vexation as a garment. My extreme misery binds me about as the collar of my coat. The Job 30:21 confirms this sense. "With thy strong hand thou opposest thyself

-- 457 --

against me." The figure here used is much like that in the Job 30:31.

Job 30:24. "Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave."] I.e. to rescue men from death. Every man must die and be retained in the grave. The redemption of the life is precious, and it ceaseth forever. God will recover men from thence to live again in this world. "Though they cry in his destruction." Though they dread death never so much, when death comes, and would never so earnestly cry to be delivered from the grave.

Job 30:27. "Prevented me."] I.e. came unexpected. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 318.

Job 30:29.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 318–19.

Job 31:11. "An iniquity to be punished by the judges."] See note on Job 31:28.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 323–24.

Job 31:12.] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 324.

Job 31:13–14.] If I despise the cause of my man or maidservant when they plead with me, and when they stand before me to be judged by me, what then shall I do when I come to stand before God to be judged by him? God may justly do by me as I do by my servant. If I despise my servant's cause, how much more may God despise my cause. I am God's servant as they are mine, and much more inferior to God than my servant is to me.

Job 31:15.] This is a good reason why servants should not be trampled on for their mean condition, because the difference of condition between master and servant is not owing to themselves, but to God. 'Tis he that makes 'em to differ in their birth and circumstances of life.

"Did not he that made me in the womb make him, and did not one fashion us in the womb?"JE deleted "What Job probably has chief." And therefore I may be sure he will have respect to his interest as well as mine, will see to it that justice be done to

-- 458 --

him as well as to me, and take care that he ben't wronged. For he will have respect to the work of his own hands, and he looks upon it to be what belongs to him, to take care to maintain the rights of his own creatures and uphold justice among them. As we both have one Maker, so we both have one Judge. As he that made him made me, so we must stand before the Judge together, who will do impartial justice between us.

The last clauseאֶחָד בֶּרֶחֶם וַיְכֻנֶנּוּ of the verse might more literally be translated, "Did not he fashion us in one womb," or "in the womb alike?" I.e. he fashioned both in an human womb. We are made of the same human race, and [God] hasMS: "have." given us the same human nature, which more clearly shows the reason why Job should not despise and abuse his servant. In these two things are contained the most forceable reasons against the master's abuse of his servant, viz. that both have one Maker, and that their Maker made 'em alike or with the same nature.This and the preceding paragraph are later additions.

Job 31:27. "Kissed my hand."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 329–30.

Job 31:28. "An iniquity to be punished by the judge."] In the Hebrew,פְּלִילִי עוֹן a "judicial," or "judiciary," or "judged punishment." This phrase used here and Job 31:11 seems to have been a phrase used to signify a very horrid and capital crime. For in the sense of our translation, it seems nothing to Job's purpose. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 330. Probably the word has no reference to the judgment of men, but of God, and means as much as a sin that peculiarly brings judgment or cries for vengeance, a phrase equivalent to our phrase of "crying sin." See Hebrews 13:4.

Job 31:30.] By this it appears that it belonged to the religion of the Old Testament as well as of the New that men should not wish evil to those that injure and hate them, and that it was agreeable to the known and professed principles of the saints of those times, which with many otherJE deleted "parallel texts." things is a very great evidences that the imprecations of curses to enemies we have in the Psalms and some other places are not of private interpretation, and are not to be understood as the expressions of personal

-- 459 --

resentments, or the penmen's expressing the desires and wishes of their own spirit. See "Miscellanies," under the word "Imprecations."This is a reference to JE's "Table" to the "Miscellanies," Works, 13, 137–38. See also note on 2 Samuel 1:17.

Job 31:31.] The "men of my tabernacle" were enraged at those that injured me. They longed to revenge the wrong. I had difficulty to restrain 'em, as David restrained Abishai from revenge when Shimei cursed him [2 Samuel 16:11.]

Job 31:34. "Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me?"] In those early days great account was made of men's pedigree, and they were kept with care. And when men's lives were so long, great numbers of the descendants of one living ancestor were alive at once, so that those that were called a family were commonly a great multitude. Job declares that he was not deterred from doing justice in his office of a judge through fear of the great multitude that were of the family of him that was to be condemned or displeased in the judgment.

Job 31:37. "As a prince."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 335.

Job 31:39. "Lose their life."] SSS.Ibid.

Job 32:8.] By the spirit that is in man, Elihu seems not to intend the soul of man, but the spirit. And the words might as well have been rendered, "But the spirit is in man."

Job 33:21. "Neither let me give flattering titles unto men."] I.e. let me not from fear or from respect of your persons, because you are my superiors, flatter or compliment you as though I approved of what you say or do, though I know it to be utterly wrong and unjust. There is much of this sort of flattery of great men in the world, which, Elihu expresses his sense, how provoking it is to God.

Job 33:6–7.] God, being about to appear to speak to Job in his awful majesty, in the first place sent Elihu, a man as he was, according to his wish that there might be no appearance, as though God would overwhelm Job by

-- 460 --

majesty and terror without giving him fair opportunity, as he desired to plead his cause with one that he need not be afraid of.

Job 33:14–16.] See no. 115.Works, 15, 83.

Elihu endeavors to adapt his discourse to the present case. He supposes that God might have thus spoken to Job in a dream, or vision, or some other way, that he did take due notice to reclaim from something displeasing and offensive to him. And therefore God now exercised him with sore affliction to open his ears, and bring him to consider and take notice of his mind and will signified to him. And he hoped he might now do the part of such a messenger or interpreter as that which he speaks of, Job 33:23, to lead into proper reflections, and a right understanding and improvement of the hand of God. And then he hoped that would be fulfilled concerning him spoken of in the Job 33:24 and following verses. And, indeed, so it proved. Elihu thus did the part of a messenger or interpreter first, and the Son of God after him, whereby Job was brought to himself, and so was delivered.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 33:18. "Perishing by the sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Job 33:22. "To the destroyers."] See Job 26:5.

"Destroyers." Psalms 17:4, no. 298.This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 15, 272.

Job 33:23.] By the "messenger" and "interpreter" here Mr. Boston understands Christ, who is "the messenger of the covenant of peace, the great interpreter of God's counsels of love to sinners, 'one among a thousand' [Ecclesiastes 7:28], 'one chosen out of the people' (Psalms 89:19), 'the chief among ten thousands'" [Canticles 5:10]. The wordמֵליץ translated "interpreter" might have been rendered "orator" or "an eloquent person," and this especially as the word is here brought in well agrees with Isaiah 50:4–6. He "hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary." "To show unto man his uprightness," Mr. Boston interprets of Christ's showing unto man his righteousness.Thomas Boston, Human Nature in its Fourfold State (4th ed., Edinburgh, 1744), 245. Boston (1677–1732) was a Scottish Calvinist divine trained at Edinburgh University. The wordיָשְׁרְוֹ here translated "uprightness" is very much of the

-- 461 --

same signification with that which is commonly translated "righteousness." Christ's work is to show his righteousness, and so to comfort the sinner after the sinner is convinced of sin and humbled, as he is here represented. The next verse confirms this interpretation. "Then he is gracious to him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit. I have found a ransom," or "an atonement" (as in the margin).I.e. margin of the KJV. Christ is that messenger in whom God finds an atonement, and that righteousness for the sake of which he delivers from going down to the pit.This remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. See Hervey's Dialogues, vol. 2, p. 335, margin.Hervey's reflections on the book of Job identify Christ as the "Messenger of the Covenant," that one of "most meritorious Uprightness, on which alone a Sinner may depend, both for temporal and eternal Salvation," who is responsible for "Deliverance from the Pit of Perdition" (Dialogues, 2, 335–36). This messenger had Abimelech when he was chastised (Genesis 20:3 ff.). See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 353–55.

Job 33:26. "Render unto man his righteousness."] SSS.Ibid., col. 356.

Job 33:29.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 357–58.

Job 34:12–13. See note on Genesis 18:25.

Job 34:17.] See note on Genesis 18:25.

Job 34:20.] Remarkably fulfilled when the first-born was slain, as there are several things in this book in which the Spirit, that in the general directed in the forming of the speeches of Job and his friends, either in them or others, which they borrowed these sayings from, had respect to those great things, which were accomplished when the children of Israel were brought out of Egypt and led to Canaan. See Job 26:12; Job 38:22–23; Job 9:7.

"At midnight." See Job 34:25, and Job 36:20, and Job 27:20; Matthew 25:6; 1 Thessalonians 5:2.

Job 34:30. "Lest the people be ensnared."] I.e. lest God's people or his elect be ensnared or offended, and ruined by overbearing temptation to sin.

Job 34:37. "Clappeth his hands."] SSS.Ibid., col. 375.

-- 462 --

Job 35:1.] SSS.Ibid., col. 376.

Job 35:4.] Elihu, in the Job 34:8–9, had charged Job with "going in company," or making himself a companion with "wicked [men]," in such saying that it is no profit to a man that he is righteous, etc., as here, Job 35:3. 'Tis these companions that Elihu means that he "will answer" with Job, those that said thus as he did, and that he went in company with.

"I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee." 'Tis as much as to say, In what I shall say in answer, I shall direct myself to thee, and also to thy companions, as proper to be taken notice of by you both, and what may be matter of satisfaction to both [of] you, as to those things you have been disputing hitherto without satisfaction to either. See SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 376–77.

Job 35:5–8 ff.] Elihu's argument with Job is that Job said it was no advantage to him that he was righteous. God required him to [do] such and such things without any benefit to him. He dealt no better by him than he did by others that neglected to obey him. But Elihu argues that it must be men's benefit that God aims at in his commands, because it must be either the creature's or his own. But it can't be his own, for he can receive no benefit by the creature's righteousness, nor damage by his sin. And so it is impossible God should be under any temptation to do the creature wrong, as he must aim at some benefit either to himself or men. It must be men's benefit, and not his own, that he aims at.

Job 35:9–10.] In these two verses Elihu seems to have respect to two things. 1. In Job 35:9 he has respect to what he himself had just now said in the foregoing verse, that man's "wickedness may hurt man," as the wickedness of oppressors. But then his mentioning the wickedness and cruelty of oppressors puts him in mind of something that Job had said of the cruelty of oppressing the innocent, and God's letting them alone, and not appearing either to punish the oppressor or relieve the oppressed when they cry to him, as particularly, Job 24:12. "Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded crieth out. Yet God layeth not folly to them." And therefore,

2. Elihu in the Job 24:10 has respect to this objection JobMS: "God." had made

-- 463 --

against divine providence, and answers. His answer is that it is true the oppressed cry out of oppression, but they don't inquire after God. Their affliction don't drive [them] to God, etc.

Job 35:15. "Yet he knoweth it not in great extremity."] The literal translationמְאֹד בַּפַּשׁ וְלְאֹ־יָדַע is, "Yet he knoweth not in great abundance," or "fullness." The meaning seems rather to be that although God has visited Job in his anger for not trusting in him, as in the foregoing verse, yet Job did not know, did not receive instruction by the divine chastisement, was not corrected by it in his great self-sufficiency, or in his confidence of his own abundance, i.e. of righteousness, wherein he was in his own eyes rich and increased with goods, etc. The wordמְאֹד translated "extremity" is a Chaldaic word that properly signifies health, fatness, and good habitude. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 381–82.

Job 36:3. "I will fetch my knowledge from afar."] I.e. I won't speak from a slighty overly view of things, but from a deep and thorough consideration, looking to the bottom of things, not judging of things from the next and most outward appearance.

Job 36:4. "He that is perfect in knowledge is with thee."] I.e. he that now had to deal with thee to instruct thee, and reprove thee, is not a poor, imperfect, ignorant, raw, young man, as you may look upon me, but he that is perfect in knowledge, inasmuch as I speak by the inspiration of God. Therefore in my reasoning with thee, thou art to look upon that God, who is perfect in knowledge in reasoning with thee.

Job 36:5.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 384–85.

Job 36:12. "Perish by the sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Job 36:14.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 387–88.

Job 36:20.] The "night," when God cuts off wicked men, for "a tempest steals them away in the night" (Job 27:20), and their punishment is often represented as coming on the wicked in the night. Don't desire it, i.e. don't

-- 464 --

act as if you desired it. Don't bring it upon you. Wicked men are represented as choosing and loving death.

Job 36:22. "Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him?"] In order to our being led to the sense of the words, they ought to have been translated, "Behold, God exalteth himself in his power," etc. The design of the words is to signify that God is absolutely perfect in power and wisdom, and is both supreme and independent, not needing the help of any, nor the instruction of any; but that he is the fountain of all power and wisdom. This agrees with the context.

The former part of the verse might as well have been translated, "He is exalted in his power." And the import of the phrase in the latter part of the verse seems to be only this, that "God is above all in wisdom."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 36:27. "According to the vapor thereof."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 395–96.

Job 36:27–28 ff., from hence to the end of the Job 37.] Elihu concludes his discourse with Job with observations and improvements of God's wondrous works on the clouds, rain, lightning, and thunder. It appears to me probable that the occasion of it was the appearance at a distance of the clouds, and lightning, and thunder of the storm that was then approaching, out of which God spake to Job. There was nothing in Elihu's foregoing discourse that seemed to lead him to it. 'Tis true that he was in the foregoing verses speaking of the greatness of God and his works, but there seems nothing that led him thus suddenly to begin about the clouds and rain in this Job 36:27. But if there then appeared to them a thunderstorm arising, that will easily account for it why he, when speaking of God's greatness, should insist on this rather than any other of God's works. The Job 36:30 seemsMS: "Seem." to confirm this. "Behold, he spreadeth light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea." The manner of expression, his calling on Job to behold, agrees with the supposition that the thing was then appearing that he was speaking [of]. And the description here given, "He spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the roots of the sea," as it is in the original,כִּסָה הַיָּם וְשָׁרְשֵׁי אוֹרוֹ עָלָיו פָּרַשׂ agrees exactly with the appearance of a thunderstorm's appearing as arising above the horizon, for the top of the clouds in such

-- 465 --

cases are commonly all spread over with an exceeding brightJE deleted "and majestical." light. Thus God spreads his light upon it. And the lower part of a storm that appears thus rising seems to cover the utmost confines and extreme parts of the sea that are next the horizon, that are here called the roots of the sea, which may elegantly be so called according to the notion they then had of the world as being a flat, and that there was first the land, and after that the sea, which they supposed bounded by the horizon, or the meeting of the firmament with the waters. See no. 149.Works, 15, 93. He certainly here speaks of a thunderstorm as it is when rising and approaching, whether there was then one approaching, or no. By the Job 36:30 and also the Job 36:32 and Job 36:33, having first observed how the cloud appears on the top of it, covered with light, and how the bottom covers the roots of the sea, he next observes how it is as it advances higher and comes nearer, how the cloud interposes between the sun and the earth, and hides its light, and how the thunder grows louder, and the notice the cattle seem to show of it. And in the beginning of the Job 37, Elihu seems to speak of what then appeared. "At this also my heart trembleth, and is moved out of its place. Hear attentively the noise of his voice," etc. And it was not the only instance of God's speaking out of a storm of rain and thunder, for so he did at Mt. Sinai. See notes on Psalms 68:8. See SSS on Job 38:1.

Job 36:29–30.] Here the clouds are represented as being spread out over the concave of the heavens, as the covering of a tabernacle, which come down as curtains and cover the utmost edge of the sea, which is the uttermost part of the pavement or ground of the tabernacle. Here the clouds are represented as one covering, and the light another, spread out upon it. As in the tabernacle built in the wilderness, there were various coverings, one without another.

Elihu probably has respect to the cloud as it now appeared. The clouds of a thunderstorm, when rising, appear at top spread over with a bright light, and at the bottom covering the utmost ends of the earth or sea.

Job 36:30.] See no. 149.Ibid.

Job 37:4. "He will not stay them."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 403.

-- 466 --

Job 37:7.] He seals up the hand of men from their work, that they have leisure and opportunity to consider his work appearing in these things.

Job 37:11. "He scattereth his bright cloud."] In the Hebrew,אוֹרוֹ עֲנַן "the cloud of his light," i.e. the cloud of his lightning. So the lightning is called, Job 37:3. The word there in the original is the same as here. See SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 406–7.

Job 37:18. "Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?"] The sky is in effect solid and firm. The ends and effects are the same as if the sky were a vault of irrefragable and impenetrable strength. It remains the same, unaltered with its beautiful azure undecayed, and with the same golden studs unaltered from age to age, through all changes and revolutions whatever—mighty storms, whirlwinds, hurricanes, thunders, and lightnings. There are all the mighty changes of heat and cold, earthquakes, volcanos, etc.

Job 37:20.] SSS.Ibid., col. 412.

Job 37:21–24.] "Elihu here speaks concisely and in haste, because it should seem he perceived that God was about to take the work into his own hands.… He observes, that God who hath said he will "dwell in the thick darkness" [2 Chronicles 6:1], and make that "his pavilion" [Psalms 18:10], is in that awful chariot advancing towards them, as if he were preparing his throne for judgment, surrounded with clouds and darkness (Psalms 97:2–9). He saw the cloud with a whirlwind in the bosom of it, coming out of the south [Job 37:9], but now it hung so thick, so black over their heads, that they could none of them see the bright light, which just before was in the clouds. The light of the sun was now eclipsed; this minded him of the darkness, by reason of which he could not speak (Job 37:19), and made him afraid to go on (Job 37:20). Thus the disciples feared when 'they entered into the cloud' (Luke 9:34). Yet he looks to the north, and sees it clear that way [Job 37:22]. And he expects that the wind will pass and cleanse them Job 37:21]. And then 'fair weather will come out of the north' Job 37:22], and all will be well. God will not always frown, nor contend forever." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 111.

Elihu, by the last observation of fair weather's succeeding the dark

-- 467 --

cloud, would signify to Job that so there is hope that he again may see prosperity after his great affliction, and that "heI.e. God. will not afflict," as in Job 37:23.

Job 37:24. "He respecteth not any that are wise of heart."] SSS.Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 414–15.

Job 38-41.] The manner of God's reasoning with Job in these chapters is agreeable to Elihu's observation, Job 33:12–13. "God is greater than man.… He giveth not account of any of his matters."

Job 38:1. "Out of the whirlwind."] The word in the originalהַסְּעָרָה don't only signify "whirlwind," but "storm" or "tempest."

See notes on Job 36:27–28 ff.This reference is a separate entry.

Job 38:7.] How the inhabitants of heaven, their beholding the progress of the work of redemption on earth, and rejoice in it, may hence be argued, see "Miscellanies," no. 811.Works, 18, 520–22.

Job 38:13. "That the wicked might be shaken out of it."] 'Tis probable that one reason why God says this of the morning is because he has in his eye that glorious morning of the light and prosperity of the Christian church, when "the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings" [Malachi 4:2], and God shall say to his church, "Arise, shine, for thy light is come, for the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee" [Isaiah 60:1]; which morning will be accompanied with that earthquake that we read of, Revelation 16:18, by which the wicked shall be shaken, of which morning the morning of the natural day is a type. What is said in the next verse is applicable to the morning of that glorious day more aptly than to the morning of the natural day, for though the face of the earth and the visible objects upon it are as it were turned, and changed, and put on a beautiful form at the rising of the natural sun, so that the sun is as it were the seal and they the clay, and they stand or appear as a beautiful garment that covers the earth, yet in the morning of that glorious day of the church when "the Sun of righteousness shall arise," the world of mankind, the inhabitants of the earth (which seem especially to be intended by the pronoun "they" in the verse), shall be turned or changed by the appearance of that Sun much more properly, as clay to the seal. They shall receive impression from him, as clay from the seal, and shall be changed into the same image, asMS: "as X." [the] 2 Corinthians 3:18. And Christ shall then put them on as a garment, as [the church] is often represented as Christ's garment. And the church shall then clothe herself with new converts, "as with a garment" (Isaiah 49:18). And what is said in the Job 38:15 is not properly applicable to the morning in any other sense than this spiritual sense, or to the morning of the church's day. 'Tis a confirmation of this explanation of these words that God, in other parts of this discourse with Job, has an eye to the future great and good things that he will do for his church. See Job 38:23 with notes.

"From the wicked their light is withholden" Job 38:15]. So it will be in the morning of the glorious day of the Christian church that light, that shall then shine forth, shall be withholden from the wicked. It will be darkness unto them. They will stumble, and fall, and won't acknowledge the work of God, or rather their light, i.e. the light of the godly that stand as a garment. The glorious light and prosperity of that day which the godly shall enjoy shall be withholden from the wicked, for they shall be slain early in that morning at the dawning of the day when the light takes hold of the ends of the earth. Then "the wicked shall be shaken out of it" (Job 38:13).

-- 469 --

The same thing is meant here that was typified by Sodom's being destroyed in the morning. See note on Genesis 23:24.

It may also be further observed, that what was called "the breadth of the earth" was the extent of the dry land in distinction from the sea, which has never yet been found out after all the late improvements and discoveries in geography.This sentence is a later addition.

Job 40-41.] In these chapters BEHEMOTH [Job 40:15], signifying land monsters or monstrous four-footed beasts, and LEVIATHAN [Job 41:1], signifying water monsters, are particularly insisted the rather, because they are images or types of the devil and perhaps of Antichrist, the chief of God's proud and haughty enemies, which are referred to in Job 40:11–12. "Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath; and behold everyone that is proud, and abase him. Look on everyone that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place." This is confirmed by what God says of leviathan in the Job 41:34. "He beholdeth all high things; he is king over all the children of pride." Behemoth is also spoken of as a beast of great self-sufficiency and self-confidence, in the Job 40:23–24. And that these mighty, terrible, and haughty beasts are mentioned to confirm what God had said of Job's insufficiency to subdue his proud and lofty enemies appears the more probable, because concerning each of these Job is put in mind how insufficient he is to subdue them. Job is put in mind of this concerning Behemoth. Job 40:19, "He that made him can make his sword to approach to him," implying that there are not sufficient for this. So concerning the leviathan, in the Job 41:11. So Job 41:25–30. See SSS on Job 40:9, as

-- 471 --

reckoned there, but Job 40:14 in our version.Ibid., col. 460. The versification in the Hebrew Bible and the King James Version differs in sections of Job. Job 41.] By "leviathan" Job 41:1] is meant any water monster. It is a general term that includes various species. The crocodile is one species; the several sorts of whales are other species. The word "whale" in English is a general [term] that includes various sorts of creatures. The word "leviathan" in Hebrewלִוְיָתָן is yet of greater extent, and includes more species. Some parts of this description agree with one species, and others with others. See note on Psalms 74:13–14.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. "Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak."] "Not speak either as plaintiff or defendant (Job 13:22), but as a humble petitioner; not as one that will undertake to teach and prescribe, but as one that desires to learn, and is willing to be prescribed to. Do not upbraid me with my folly and self-sufficiency (James 1:5). Now he is brought to the prayer Elihu taught him. 'That which I see not, teach thou me' [Job 34:32]." Job 42:7.] Job's three friends were exceeding confident that they were in the right and Job altogether in the wrong. They were confident that they had truth and justice onMS: "of." their side, and that they were pleading the cause of God, and stood up in his vindication. They thought they had great evidence of it, and that God's saints of old were with them on their side in this dispute. And yet we see when God appears and comes to pass sentence, he chiefly condemns them, and in the controversy between them and Job mainly justifies Job. So now in controversies that are managed in religious matters, doubtless many may be very confident that they are in the right, and think they are strenuously pleading the cause of God, that yet will be condemned when God comes to judge. And yet those that God in the main will justify may much miss it in many things in their spirit, and temper, and talk, and behavior, and be truly unreasonable as Job was.

"My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." "They had wronged God in making prosperity a mark of the true church, and affliction a certain indication of God's wrath (Ecclesiastes 9:1). They had censured and condemned Job upon a false hypothesis, had represented God fighting against Job as an enemy, when really he was only trying him as a friend; and this was not right. It is a dangerous thing to judge uncharitably of the spiritual and eternal state of others, for in so doing we may perhaps condemn those whom God has accepted, which is a great provocation to him. It is offending his little ones, and he takes himself to be wronged in all the wrongs that are done to them.… God is very angry with those who despise and reproach their brethren, who insult over them, and judge hardly of them, either for their calamities or for their infirmities." Henry.This paragraph is a separate entry. Exposition, 3 (1725), 133–34.

Job 42:8.] See note on Hebrews 5:7.

Job 42:10. "And the Lord turned again the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends."] When he forgave their trespass that had injured him and called him an hypocrite, then God forgave him those sins he had been correcting him for. When he exercised charity to them in heartily praying for their good, then God opened his bountiful hand to him. Job was brought to this spirit by being humbled by what Elihu first, and afterwards God, had said to him. A deep humiliation for our own offenses

-- 474 --

against God will bring us to a disposition to forgive the trespasses of others against us, and our forgiveness of them is a proper expression of our own repentance which God waits for.

Job 42:11.] Probably the remarkable alteration that appeared in his spirit and behavior after God had humbled him, his amiable lowliness, submission, patience, meek and quiet and charitable spirit, was the means by the concurrence of a divine influence on their minds wonderfully to melt and draw their hearts towards Job, together with what his three friends might say to himMS: "them." after they were convinced to alter their minds about Job's affliction, which might cause them to repent their having so slighted his affliction heretofore. A conviction of their error might have influence to cause their hearts to be in the more tender frame now, and to be opened the wider towards Job.

Hence we may note, that makes the virtue itself a means of that which God intends as its rewards. Note also, that it is proper in doing deeds of charity not only to have respect to men's poverty, but to have respect to the greatness of their losses. Thus a rich man that has met with great losses may be more an object of charity than those that are as poor as he, that han't been brought to poverty by such losses. Job doubtless had much more given then, enough to make him equal with many of his poor neighbors.This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 1:6. "The way of the ungodly shall perish."] I.e. they lead to perdition. He shall perish that walks in them, the "way" being put for him that walks in that way, by such a metonymy as is used, Psalms 17:5. "Hold up my goings in thy paths," i.e. hold me up in my goings, and keep me from falling.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. Psalms 37:38, "The end of the wicked shall be cut off," i.e. the wicked at their end shall be cut off. Psalms 140:4, "Who have purposed to overthrow my goings," i.e. to overthrow me in my goings. This sense is confirmed by the next verse, "They have spread a net by the wayside." 2 Samuel 1:27, "And the weapons of war perished," i.e. by their perishing who use the weapons of war. Or this verse may very naturally and probably be interpreted thus. God in the judgment will own the way or works of the righteous. They shall be approved of by him, and found to glory and honor to be true gold; but the way and work of the wicked shall perish in the judgment, however fair it might appear. It shall vanish away, and all its seeming goldness disappear when it comes to be tried. Like shining dross, it shall perish when tried by the fire. 'Tis said, Psalms 1:5, the wicked "shall not stand in

-- 476 --

the judgment," and the reason is here given, viz. that their way will not stand in the judgment. His work shall be destroyed: the building that he hath built on a sandy foundation shall fall and perish, and he shall perish in it.

"Because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger." 'Tis pretty manifest that "the enemy and the avenger" here spoken [of] must be the devil, for 'tis evident the "babes and sucklings" here spoken [of] are mankind that God had put such great honor upon in and after his creation. And thereforeJE deleted "the scope and argument of the Psalmist requires." the import of what the Psalmist here declares of God's end in thus exalting mankind, requires that we understand "the enemy and the avenger" to be someone in natural capacity and strength vastly superior to mankind, and in comparison of

-- 478 --

whom men are but "babes and sucklings." For God's ordaining strength "out of the mouths of babes and sucklings" is to pour contempt upon the great and proud enemy and avenger, to conquer him and obtain a glorious triumph by so weak and despicable an instrument, and thrusting him down below babes and sucklings, and subduing him under their feet, and so causing his glorying to cease.

Psalms 8:5–9. "For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels." The Psalmist is here admiring and praising the wonderful goodness and condescension of God to man in advancing the human nature to such dignity and honor. Now the advancement of the human nature, or crowning of it with glory and honor, is twofold. There was that that was done at God's first work, when God first created man, whereby God gave him dominion over this lower world and the other creatures in it, herein making man but a little lower than the angels, those thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers above [Colossians 1:16]. And as man was made in the image of God, so hereby he had given him an image of God's authority and dominion. He was placed here as God's vicegerent, and hereby there was given a specimen and shadow of the second and greatest exaltation, which God designed the human nature for; which design of God probably had been declared in heaven among the angels before now, then now saw a specimen of it in man's dominion over the creatures. And

Secondly, the second exaltation, or crowning with glory and honor, of which this was but a shadow, is that which is performed in God's second work in actual uniting the human nature to the divine, whereby the human nature was exalted not only to an honor and dominion that was an image of God's, but actually toMS: divine ‹Gods›. God's honor and dominion, whereby he

-- 479 --

had indeed in the most extensive sense dominion over all the works of God's hands, and had all things put under his feet. That person in the human nature, that is the head and representative of the rest, is thus exalted; and the rest that are his members, and are united to him, are partakers with him in this exaltation.

Now the Holy Ghost in this place has respect to both these exaltations of the human nature, as it is exceeding common for the Holy Ghost to speak of the shadow and the thing shadowed forth, of the lesser and the greater, of the same kind both under one. He speaks most directly and expressly of the first, but he has an ultimate and perhaps a principal respect to the latter. I believe he has a principal respect to the latter in the Psalms 8:2, "Out of the mouth," etc., and that "the enemy and avenger" there spoken of is the devil, who can't bear to see the human nature so exalted.

These words in the Psalms 8:5, "Thou madest him a little lower than the angels," are spoken in different senses as they relate to man in his first creation and to the man Christ Jesus, but yet in both as a great work of bounty and condescension to the human nature or mankind.

Hence we may understand why the Apostle applies this place as he does, Hebrews 2:6 ff.

The first words in the Psalms 8:5 are spoken with a more special reference to man's first exaltation, and best agrees with that as where Christ, in the Matthew 24, prophesies of the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the world under one. There are some expressions do much best agree with the one, others with the other. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, sec. 2, (3), 2.Works, 18, 286–89. In no. 702 JE provides numerous examples in which the "creation of man" shadows forth "his new creation."

Psalms 11:6. "Snares."] I.e. this destruction shall come suddenly and unexpectedly upon them, while they are saying, Peace and safety; while they are eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and gratifying their lusts, as a bird that is securely feeding on the sweet bait, suspecting no harm nigh, and is suddenly caught in the snare. For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the earth." See also Matthew 24:36–39 and 1 Thessalonians 5:6. Psalms 16.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 617–29.

Psalms 16:3. "But to the saints that are in the earth."] Their being "in the earth" is mentioned, because hereby they were within the reach of his goodness. God was in heaven, and so far out of the reach of his goodness; his goodness extended not to him.

Psalms 16:4. "Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god. Their drink offerings of blood will I not offer."] Here is respect [had] to the customs of idolaters in offering "drink offerings of blood," and sometimes offering and drinking human blood. But as the psalm is prophetical, and as the Psalmist speaks in the name of Christ, the Spirit of God here probably has in view the cruel religion of the false, idolatrous, self-righteous church, which drinks and offers to God the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus, supposing or at least pretending that they do God service by killing their fellow creature, and shedding Christ's own blood, and the blood of those that are truly Christ's followers, as it was with the corrupt church of the Jews and the Church of Rome. The description of the persons here spoken of agrees with both those, viz. that they are those "that hasten after another," which the Jews did when they rejected Christ, and so rejected God as their Savior, and were set in their own way of trusting in other saviors, and sought another portion, had confidence in the flesh, trusted in their own righteousness, trusted in their false teachers, and were in earnest expectation of another messiah, and were in eager expectation of great earthly prosperity and glory under the messiah which they chose for their portion. The multiplying of the sorrows of these was remarkably fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem. All their sacrifices of beasts, and all their legal services, and legal righteousness, which they trusted so much in, which they offered with a libation of Christ's blood and the blood of his saints, could not save 'em from God's wrath which then came upon them to the uttermost.

'Tis evident that the psalm has reference to the persecution of enemies exercised against him in whose name the psalm is uttered.

Psalms 16:5. "And of my cup."] "It was customary among the ancients, to assign to each guest at a feast a particular cup, as well as dish; and by the kind and quantity of the liquor contained in it, the respect of the entertainer

-- 482 --

was expressed. Hence 'cup' came in general to signify a portion assigned, whether of pleasure or sorrow. Compare Psalms 23:5, and Psalms 11:6, and Psalms 73:10; Isaiah 51:17, Isaiah 51:22; Jeremiah 25:15, Jeremiah 25:17; Zechariah 12:2; John 18:11; Matthew 26:39, Matthew 26:42, and Matthew 20:22–23." See Doddridge's note on Matthew 20:22.Family Expositor, 2, 266–67. See SSS on this verse.This sentence is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 622–23.

"The Lord is the portion of mine inheritance," etc. As this psalm is concerning Christ,JE deleted "our great high priest." the Psalmist speaks in his name. So this is the more properly said, that which was said of the priests and Levites of old, "The Lord is their inheritance" [Deuteronomy 10:9], being true in a sense the most eminent and highest possible.

"Thou maintainest my lot." This is the most fitly mentioned because, as was observed before (Note on Psalms 16:4.), the psalm has reference to the persecution of Christ's enemies, who endeavored to deprive him of happiness, and make him miserable.These last two paragraphs are a later separate entry.

Psalms 16:9. "My glory rejoiceth."] The following reasons may be given why by "glory" here and in Psalms 57:8 and Psalms 108:1 is meant the soul. 1. This seems agreeable to the use of the same word in the originalכָּבוֹד in Genesis 49:6. "O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, my honor" (or "glory"), "be not thou united." Here the words "soul" and "glory" seem only two different words used to signify the same thing for eloquence sake, as is very frequent in the Old Testament. And so in Psalms 7:5, "Let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it; yea, let him tread down my life, and lay mine honor" (or "my glory") "in the dust." Here those three words, "soul," "life," and "glory" seem all to signify much the same thing. 2. So here in Psalms 16:9, "heart" and "glory" seem to be two words that are of like signification, as "heart" and "soul" are. And so again in Psalms 108:1, "O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory." In the originalאַף־כְּבוֹדִי וַאֲזַמְּרָה אָשִׁירָה the words are, "I will sing and give praise, even my glory," or "also my glory," which manner of expression are much moreJE deleted "emphatical." elegant and forceable, if we understand "even my soul" than "even my tongue." 3. The soul of man is much more properly his glory than his tongue. It was by his soul, that breath of life that God breathed into him, whereby he became a living soul, that he was set in honor above the

-- 483 --

beasts that perish. And he becomes "like the beasts that perish" because he understands not (Psalms 49:20). He don't improve the faculties of his rational soul, by which God made man wiser than the beasts of the earth and gave him more understanding than the fowls of heaven. God crowned Adam with glory and honor by setting him above the beasts in understanding and dominion. See Psalms 8:4. As Christ, the wisdom and reason of God, is called his "glory," so is the rational soul of man called his "glory."

But yet Acts 2:26 seems to show that by "glory" here is meant the tongue. I would therefore rather conclude that by man's glory is meant his logos, including both the internal and external logos, his reason or understanding and his word, as the Logos of God is his glory, the brightness of his glory. And sometimes man's glory is put chiefly for his inward logos, and sometimes for his outward.This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 16:10.] What came to pass with respect to the real body of Christ is what likewise comes to pass with respect to the church, the mystical body of Christ. It sometimes seems to be dead; it is brought so low that [it] is as it were hid in the grave. It is buried out of sight as if dead, but yet never will suffer it to be wholly destroyed. It shall not see corruption, and it shall come to life again. So it was with the church in the time of Antchrist. God's two witnesses were as it were slain, and their bodies lay dead in the street of the great city three days, and then came to life, and stood on their feet, and ascended into heaven, as in the eleventh of Revelation.

Psalms 16:11. "Show me the path of life."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 628–29.

Psalms 17:3. "Thou hast visited me in the night."] To see how I behave myself in secret, which is a much greater discovery of the heart than the behavior before men. "I have purposed my mouth shall not transgress." This confirms what the apostle James says, that he [that] bridles the tongue "is a perfect man" [James 3:2], and it is a good sign of his sincerity; and what Christ says, "By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" [Matthew 12:37].

Psalms 17:4. "The destroyer."] No. 298.Works, 15, 272.

-- 484 --

Psalms 17:8.] By "shadow" here is not meant the same as is signified by shadow or shade, according to the common use of the word in English, but thereby is intended no other than covert; as Isaiah 34:15, "Lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow." So an arrow, or instrument, is said to be hid "in the shadow of the hand," i.e. 'tis held or grasped in the hand (Isaiah 49:2 and Isaiah 51:16). So we read of coming under the shadow of a roof (Genesis 19:8).

Psalms 18:7–15.] The things here spoken of, God probably had at some time or times literally accomplished for David and against his enemies. He had at some time wondrously appeared on David's side in the time of battle, and fought against his enemies, when they were too strong for him and he cried unto him, with mighty thunder [and] lightning, as he did against the Philistines (1 Samuel 2:10), and as he did against the Egyptians at the Red Sea (Psalms 77:16–18), and as he did against the Amorites when Joshua was fighting with them. See note on Habakkuk 3:11, no. 208.Ibid., 131–34. And as he probably did against Sisera when Deborah and Barak fought with him. See note on Judges 5:20.Ibid., 140–42. And as Hannah prophesies that God would do for his people and "his anointed" [1 Samuel 2:10]. But David was God's anointed, the most eminently of all the temporal princes of Israel. It seems also that God had fought against his enemies with hailstones, with thunder and lightning, as he did against the Amorites when the sun and moon stood still. And particularly it is probable that God thus appeared and fought for David against the Philistines at Baal Perazim, in one or both those battles that he fought with them there, that we read in the latter end of the 2 Samuel 5. For both those battles seem to be fought in the same place, and the history gives us an account that God did miraculously there appear for David against his enemies (2 Samuel 5:20, 2 Samuel 5:24). And it appears very probable that God appeared for him with thunder, lightning, and hail, by Isaiah 28:21, where this instance of God's appearing against David's enemies at Perazim is mentioned as parallel with what he did against the enemies of Joshua at Gibeon: "For the Lord shall rise up as in mount Perazim; he shall be wroth as in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his work, his strange work, and bring to pass his act, his strange act."

Psalms 18:33. "My high places."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 648–49.

-- 485 --

Psalms 18:35.] "Thy gentleness," or thy humiliation or affliction. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 649–50. This teaches that the exaltation of God's people is by the humiliation and suffering of their Savior.

Psalms 19:4–6.] See no. 328.Works, 15, 311–13.

Psalms 19:5. "As a bridegroom coming out of his chamber."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 658–61.

Psalms 22.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 676–95.

Psalms 22:6. "I am a worm."] "The word,"תּוֹלַעֵת as Mr. Henry observes, "signifies a worm used in dyeing scarlet," which more livel[il]y signifies his suffering and dying state.Exposition, 3 (1725), 180.

Psalms 22:9–10.] In this verse there is probably a reference to the manner of Christ's birth being in a stable, where the blessed Virgin was alone without the help that is usual in time of travail. There she committed herself and the fruit of her womb to God, and received strength to bring forth by faith, as it had been by faith that she conceived, though she knew not a man. And also to the blessed Virgin's committing him to God, when Herod persecuted him and sought to destroy him, and God's wonderful preserving him on that occasion.

Psalms 22:10.] By this it appears that 'tis fit that God's people should give up their children to God in infancy, and also that by such an act of the parents God becomes the child's covenant God. Whence I would argue that these things ought to be visible: that which should be really by all God's people, should be visibly among them. It should be visible to the public that they do give 'em up to God. And then the public should look upon those infants as some of the covenant people of God; or which is the same thing, those children are actually some of the visible church. Nothing seems more reasonable: that a people that are devoted to the worship of a God should visibly give up their children to their God. This is what the heathen nations do, and certainly it is very manifest by the Scripture that

-- 486 --

'tis agreeable to God's will that his people should do so. And if so, then it follows from this text that when parents have visibly given up their children to God, they ought to be looked upon by the public as God's, or some of God's covenant people, or which is the same thing (as the Apostle expresses it), they are holy [1 Corinthians 7:14]

Psalms 22:14. "All my bones are out of joint."] This seems to be spoken of Christ in the time of his crucifixion, by the Psalms 22:16 and Psalms 22:18, and probably at that time literally fulfilled of Christ, his limbs being so stretched forth, and bearing all his weight on them so long, and his nerves and other ligatures so weakened and relaxed with extremity of pain, that it probably drew his bones out of joint. See how the rest of the verse was fulfilled, in notes on John 19:34.

Psalms 22:15. "My strength is dried up like a potsherd."] This was remarkably fulfilled in Christ, whose body was drained of its moisture and animal spirits by a gradual shedding of blood, and want of sleep, and continual pains of body and agonies of mind, from the beginning of his agony in the garden till he expired on the cross.

"My tongue cleaveth to my jaws." "The clamminess of the mouth is an usual symptom of approaching death. This was fulfilled both in Christ's thirst upon the cross (John 19:28), and in his silence under his sufferings." Henry.This paragraph is a later entry. Exposition, 3 (1725), 181.

Psalms 22:17. "I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me."] We must understand the person here speaking as stripped of his garments so that naked body appeared, as it follows in the next verse. "They part my garments among them." "His blessed body was lean and emaciated with labor, grief, and fasting, during the whole course of his ministry, which made him look as if he were near fifty years old (John 8:57)." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 181.

Psalms 22:20. "My darling" (or, "my only one," as in the original)יְחִידָתִי "from the power of the dog."] As these are meant by the Holy Ghost to be the words of Christ, by his "only one" here is doubtless meant the church. In Christ's soul's being delivered, the church was delivered, for he was not delivered as a private person.

-- 487 --

Psalms 22:26. "The meek shall eat."] I.e. of "my vows," or sacrifices that I have vowed, spoken of in the foregoing verse.

Psalms 22:29. "All they that go down to the dust shall bow before him."] Christ came to save from death, and he does as it were bring his people up out of their graves (Isaiah 26, Isaiah 29; Ezekiel 37). They are saved from a state of spiritual death and from eternal death, which they are condemned to; and he actually brings 'em out of their graves at the resurrection. Those that are thus saved shall worship Christ as their Savior from death, without whom they must have forever died; and therefore it is added, "and none can keep alive his own soul." And others "that go down to the dust," that are not saved, shall bow before Christ, as he will be their judge (Philippians 2:10). They shall bow before [him], as they shall be forced to be subject to his condemnation and almighty power in executing the sentence. He'll destroy them; they must "go down to the dust," for none of 'em shall be able to keep alive his own soul.

"Eat and worship." I.e. shall eat sacrifices; that was that eating, that worshipping.

Mr. Henry thus. "Even they that live in pomp and fare deliciously, when they have eaten and are full, shall bless the Lord their God for their plenty and prosperity."All three paragraphs are separate entries. Exposition, 3 (1725), 182.

Psalms 23:2. "He leadeth me beside the still waters."] In the original,מְנֻחוֹת עַל־מֵי "the waters of rest, or quietness." This seems not to have reference so much to the stillness of the waters as to the rest, comfort, and satisfaction which is found in drinking the waters, being such as greatly refresh and give satisfying delight. As Christ says, "He that drinketh the water that I shall give him shall never thirst" [John 4:14]. The word "rest" is sometimes used to signify such refreshment as one has in food or drink, and in gratifying the taste or smell. So in Job 36:16, "That which should have been set on thy table should have been full of fatness"; in the original,דָשֶׁן מָלֵא שֻׁלְחָנְךָָ "the 'rest' of thy table." The word is of the same root as in this place. So in places innumerable, the sacrifices which are called the "bread of God" are said to be "a savor of rest." See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 696.

-- 488 --

Psalms 23:4. "Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."] By God's "rod and staff" in this place seems to be meant two things. 1. The rod with which he that is here said to be comforted walks, the staff on which he leans and supports him in walking through this dark, difficult, and terrible valley, and comforts him as it supports him, and keeps him from stumbling and falling, which is "faith." The same that is often represented by a staff was typified of old by Jacob's staff and Elisha's staff. See note on Numbers 21:18. This may be called "God's staff," as it is a staff given by God; and so when it is said, "thy rod and staff comfort me," 'tis as much as to say, "the staff which thou hast given me comforts me."

2. Another thing meant is the rod in the hand of Christ, which he uses as a shepherd. Both these things are signified by Moses' rod. See "Notes on Scripture," nos. 195 and 442.Works, 15, 106–8, 524–25. Moses' rod was a shepherd's rod. It was the rod he was found with, or that he had in his hand, as he was feeding the flock of Jethro [Exodus 3].

Or as here are two words, "rod" and "staff." The first may signify the rod of the shepherd; the second may signify a walking staff, or faith. It favors this interpretation, that a plural pronoun and plural verb agree with rod and staff, which seems to suppose 'em to be two things.

Psalms 23:5. "Thou anointest my head with oil."] This may probably not only signify God's exalting him to glorious dignity, as God's saints are made kings and priests, but his testifying his love to him by giving a most friendly entertainment in his house, as this was one way in which they used of old to bid their friends welcome, to anoint 'em with oil (Luke 7:46), as well as spread a table before 'em, and give 'em a full cup.

"Anointest my head with oil." SSS.This line is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 697–98.

Psalms 23:6. "I will dwell in the house of the Lord forever."] "Being there not merely as a servant, or as a guest kindly entertained for a little while (see note on foregoing verse), but as a child adopted into the family. For as Christ says, "The Son abideth in the house forever" [John 8:35].

Psalms 24:5. "And righteousness."] I.e. the reward of righteousness, or a being treated as righteous. He shall be justified, accepted of God, and acknowledged and rewarded by him as righteous. See Psalms 37:6.

-- 489 --

Psalms 24:6. "This is the generation of them that seek him."] Therefore the promises that are made to them that seek in Scripture are to such as seek thus, viz. graciously.

Psalms 24:7–10. "Lift up your heads, O ye gates."] This is the will or command of God the Father. God the Father himself opened the gates of heaven to receive his Son after his passion in token of his great acceptance of what he had done.
