"Be ye lift up." This has respect to God's, or Christ's, triumphant ascension into heaven after a battle and victory over his enemies here on earth, agreeable to the representation, Psalms 47:5. The representation is of an entrance into heaven from the earth through that vault which is conceived as the pavement of heaven. And the doors are represented as opening upwards, raised or lifted up, when they are opened. And they are called upon to open as of themselves, or to lift up themselves, when the King of Glory [approaches], as most readily receiving the King of Glory as a most proper inhabitant, the rightful owner of the house, one infinitely worthy to be received. The very stones will as it were cry out, and a dumb ass speak, when there is great occasion. So the doors of heaven will open of themselves, when the King of Glory approaches.This paragraph is a later addition.

See no. 308.Works, 15, 281–83. SSS.Both references on this line are separate entries. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 703–4.

Psalms 25:9. "The meek," etc.] This was remarkably exemplified in Moses. See Numbers 12. Compare Numbers 12:3 with Numbers 12:6–8.

"He will guide in judgment."] I.e. into righteousness, or into the right way. This is agreeable to the use of the word mispatמִשְׁפָּט in the Hebrew Bible.This paragraph is a later entry. See Works, 21, 349–50.

Psalms 25:11.] His iniquity's being "great" is here mentioned as a reason why the Psalmist asks God to pardon him only for his "name's sake," and not for any worthiness in him.

Psalms 25:22. "Redeem Israel," etc.] Such passages as these in many of the psalms show that although the Psalmist speaks in the first person singular, yet he speaks in the name of Christ or his church, or rather in the

-- 490 --

name of Christ mystical. See Psalms 44:15, JE deleted "Psalms 22:26, Psalms 9:6, Psalms 9:8, Psalms 7:7–8, Psalms 11, and Psalms 11:38, and Psalms 28:9, and Psalms 40:16. Psalms 44:15." compared with the foregoing and following parts of the psalm. Compare Psalms 60:12MS: "Psalms 66:12." with the rest of the psalm.JE deleted "Psalms 10:17, and Psalms 12:7, and Psalms 32:6–11, Psalms 40:5."

For this reason David in many psalms, speaking of hisJE deleted "enemies." persecutors, represents 'em as heathen and aliens. So Psalms 54:3, Psalms 59:5, Psalms 32:8, and Psalms 9:5, Psalms 9:15, Psalms 9:19–20, and Psalms 10:16.

So David speaks of God's making known his dominion to the ends of the earth, or over all nations, by avenging him (Psalms 59:17).MS: "Psalms 59:17." JE marked this entire entry with a vertical line on the left side. The last two paragraphs of this entry are a later addition.

Psalms 26:12. "An even place."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 717.

Psalms 27:13. "Land of the living."] See note on Ezekiel 26:20.

Psalms 29:3.] Lightning and thunder is a very lively image of the word of God upon many accounts. 'Tis exceeding quick, and exceeding piercing, and powerful to break in pieces, and scorch, and dissolve, and is full of majesty.

"The voice of the Lord is upon the waters." Thunderstorms in Canaan generally come out of the west, from off the Mediterranean Sea. So perhaps the voice of God in his word in the latter days, of which this psalm seems to be a prophecy (see Psalms 29:1–2, Psalms 29:10–11), will probably come from the west and over the sea. See 1 Kings 18:41–46.This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 29:7.] The "voice of the Lord" here probably includes both thunder and earthquakes.

Psalms 29:10. "The Lord sitteth upon the flood."] There may probably be here an eye to Noah's flood, and things typified by it (not exclusive of the ocean and other floods). Mr. Henry observes that the wordמַבּוּל "is never used but concerning Noah's flood."Exposition, 3 (1725), 196. In the time of that flood probably were extraordinary thunders and lightnings.

-- 491 --

Psalms 30. Title.] David's entering into his house, where was his throne and where he reigned over Israel, was a type of hisI.e. Christ's. entering into heaven, and entering into his spiritual house, the Christian church, after his sufferings. And the dedication of David's house is a type of the new glory added to heaven by Christ's entering into it, and establishing and dedicating the Christian church. And therefore the psalm is accommodated to the latter event rather than the former.

Psalms 31:20. "In the secret of thy presence."] As it were in the holy of holies. See SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 741–42.

Psalms 31:22.] For the import of the wordחָפַז here translated "haste," see note on Psalms 116:10–11.

Psalms 33:18.] Psalms 119:166, Psalms 147:11, Psalms 40:3; Isaiah 50:10–11.

Psalms 34.] This psalm remarkably shows that a dependence on God for his protection and help should not cause us to neglect any proper endeavors, or the utmost use of our own strength and wisdom for our own preservation, deliverance, or any benefit we stand in need of. This psalm shows that David looked to God and trusted in him, when he was in such great danger in the land of the Philistines, and that God accepted his trust in him, and accordingly remarkably interposed and delivered him. "The angel of the Lord encamped round about him" Psalms 34:7]. And yet David made use of the utmost of his own contrivance and cunning for his own deliverance. "He changed his behavior," and "let his spittle fall down on his beard," and feigned himself distracted [1 Samuel 21:13]; and God made use of this as the means of his deliverance.

Psalms 35:13 "When they were sick."] "When Saul was ill and melancholy," David was his physician to relieve him, and probably not only made use of "his harp, but his prayers." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 209.

Psalms 35:16.] An hypocritical mocker is one that pretends respect out of mockery. Thus they that bowed the knee to Christ, and cried, "Hail, King of the Jews" [Matthew 27:29], were "hypocritical mockers."

-- 492 --

Psalms 36:7–9.] See "Discourse on the Doctrine of the Trinity," third sheet this mark ♀, p. 9.JE declares that God's lovingkindness (Psalms 36:7) "is the same with the Holy Ghost," which he also links with "the fatness of God's house and the river of his pleasures" (Psalms 36:8) as well as with "the fountain of life" (Psalms 36:9). He ties these verses to similar images in Ezekiel, John, and Revelation (Works, 21, 128). Compare these verses with Revelation 21:23–24, and Revelation 22:1, Revelation 22:5; and see note on Revelation 21:23–24. See note on Psalms 36:8.JE wrote the three sentences in this paragraph at different times.

Psalms 36:8.] By partaking of God's "pleasures," here is meant the pleasures which God enjoys, even in like manner as by entering into God's rest in Psalms 95:11, is meant entering into the rest which God enjoys, as the Apostle explains it. See note on Hebrews 4:5.

Psalms 36:8–9.] See Revelation 21:23 and Revelation 22:1, Revelation 22:5.

Psalms 36:9 "In thy light we shall see light."] We shall not only enjoy light, but thou thyself wilt be our light, as 'tis said, Revelation 21:23, "The city had no need of the sun, nor the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof." And Revelation 22:5, "And they need no candle, neither light of the sun, for the Lord God giveth them light." We shall see light, and not only so, but the light that we shall see and dwell in is thy light, the light of thine own glory that shines round about thee, which was represented by the light of the Shekinah. The Psalmist seems to have the light of the Shekinah in the temple in his eye, for he is speaking here of the pleasures and good things of God's house, as in the foregoing verse, the river of God's pleasure spoken of there is the same that in Ezekiel's visions is represented as proceeding forth from the temple (Ezekiel 47), and in the twenty-second of Revelation as "proceeding out of the throne of God and the Lamb" Revelation 22:1].The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. 'Tis God's light in two respects. 1. As 'tis the light of the glory that shines forth from God, 'tis the light of God's glory. And 2. 'Tis the light that God enjoys, the light in which he is happy. So the saints have fellowship with God in his happiness. The same is meant by the other expression in the verse foregoing, "thou shalt make them to drink of the river of thy pleasures" [Psalms 36:8].JE mistakenly linked an additional paragraph to this entry which belongs with comments on Psalms 72:6. It has been transferred to that location.

Psalms 37:6. "Thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment," etc.] I.e. he, by his treatment of them, shall openly and plainly declare his acknowledgment

-- 493 --

of that as righteous, and that in judging he justifies and accepts thee. See Psalms 24:5. "Thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noon day." I.e. though now it be a time of darkness and trouble, and be as it were a time of night with thee, as the foregoing verses imply, yet God will judge righteously between you and your enemies, and bring forth of his righteous judgment, or the fruit of his judgment agreeable to thy righteous cause (And this is frequently the meaning of the word "righteousness" as used in the Old Testament, and called "their righteousness." It signifies the righteousness of their cause in that strife their enemies have with him, as pleaded and manifested by God, their righteous judge.),This parenthesis is a later addition. as the light of the morning after your dark night that has seemed long to continue, yea, and shall at last bring the light to the brightness of noon day. See Psalms 46 and Isaiah 58:8.

Psalms 37:11.] The "meek" spoken of in this verse are those that don't fret themselves, that "rest in the Lord and wait patiently for him" Psalms 37:7], that "cease from anger and forsake wrath," that "fret not themselves in any wise to do evil" Psalms 37:8], spoken of in the foregoing verses. "The meek shall inherit the earth." This [is] accomplished in the glorious times of the church on earth, and proves that departed saints shall have the benefit and enjoy the glory of these times. See "Miscellanies," no. 811.Works, 18, 520–22. That which is spoken of in this and the two foregoing verses had its more immediateMS: "immediately." accomplishment in Solomon's reign, a type of the glorious day of the gospel church, when all David's enemies and all the enemies of the church were cut off, and were no more found. But the righteous inherited the land and the earth in a sense, as Solomon reigned over great part of the earth, and was honored and sought to by the whole earth. This was indeed to be in a "little time." See Psalms 72:7, and "Miscellanies," no. 871.Works, 20, 110–11. From hence we may infer that when those glorious times shall begin, God's people shall be brought off from censoriousness and bitter complaint of persecution, and other things inconsistent with meekness, that do now too much prevail amongst godly people and ministers. See Proverbs 10:30.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. "Abundance of peace." See Psalms 72:7 and Jeremiah 33:6.

Psalms 38.] By this psalm it seems evident that David labored under some very painful and loathsome disease in his loins, that was brought upon

-- 494 --

[him] as a punishment of his sin with Bathsheba, at the same [time] that Absalom rebelled against him, and he fled from him, and Shimei cursed him (which he seems to have respect to, Psalms 38:13–14), and Absalom defiled his concubines. This psalm, according to the title, is to bring that sin "to remembrance."

Psalms 39:7. "And now, Lord, what wait I for?"] I.e. I don't wait for any earthly happiness, for such things as are mentioned in the preceding verse, for which men are disquieted in vain. I don't wait for riches, which men heap up and know not who shall gather them. I don't expect happiness in those things that death will soon separate all men from, but "my hope is in thee."

Psalms 39:12. David asks mercy as a stranger, having reference to the law, often repeated in the Pentateuch, of showing mercy to strangers (a sojourner with thee), alluding to that which is said, Leviticus 25:23, "The land is mine, and ye are strangers and sojourners with me." See SSS.Synapsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 799–800.

Psalms 40:6.] See nos. 62 and 171.Works, 15, 67, 99–100.

"Mine ear hast thou opened." Rawlin on Justification, p. 87, observes that the word כָרָה, translated "opened," "signifies not only to dig or bore, but alsoMS: "more generally ‹also›." Rawlin reads "more generally." to adapt, fit, or make ready," which also appears both by the Hebrew lexicon and concordance.See Buxtorf, Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum (6th ed.), pp. 354–55. See also Taylor, Hebrew Concordance, I, entry 890 on כרךְ. So that if we suppose the word is here used so as to imply both these significations, they do the more naturally signify Christ's incarnation or taking on him the human nature, of which the Apostle interprets; for by that he willingly "took on him the form of a servant" [Philippians 2:7], and has his ear bored as such, and by that he had an ear prepared or fitted, by preparing a proper nature for him to receive and obey God's commandments in.This paragraph is a later entry. Richard Rawlin, Christ the Righteousness of his People; or, The Doctrine of Justification by Faith in Him. Represented in several Sermons, Preached at the Merchants Lecture at Pinner's-Hall (London, 1741), p. 87, note. The interpretation of Rawlin (1687–1757), an Independent minister at Fetter Lane, London, rests on the "easy and common figure of a part for the whole, by Christ's having his ear hollowed or framed, we are to understand his having a proper human body given him."

-- 495 --

Psalms 40:6–8.] See Isaiah 50:5–6.

Psalms 40:7. "In the volume of the book it is written of me."] See Matthew 26:54.

Psalms 45.] See the evidence there is that this psalm is no epithalamium relating to any marriage of David or Solomon, §46 of the "Prophecies of the Messiah," "Miscellanies," no. 1067.JE offers a detailed refutation of the notion that the person spoken of in this psalm is either David or Solomon. The account is "inconsistent" with David's marital history, and Solomon was never "a mighty hero in the field of battle and a great conqueror," as the object of this song is described. Furthermore, "the person here principally intended… is spoken of as one above mere men" ("Miscellanies," no. 1067, pp. 16–17).

Psalms 45:1. "My tongue is as the pen of a ready writer."] I.e. I am not any more at a loss for words and expressions than a ready scribe who writes from a copy, where all the words are already set before his eyes.

Psalms 45:7.] See no. 163.Works, 15, 97.

Psalms 45:8.] Ivory is a white substance, and these spices coming "out of ivory palaces" representMS: "represents." the same as Mary's precious ointment, perfumed with spices, out of an alabaster box. See note on Mark 14:3. Ivory is evidently used in Scripture as a type of spiritual purity by reason of its whiteness. So Solomon's throne of judgment was of ivory (1 Kings 10:18), to signify the righteousness and purity of his judgment, and righteousness of his government, as Christ is represented at the day of judgment as sitting on a great white throne (Revelation 20). The same may be argued from Canticles 5:14, "His belly is as bright ivory." And Canticles 7:4, "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory." By the "ivory palaces" is probably meant heaven. So SSS.This reference and the preceding sentence are a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 841–42.

Psalms 45:10. "Forget also thine own people, and thy father's house."] By which may be intended sin, and the pleasures and profits thereof, the objects of our lusts; which may well be compared to our father's house and natural kindred, both because sin and corruption is what we have naturally, that which we are born with, and that we derive from our parents. 'Tis that which we have by the first birth, whereby we are born of earthly parents, for "that which is born of the flesh is flesh" [John 3:6], and also because

-- 496 --

sin is naturally dear to us, as those relations that we are akin to by birth, that we are born of or amongst, and are nourished and brought up by and with.

By her "father's house" may be intended also this world, which is our native country. We are naturally, and by our first birth, of the earth, earthly. We must forsake this country in our hearts for Christ. See Ephesians 5:30–32.This reference is a later addition.

Psalms 45:13. "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold."] So it was with the tabernacle that Moses erected. Its inward clothing or curtains were of fine linen, embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet, coupled together with taches of gold; but its outward coverings were plain, of rams' skins and badgers' skins [Exodus 25:4–5]. The church is "black, but comely," outwardly of a mean appearance, "as the tents of Kedar," and inwardly beautiful and glorious, "as the curtains of Solomon" [Canticles 1:5].

Psalms 46:9. "He maketh wars to cease unto the ends of the earth. He breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder. He burneth the chariot in the fire."] We have a more particular prophecy of this, and of what is spoken of in that parallel text, Psalms 76:3–6, in Ezekiel 39:8–10.

Psalms 47:4. "The excellency of Jacob."] It seems as though the tabernacle and temple used sometimes to be so called (See Amos 6:8.), but more eminently that divine person who dwelt in the tabernacle and temple. See "Controversies Book."JE identifies the "excellency of Jacob" with the person "elsewhere called the excellency and beauty and glory of the Lord, and the glory of Israel." Then he adds, "But that which was eminently the glory and excellency of Israel, was that divine person who dwelt in the temple over the ark" ("'Controversies' Notebook: Justification," Works, 21, 386).

Psalms 47:9.] The angels, those principalities and powers, were "gathered together" to attend on Christ at his ascension and entrance into heaven. They were as it were his royal guard who as it were bore "the shields of the earth." As at a king's coronation in Israel, "the princes of the people," and their chief captains, and men of war used to be gathered together to attend upon the king to his palace and to the temple, probably bearing before him the public shields (1 Kings 14:27–28).

-- 497 --

Psalms 48:7.] See no. 16.Works, 15, 52.

Psalms 49:3–4.] See no. 17.Ibid., 52–53.

Psalms 49:4.] This psalm may be called a parable, and what it contains a "dark saying," because the main subject of it is a future state of rewards and punishments after death. This doctrine under the old testament was enveloped in parables and dark sayings. But Jesus Christ has "brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" [2 Timothy 1:10]; and the New Testament speaks of these great things not in dark speeches, but it uses great plainness of speech. SSS.This reference, which JE repeated on the margin of the Bible, is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 859.

Psalms 49:5.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 859–60.

Psalms 49:8.] SSS.Ibid., col. 862.

Psalms 49:14. "Dominion over them in the morning."] See no. 366.Works, 15, 356–57.

"Death shall feed upon them." See note on Job 24:20, and Job 21:32–33, and Isaiah 14:9.

"In the morning." SSS.Each of these paragraphs is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 866–67.

Psalms 49:15. "But God shall redeem my soul from the power of the grave, for he shall receive me."] The wordלָקַח "receive" here is the same with that translated "took" (Genesis 5:24). "And Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him," which confirms two things, viz. 1. That the souls of the saints do not die when their bodies die, but are received to a state of happiness in more perfect union and communion with God. 2. That the souls of saints at death are received to heaven, the abode to which Enoch, and Elijah,The following three words are a later addition. and Jesus Christ are gone.

-- 498 --

Psalms 49:18. "And men will praise thee."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 869.

Psalms 49:19. "Never see light."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 869–70.

Psalms 50.] This psalm is a prophetical description of the nature of that new dispensation that is in the New Testament so often called the "kingdom of heaven," including the whole of it from Christ's coming in the pouring of his Spirit after his ascension till the consummation of all things after his coming to the last judgment. This dispensation is a dispensation wherein the word of God is not confined to one nation only, but the law goes forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. From thence the light of the gospel shines forth to the Gentile nations into all the earth, "from the rising of the sun to the going down" of the same, which is prophesied of, Psalms 50:1–2.

Under this dispensation the Son of God comes to set up his kingdom on the world, and to reign and judge amongst all nations, which is prophesied of, Psalms 50:3–6. From the Psalms 50:7–16 there is a description of this gospel dispensation with respect to God's church and people, showing that the worship of God's church shall not consist in legal ceremonies and external forms, but in a spiritual service, as Christ says, John 4:21, John 4:23. "But the hour is coming, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.… But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth; for the Father seeketh such to worship him."

And nextly, the nature of this dispensation is described as it respects wicked men, when the church of God would be so constituted that visibly wicked persons should more effectually be shut out from that people that are called the Israel of God, that come and join in his visible worship (Psalms 50:16–20), and when God should bring more terrible wrath against wicked men (Psalms 50:21–22), and lastly, in the Psalms 50:23, what those things are that God looks at in order to acceptance. See SSS.This reference, which JE duplicated on the margin, is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 871–79.

Psalms 50:1. "Mighty God."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 872.

Psalms 50:2. "Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, hath God shined."] This is mentioned as a great distinction between the glorious new dispensation

-- 499 --

or revelation given in the days of the gospel of Jesus Christ, from that delivered from Mt. Sinai when God gave the Law in the wilderness. It is said, Deuteronomy 33:2, "He came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir, and shined forth from Mt. Paran, and came with ten thousands of his saints; and then from his right hand went a fiery law." But in the days of the gospel we are not come to Mt. Sinai, but we "are come to Mt. Zion, the city of the living God, to the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:18–22). Compare Galatians 4:26–27 with the context. See Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:1, Psalms 80:1.

Psalms 50:3.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 872–73.

Psalms 50:5. "By sacrifice."] SSS.Ibid., col. 874.

Psalms 50:16–22.] The Spirit of God, in what is said in these verses, seems to have a special regard to the scribes and Pharisees in Christ's time, and to the popish priests afterwards.

Psalms 50:21.] I won't let thy sins pass as little things not worthy to be taken notice of, as thou thyself didst, and was ready to think that I did, because "I kept silence." But I will by no means clear the guilty, or acquit the wicked. I am an "holy God" and "a jealous God"; I "will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins" (Joshua 24:19).

Psalms 51:4. "That thou mayest be justified when thou speakest," etc.] "Justified" in that "sentence passed upon him: 'The sword shall never depart from thine house,' etc. (2 Samuel 12:10–11)." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 248.

Psalms 51:7. "Purge me with hyssop."] "The expression alludes to the ceremony of cleansing the leper, or those that were unclean by a dead body, by sprinkling water, and blood, or both, upon them with a bunch of hyssop, by which they were at length discharged from the restraints they were laid under by their pollution. 'Purge me with hyssop,' i.e. with the blood of Christ applied to my soul." Henry.Ibid., 249.

Psalms 51:12. "Uphold me by thy free spirit."] The same that in the New Testament is called the "Spirit of adoption," and set in opposition to a "spirit of bondage" [Romans 8:15], which David's sin had brought him under.

-- 500 --

"By thy free spirit." The word rendered "free"JE deleted "in the original." נְדִיבָה signifies "voluntary, ingenuous, generous." The Spirit of God is a spirit of love and not of fear, and therefore disposes to an ingenuous, free obedience. Therefore the Apostle says, "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" [2 Corinthians 3:17].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Psalms 51:16.] The law of Moses made no provision of any sacrifices for such sins as David committed, nor accepted any sacrifice of beasts for them.

Psalms 51:18.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 888–89.

Psalms 51:18–19. "Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion. Build thou the walls of Jerusalem," etc.] Here the Spirit of GodMS: "David ‹the Sp. of G›." has respect to the accomplishing the work of redemption by Jesus Christ, which shall be accomplished for such vile rebels as David, not for any sacrifice, but of sovereign mercy and of God's good pleasure. When that time should come, then should a sacrifice be offered to God, which was the antitype of the sacrifice of bullocks, which indeed should be pleasing to God, and sufficient to atone for such sins as David's. And therefore it follows, Psalms 51:19, "Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices," etc. Note there was a typical accomplishment of this, which David prays for, when the temple was built in Jerusalem with its courts, and dedicated with such a vast number of whole burnt offerings, and God manifested his acceptance of the sacrifice by fire coming down from heaven in so wonderful a manner in the sight of all the people—and at the same time the city of Jerusalem [was] so fortified and beautified with many magnificent buildings by Solomon—which abundance of sacrifices at the building of the temple was a type of the greatness, preciousness, sufficiency, and infinite fullness of the sacrifice that was offered, when Christ was incarnate, and the temple of his body built (1 Kings 8:5, 2 Chronicles 7:4–5), and which the spiritual Solomon offered to God, whenMS: "which." the church, the spiritual temple of God that he built, was sanctified and dedicated to God. But this has its ultimate and proper accomplishment in the redemption of Christ, which so often [was] prophesied of under such figures as "building up Zion" [Micah 3:10], "building the old wastes" [Isaiah 61:4], etc.

-- 501 --

Psalms 52:8. "Olive tree in the house of God."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 893.

Psalms 58:1. "O congregation."] See Numbers 35:12 and Joshua 20:6.

Psalms 58:5.] I.e. that "will not be charmed," but will bite, notwithstanding any enchantment that can be used. See Jeremiah 8:17 and Ecclesiastes 10:11. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 916–17.

Psalms 58:9.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 918.

Psalms 59.] Concerning David's PRAYING AGAINST HIS ENEMIES. 'Tis evident by this psalm and several others that when DavidJE deleted "prays against his enemies." seems to pray against his enemies, the enemies that he speaks [of] are not his personal enemies. That however he takes occasion to pray, as he does from the malice of his personal enemies, yet that the enemies he has respect to in his prayer are principally not those personal enemies that give the occasion of his prayer, but they are the enemies of the church of Christ. He speaks as the head of the church and in the person of Christ, of whom he was the great type. Thus in this psalm the occasion of this prayer was Saul's sending to watch the house to kill him, as the title declares; but 'tis evident that the enemies that he prays against are not Saul and others in Israel that were his personal enemies, but the heathen, as Psalms 59:5 and Psalms 59:8. See "Miscellanies," nos. 600, 640.Works, 18, 141–42; 173–75.

Psalms 59:6.] They spent the daytime in pursuing him, and at evening they retired to some city. And there they spent the evening in reproaches, injurious slanders, and bitter invectives, which is compared to the spiteful barking of a dog. They "go round about the city"; that is, they go about the town into all parts of the city, filling it with the noise of their reproaches and exclamations against him, as though he were a man of ill designs and traitorous heart, etc., if possible to destroy his reputation and incense the multitude against him. See Psalms 59:14–15.This reference is a later addition.

Psalms 59:13. "Consume them in thy wrath that they may not be."] The title of the psalm shows that the occasion of David's penning this psalm was

-- 502 --

Saul's persecuting of him. Here seems therefore to be an imprecation of God's wrath on Saul to consume and cut him off from the earth. And yet when Saul was cut off from the earth,The next eighteen words and the following reference are later additions. how did heI.e. David. rend his clothes, and mourn, and weep, and fast for Saul as well as Jonathan (See 2 Samuel 1:11–12.); and how did David revenge his death on the Amalekites that slew him; and how did he lament Saul's death as the death of one that he greatly loved and was very dear to him in his elegy, which is a great evidence that David's imprecations of God's vengeance on his enemies in the book of Psalms are not the expressions or breathings of his own spirit, but prophecies uttered, prophetical curses denounced, by the Spirit of God. See note on David's elegy, 2 Samuel 1:17.

Psalms 59:14–15. "At evening let them return."] After they have been vanquished and utterly confounded abroad, when they return miserably disappointed. "And let them make a noise like a dog; let 'em go round about the city." "When they were in quest of David," and of God's saints, "they made a noise like an angry dog, snarling and barking. Now they make a noise like a dog in misery, howling and wailing. Those that repent of their sins when they are in trouble, mourn like doves. Those whose hearts are hardened when they are in trouble, make a noise like dogs, 'like a wild bull in a net, full of the fury of the Lord' [Isaiah 51:20]. See Hosea 7:14. 'They have not cried unto me with their hearts, when they howled upon their beds for corn and wine.' They shall meet with little relief. 'They shall go round about the city, and wander up and down for meat.'" Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 263.

Psalms 59:15.] Or rather, they will "wander up and down" to devour. See Hervey's Dialogues, vol. 2, p. 223, margin.Hervey, seeking to clarify an obscure passage, writes, "David, to set forth the barbarous Assiduity of his Persecutors says, They wander up and down, They pry into every Corner; they search the City, and examine the Country; לאבל not for Meat; which in this Connection, gives a very jejune Sense, and quite foreign to the Subject: but to devour. To devour me the destined Victim of their Rage" (Dialogues, 2, 223, note).

Psalms 60:7. "Ephraim also is the strength of my head."] See note on Ezekiel 5:1–4. Perhaps that we now call a king's life guard was then called "the strength of his head."This sentence is a later addition.

-- 503 --

Psalms 60:8. "Philistia, triumph thou because of me."] In the marginI.e. of the KJV. is "triumph thou over me." Here is a notable and strange difference in our translation between the expression here and in Psalms 108:9, The versification in the Hebrew Bible and the King James Version differ. In the former the verse is Psalms 108:10. though it be evident that there is a repetition of the same song. There the expression is, "Over Philistia will I triumph." The words in the original(Psalms 108:110) אֶתְרוֹעָע עֲלֵי־פְלֶשֶׁת (Psalms 60:8) הִתְרֹעָעִי פְלֶשֶׁת יָלַי are the very same in both places and in the same order, excepting that the word "triumph" here is in the second person imperative, and there 'tis in the first person future. And one vowel is different in עלי, "over," being paragogical, so that the manifest truth seems to be this. The very same thing is expressed in both places, viz. a prediction that God or Christ would triumph over Philistia. Only in Psalms 108, God speaks in the future tense first person, "I will triumph." And here, changing the person as is very common and speaking to himself by an apostrophe, he speaks in the imperative second person, "Triumph thou over Philistia." This is not at all strange nor disagreeable to the style of Scripture. 'Tis very much like that apostrophe in Judges 5:21, "O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength." We have just such a change of the person, from the first person to the second, where the person speaking speaks to himself, in Psalms 121:1–2. Or it may be as speaking to the church, or to Christ, or David, the same that speaks in the next verse. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 940.

Psalms 61:2.] "When my heart is overwhelmed," when the waters surmount my low stature and so overwhelm me, then "lead me to the rock that is higher than I," upon which I may yet be above the waters.

Psalms 61:3. "For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy."] This verse shows what was that high rock spoken [of] in the preceding verse.

Psalms 63:10. "By the sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Psalms 63:11.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 955–56.

Psalms 65:7. "Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves."] Many of the miracles of Christ are such as are mentioned in the Old Testament

-- 504 --

as the peculiar glorious works of God, as here the stilling the tempestuous sea, treading "on the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8), opening the eyes of the blind, unstopping the ears of the deaf, healing the lame, giving speech to the dumb (Isaiah 35:5–6, Isaiah 29:18, Isaiah 42:7; Psalms 146:8), raising the dead (Isaiah 26:19, Ezekiel 37:1), etc.

Psalms 65:8.] See no. 54.Works, 15, 66.

Psalms 68.] Concerning the removal of the ark as a type of Christ's ascension, see no. 319.Ibid., 297–302.

Psalms 68:8–9.] See no. 210.Ibid., 135–40.

Psalms 68:12.] "She that tarried at home" was the church of Israel.

Psalms 68:14. "White as snow in Salmon."] This has respect to the holiness of that generation that first entered into Canaan under Joshua. It was with the church of Israel, after she was brought out of her Egyptian bondage, and after God had fully washed away from her the pollutions of Egypt, as it is promised it shall be with the church, after she is delivered from her bondage under Antichrist and is fully purged from all remaining pollutions from that spiritual Egypt. To her shall be granted that she shall be clothed in fine linen, clean and white. See verse foregoing.

Psalms 68:15. "The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan, an high hill as the hill of Bashan."] Mt. Zion was but a small hill in comparison of the hill of Bashan and many other hills in the world, and appeared barren and mean in many respects in comparison of them, being a dry place, as the word "Zion" signifies "drought," whereas the hill of Bashan was very fruitful, and covered with flocks and herds. But yet with respect to the dignity which God had put upon, and the spiritual privileges that were annexed to it, it might be looked upon as the highest, the noblest, most fruitful and pleasant hill in the world. So the church of God appears to a carnal eye, low, mean, and contemptible in comparison of many of the great and mighty kingdoms and the magnificent and opulent cities of the world, but yet indeed is the highest, most exalted, most rich and glorious

-- 505 --

city and kingdom on the earth, being "the perfection of beauty" [Psalms 50:2], the city of the great king, an eternal excellency, "the joy of the whole earth" [Lamentations 2:15].

See note on Psalms 68:16.This reference is a later addition.

Psalms 68:16. "Why leap ye, ye high hills? This is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the Lord will dwell in it forever."] Though Mt. Zion appeared so small and barren, contemptible in comparison of some other mountains, it not only might be looked upon as really higher, and more fruitful and pleasant than they, but stronger and more stable. Other mountains, the greatest of them, are liable to be moved. They were greatly shaken, many of them, when God gave the Law; and "even Sinai itself was moved at the presence of the Lord" (Psalms 68:8). Yea, the time will come when the greatest mountains will, at the presence of God, skip like rams. But Zion, being the place which God has chosen to dwell in, and where he will dwell forever, never shall "be removed but abideth forever" (Psalms 125:1). Here God has fixed his everlasting throne which never can be shaken. The church of God, the spiritual Zion, though it appears weak and despicable, is the strongest city in the world. No city has such bulwarks. God is a wall of fire round about her. Salvation has he appointed for walls and for bulwarks. "God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved" [Psalms 46:5]. The greatest and strongest cities in the world come to an end and are overthrew, but this city shall never be destroyed. The people of Zion need not fear, "though the earth be removed, and the mountains carried into the midst of the sea" [Psalms 46:2].

Psalms 68:18.] The reason why the Psalmist mentions God's ascending here is that the ark was now ascending. David was removing of it, and carrying of it up into the hill of God, the high hill or the hill of Bashan, which was to be God's settled abode, mentioned in the Psalms 68:15–16. This hill is a type of heaven, and the ark's ascending into it is a type of Christ's ascension into heaven.The remainder is a later addition.

"Yea, for the rebellious also." By the "rebellious" here is probably meant the heathen nations. Dr. Watts, Glory of Christ, God-man, p. 73.Isaac Watts, The Glory of Christ as God-man, 73. Watts comments extensively on Old Testament texts applied to Christ by both Jewish and Christian writers.

"Thou hast led captivity captive." The words in the original,שֶּׁבִי שָׁבִיתָ according

-- 506 --

to the Hebrew idiom, properly denote a doing something very great and notable of this kind, viz. in taking enemies captive, either by taking captive a great multitude (agreeable to the marginalJE deleted "reading." rendering of the Apostle's citation of this place in Ephesians 4:8),The marginal reading at Ephesians 4:8 in the KJV is "a multitude of captives." or taking captive great and strong enemies, or leading them into a great captivity, subduing and captivating them effectually, or implying several or all these things. The same verb and noun, which are used here, are used, Numbers 21:1, where in our translation the king of Canaan is said to take some of the people captives, which should have been rendered, "He took a great number captives."Each of these paragraphs is a separate entry.

Psalms 68:22. "From Bashan."] The kingdom of Og, that mighty giant. Bashan was also the country of that "multitude of bulls," spoken of, Psalms 68:30. See Psalms 22:12, Amos 4:1.

Psalms 69:5.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1007–8.

Psalms 69:9. "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up."] I.e. it has so prevailed as entirely to govern me, and swallow me up, and cause me to renounce myself, and has caused me willingly to expose myself to be consumed by mine enemies, and hath actually been an occasion of my being devoured by them. That this is the meaning is evident by the next words, as also by all the context. So Christ's zeal consumed him, his being so zealous in opposing the corruptions and wickedness of the Pharisees, and other Jews, and especially his taking so much upon him in the temple in driving out the buyers and sellers (and otherwise), which he did once a little before his crucifixion, provoked them, and was the occasion of his own sufferings. Therefore these words are applied to Christ (John 2:17). See also Psalms 119:139.

Psalms 69:13. "In an acceptable time," or as it might have been rendered, "in the time of thy good will or favor."] 'Tis an Hebraism, and is no more than to say, "and then I found acceptance," or "so I found acceptance." See Ezekiel 16:8. See SSS.Ibid., col. 1010.

-- 507 --

Psalms 69:22–28.] See concerning such imprecations, 2 Samuel 1:17 note.

"Let their table become a snare to them; and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap." This was fulfilled to the unbelieving Jews, who rejected and crucified the Lord of glory, by a curse being made to attend. But more especially did their table become a snare and a trap to 'em as their altar in the temple (which was called God's table), and the table at which they eat their sacrifices on their feast days and at other times became an occasion of a great increase of their guilt and misery. This was remarkably fulfilled at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, when the Romans took that opportunity when the people were gathered to Jerusalem to that great feast of the Passover (which was a feast that, in the original design of its appointment, was to be for their preservation from the destroying angel, when their enemies were destroyed for their sakes): I say, when the Romans made this their opportunity to lay the land waste, being left of those that should defend it, and shut the people up in Jerusalem, where they were taken as in a trap, and the paschal table became a snare to 'em.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Psalms 71:16. "Strength… righteousness."] See Isaiah 45:24.

Psalms 72:3. "The mountains shall bring peace," etc.] I.e. this shall be as it were the natural produce. In the land of Canaan, that hilly country, their fruitful grounds were mountains and hills. In the Psalms 72:16 we read of "an handful of corn" on the mountains, and in innumerable places we read of the produce of the hills and mountains. This figure of speech concerning the mountains'; bringing forth peace is like many others in the Scripture, such as the earth's opening, and bringing forth salvation, and righteousness springing up together (Isaiah 45:8), and truth's springing out of the earth (Psalms 85:11).

Psalms 72:6. "He shall come as rain on the mown grass."] Man is first cut down by the fall before he is redeemed by Christ. The soul, before it is refreshed and renewed with the consolations of Christ, is wounded and as it were cut down with the scythe of the law. And in order to our having the benefit of Christ's salvation, we must be cut down; we must be cut down as to our former sinful life. We must die to sin that we may live to Christ. We must be cut down as to our worldly happiness; those things that we used to place our happiness in, we must renounce, and sell all

-- 508 --

for Christ. We must be crucified to the world, and the world must be crucified to us. We must cut ourselves down as to these things. He that would find his life must lose it [Matthew 10:39]. We must be cut down as to our pride, must be made low and level with the ground as to our own righteousness, cut off from our own stock that we may be engrafted into Christ, cut off as to that life that we live by nature, in order to renewed life by Christ, as the grass that grows again and is renewed by rain after it is mown. So Christ comes down as rain on those that are cut down by affliction, and on his church when cut down by her oppressors and persecutors. See Psalms 72:2 and Psalms 72:4. Grass is a very low, feeble, tender plant; it vastly differs from tall trees. It is easily cut down; many hundreds of spires of grass may be cut down at one stroke of the scythe. 'Tis easily devoured and commonly trodden under foot. Yet this is remarkable concerning it: that when it is cut down, it will sprout again when watered by the showers of heaven, and will flourish not less than it did before. Cutting of it down, though it be year after year, and many times in a year, don't at all put it out of hope. If it be devoured from day to day by the beasts that feed upon it, yet it will live and grow by the dew and rain. When a field is mown close to the ground, yet the rain as it were heals the wound of the scythe, and raises it from the dead; and presently it appears green, and flourishing, and joyful again. The church of God in the world is very much like grass in this respect: it can't be killed by cutting down, or by being devoured by the beasts that are greedy of it. Let it be never so often wounded, cut off, or mown down, it will live and grow again by showers of heaven. There quickly comes up a multitude of new spires in the room of old ones that were cut down. Often has that been verified in Isaiah 37:31, "And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward." And that in Isaiah 26:19, "Thy dead men shall live; together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in the dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast forth her dead." And Hosea 14:5–7, "I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. His branches shall spread, his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine. The scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon."

When the grass is mown, it is killed. The growing of the grass, after it is cut down with the scythe, is a kind of resurrection from the death. So by Christ's word and spirit, which is spiritual rain, the soul rises from the dead after it has died to sin, to the world, and to the law; it is quickened

-- 509 --

together with Christ. And their dead bodies at last shall rise, so that when he comes at the end of the world, he will come down on the dead bodies of the saints "as the rain on the mown grass" [Psalms 72:6]. And whenever he revives the saints, either their bodies or spirits, it is as [rain] coming down from heaven.This paragraph has been relocated from its mistaken location at Psalms 36:9.

Psalms 72:7. "Abundance of peace."] Psalms 37:11; Jeremiah 33:6.

Psalms 72:8. "And from the river unto the moon."] See notes on Zechariah 9:10.

Psalms 72:15.] It might have been rendered, "Prayer also shall be made through him continually, and daily shall he be blessed." The wordבָּרַךְ rendered "praised" is that which is commonly rendered "blessed" when speaking of an act of worship towards God. And the wordבְּעַד translated "for" is sometimes used for "through," as Joshua 2:15. "Then she let them down by a cord through the window." If we hold translation "for him," then it must be understood of the saints' praying for the Father's accomplishment of the promises made to the Son in the covenant of redemption, that his kingdom may come, his name glorified, and that he may see his seed, and that the full reward may be given him for his sufferings, and so that he may receive "the joy that was set before him" [Hebrews 12:2].

Psalms 73:1. "To Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart."] See John 1:47.

Psalms 73:4. "There are no bands in their death."] I.e. they don't die as prisoners or bound malefactors, as the righteous do that are persecuted by them. They remain in a state of liberty all the days of their lives, and die free men.

In the original,לְםוֹתַם חֵרְצֻבּוֹת אֵין the words are ein chartzutboth lemotham, which might more properly have been translated, "Their death hath no bands," the Hebrew of the Latin verb sum, with the prefix lamed following, being used for "have." And the meaning seems to be that they seem to be at liberty from death, as though they were out of its reach. Their death is here represented as a person that is indeed their enemy, or an officer of vengeance that they greatly deserve to be delivered up to, and that has a commission against them, and would feign seize them, and make 'em his prisoners,

-- 510 --

but has no bands to bind them, so that they live long and live without the fears of death, which are as it were the bands of death, by which some are all their lifetime subject to bondage, and also without those diseases and pains that are the forerunners of death and as it were its bands, by which death holds some persons its prisoners a long time before he executes them. That this is the meaning is confirmed by the following words of the sentence, "but their strength is firm." See SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. This closing reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1034–35.

Psalms 73:9. "Their tongue walketh through the earth."] I.e. they give their tongue an unbounded liberty to go where it will, without confining it by any enclosure at all.

Psalms 73:10. "Therefore his people return hither."] I.e. after they have gone forth in the time of their affliction and persecution, out of their city or dwelling place, to seek God who is departed from them, and to cry to him to judge their cause, and avenge them of their oppressors, they return back again disappointed, not having found God. See Psalms 74:21, "O let not the oppressed return ashamed."

Psalms 73:17–24.] See "Places of the Old Testament which Intimate a Future State."JE's entry on these verses in the "Intimations" manuscript (Andover Coll.) includes several observations. The destruction of the wicked described in Psalms 73 "can't be meant only [of] their temporal death, for the godly died as well as they." Nor can it be intended "of any temporal calamity God brings upon 'em in their lifetimes." The antithesis of this continual destruction is the "salvation of the righteous" which is "their portion forever" (pp. 8–9).

Psalms 73:20. "As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image."]JE deleted "It might as well have." The word in the originalבָּעִיד is "in awaking," which most probably means their awaking from their dream in passing out of time into eternity, or when God comes to awaken them from their graves at the day of judgment. "'In the day of the great judgment,' so the Chaldee ParaphraseAn Aramaic Targum, or tradition of interpretation of scriptural texts. reads it." (Henry).Exposition, 3 (1725), 295. "Thou shalt despise their image," or shadow. Their prosperity in this world is but an image or shadow of happiness, like the images in a dream that are contemptible,

-- 511 --

little worth, and appear so when one awakes. So God will make the enjoyments of this world to appear when he comes to awaken wicked men that trusted in their worldly prosperity. God will then as it were laugh at their imagined happiness.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1041.

Psalms 73:24.] That by "glory" here is meant that glory that the saints shall be received to in a future state, is confirmed by Psalms 149:5.

Psalms 74:8. "All the synagogues of God in the land."] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, pp. 555–58.Prideaux contends that this verse does not prove the existence of synagogues before the Babylonian captivity because these words in the original can be translated "all the assemblies of God," referring simply to places where people assembled to worship God (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, pp. 555–58).

Psalms 74:13–14. "Thou breakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou breakest the heads of leviathan in pieces."] Christ then obtained a signal victory over Satan, that old serpent, the leviathan, that crooked serpent, when he overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea. Then was in a measure fulfilled that curse on the old serpent, Genesis 3:15, "Her seed shall bruise thy head." Here it is said that God broke "the heads of the dragons." So it is said, Isaiah 51:9, "Art thou not it that cut Rahab, and wounded the dragon?" Now the dragon is a serpent. So here it is said, "Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces"; leviathan is also a serpent, as Isaiah 27:1. This is a confirmation that the serpent, spoken of Genesis 3:15, "It shall bruise thy head," is the same serpent whose head God here is said to have broken, viz. the devil, and that the bruising of his head that was threatened was to be in the redemption of his people. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was typically that dragon and leviathan, as is confirmed by Ezekiel 29:3. And by comparing in this psalm with that in Ezekiel, we may gather that the crocodile that was wont to keep in the river of Egypt was called a leviathan; for Pharaoh is here called leviathan, and without doubt 'tis as comparing him to that dragon that kept in the river of Egypt, as it is expressly said in Ezekiel 29:3. And in Ezekiel 32:2, he is calledMS: "called to." a whale that has feet, which must doubtless be meant of the crocodile. This confirms that respect is had to the crocodile in the description of the leviathan in Job, though probably not only to that [Job 41:1].

-- 512 --

Psalms 74:15. "Thou didst cleave the fountain and the flood."] God, in dividing Jordan, did not only divide the water that ordinarily belonged to the river, or the water which came from its fountains, but also the extraordinary additional water by the great rains a little before harvest. So God cleaved both the fountain (i.e. the fountain water) and the flood.

Psalms 75:3. "I bear up the pillars."] See note on Isaiah 65:17–18.

Psalms 75:8. "A cup."] The same that Christ drank (Matthew 26:39, Matthew 26:42).

Psalms 76:9.] 2 Thessalonians 1:5–7.

Psalms 77:13. "Thy way is in the sanctuary."] In the original,בֵּקֹּדֶשׁ bakkodhesh, "in holiness," so that this scripture seems to be parallel with that, Psalms 145:17. "The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works."

Psalms 77:15. "The sons of Jacob and Joseph."] God's church in Israel is called not only by the name of Jacob, but Joseph, both being eminent types of Christ. Joseph was so in an especial manner beyond most persons that we have an account of in the Old Testament. And he was an eminent example of the spirit and practice of all true saints, so that all of that character are fitly called "sons of Joseph." See note on Psalms 80:1.

Psalms 77:16. "The waters saw thee, O God."] See notes on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210, Corol. 2.Works, 15, 139–40.

Psalms 77:17. "Water." SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1068.

Psalms 77:17–18.] Shuckford, in his Connection, vol. 2, p. 455, says that Artapanus, an ancient heathen historian,Artapanus, in fact, was a syncretistic Hellenistic Jewish writer in the second century B.C.E. takes notice that the old Egyptian priests, speaking of the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea and the overthrow of the Egyptians, speak of lightnings that were at that time.Sacred and Prophane History (2nd ed.), 2, 455–56, n. r.

Psalms 78:2.] The rehearsal made of the wonderful things which God had done of old for Israel in their redemption of Egypt, settlement in Canaan, etc.,

-- 513 --

are called a "parable" and "dark sayings," because all these things are typical of gospel things. And with an eye to gospel things, this psalm (as almost all the rest) was indited by the Spirit of God.

Psalms 78:5.] The meaning of this verse is this: he established this for "a testimony in Jacob," and made it "a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make" the things forementioned (viz. the wonderful works that he hath done) "known to their children."

Psalms 78:9. "The children of Ephraim," etc.] This seems to refer to that shameful defeat which the Philistines gave them in Eli's time when they carried the ark into captivity, the same thing that mention is made of again, Psalms 78:56–64. It appears that that sorrowful event was very much in the Psalmist's mind, and that forgetting of God's wonderful works which was the occasion of it, which things gave occasion to that dispensation of glorious and sovereign grace with which the psalm concludes, viz. God's refusing the tribe of Ephraim and choosing the tribe of Judah, and Mt. Zion, and the family of David Psalms 78:67–70]. The defeat of the children of Ephraim may be taken notice of the rather because they were eminently a warlike tribe. There chiefly lay the strength of Joseph's posterity, of whom such things are said, Genesis 49:23–24. "The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him. But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob." But now his posterity, armed with bows, turned back their bow, did not abide in strength. The arms of their hands were weakened. Joshua and Gideon were of that tribe.

Psalms 78:25–26.] See no. 210, Corol. 1, in that part of it that is there noted in the margin.Works, 15, 138.

Psalms 78:30. "They were not estranged from their lust."] The wonderful work God had wrought in thus bringing quails did not bring 'em to repentance. The goodness of God did not lead 'em to repentance, but they only improved the fruits of his goodness to humor their lusts, to nourish and increase 'em. Therefore God's wrath came upon them with their meat while they were eating it.

Psalms 78:39. "A wind that passeth away, and cometh not again."] The Holy Spirit here seems to allude to the breath (which is as it were the life),

-- 514 --

which when a man dies "goeth forth," as the expression is, Psalms 146:4. It then passes away, and "comes not again." See note on James 4:14; and "Images of Divine Things," no. 141; Ibid., 2, 100. and also note on Job 7:7.

"A wind that passeth away." Note on Proverbs 10:25.

Psalms 78:43. "A field of Zoan."] No. 254."Ibid., 2, 204.

Psalms 78:49. "By sending evil angels among them."] Note on Exodus 21-23, no. 388.Ibid., 372–73.

Psalms 78:54. "Even to this mountain."] Jeremiah 17:3.

Psalms 78:57.] They were like a rotten bow, that though it looked well, yet would not bear straining; but when the archer strained, and just as he was about to let the arrow fly, and expected that the bow would do execution and accomplish the archer's purpose, then it fails, breaks on a sudden, and deceives and disappoints the archer's expectation. The trial of the strength and goodness [of] a bow is in straining of it. When God in his providence calls a professor to hard labor, or great self-denial and suffering for him, it is like an archer's straining a bow. If the bow will bear straining, then is it like to do service. So if a professor of religion will bear self-denial, then in going through with great trials does he do God most service, and does most glorify his name.

The comparison is very much like that, Proverbs 25:19. "Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint." And Isaiah 36:6, "Thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt." So Ezekiel 29:6–7. God's people are represented as his bow, by which he prevails against his enemies (Zechariah 9:13).This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 78:69. "Like the earth which he hath established forever."] The temple was not finally destroyed till the Messiah came, and the kingdom of heaven was introduced after his resurrection, and the Christian church established. The type did not cease till the antitype came, and the shadow was succeeded by the substance. And thus the temple in effect remained forever.

-- 515 --

Psalms 78:71. "From following the sheep great with young."] "He doth not say, 'from leading the ram,' but 'from following the ewes,' especially those 'great with young,' which intimates that of all the good properties of a shepherd, he was most remarkable for his tenderness and compassion to those of his flock that most needed. This temper of mind fitted him for government, and made him a type of Christ, who when he 'feeds his flock like a shepherd,' doth with a particular care 'gently lead those that are with young' (Isaiah 40:11)." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 310.

Psalms 80:1. "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph as a flock."] The Ten Tribes are commonly called by the name of Ephraim. But when that part of God's true church that was to be found among the Ten Tribes is spoken [of], it is rather called by the name of Joseph, out of respect to the eminently pious character of Joseph and the peculiar blessings given to him by Jacob and Moses, of which these were especially the heirs, and as to many of them the only heirs. See Ezekiel 37:16–17, Ezekiel 37:19; Amos 5:15 and Amos 6:6; Revelation 7:8. And one reason why Joseph is mentioned as led by God as "a flock," when God is spoken of as the "Shepherd of Israel," may be a respect to what is said by Jacob in blessing of Joseph. Genesis 49:24, "From thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel," where there was a special respect to Joshua, which is the same name with Jesus. He that is here spoken of is the true Jesus, the antitype of that Jesus that led the people into Canaan. See note on Psalms 77:15.

"Thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth." See observations on this in my discourse on the "Prophecies of the Messiah," "Miscellanies," no. 1067, §84, at this mark in the margin

.This paragraph is a separate entry written earlier than the preceding paragraph. JE's marginal reference points to his interpretation of this passage as an "earnest request of the church and a prophecy" that God, who had hid himself during the Mosaic dispensation under the veil of the temple and between the cherubim, would "openly manifest his glory" and give free access to all ("Miscellanies," no. 1067, p. 76).

Psalms 80:2. "Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh," etc.] Ibid., at this mark,∗.JE ties this passage, which speaks of deliverance from captivity and bondage, with prophecies of redemption by the Messiah. The latter action is, in particular, compared to the deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt and their march toward Canaan under divine leading ("Miscellanies," no. 1067, p. 77).

Psalms 81:5. "This he ordained in Joseph."] See note on Psalms 77:15, and Psalms 80:1.

-- 516 --

Psalms 81:7. "The secret place of thunder."] I.e. the pillar of cloud, the thick darkness, where God was, out of which God thundered on the Egyptians when they were pursuing the Israelites in the Red Sea, which was the time of their final and complete deliverance from their ancient taskmasters. See Psalms 77:15–20.

Psalms 82:5. "Foundations of the earth."] See note on Psalms 82:8, at the end.

Psalms 82:6.] See notes on John 10:35.

As those kings of Israel were said to sit upon "the throne of the Lord," as 1 Chronicles 29:23, so reciprocally the Lord himself (Jesus Christ) is said to sit upon "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32).

"Ye are gods." See 1 Chronicles 29:23, and 2 Chronicles 13:8; Luke 1:32.This paragraph and the preceding are later separate entries.

Psalms 82:8.] "Arise, O God, judge the earth; for thou shalt inherit all nations."] The design of these words, and their connection with the two foregoing verses, confirms that the princes of Israel are there called gods and sons of God, with reference to Christ, the true king of Israel or of God's people, and as being types of him. The three verses in their connection impart thus much: as to these temporal princes and judges, God has given 'em the name of gods and sons of God, being exalted to the place or seat of kings, judges, and saviors of God's people, that is, God's heritage and kingdom; but they die like men, whereby it appears that they are no gods, nor are the true Son of God, but mere men, and no more than images and shadows of him. But O, that he that is truly God, who is indeed the Son of God, the true King, and Judge, and Savior of God's people, the antitype of these, would come andJE deleted "judge." reign not only over the land of Israel, but over the whole earth, when God's Israel shall fill the earth, and all nations shall be God's people. It is observable that when it is said in this verse, "Arise, O God," the word "God" is Elohim, the same that is used Psalms 82:6. "I have said, Ye are gods." They were called Elohim. But Christ is the true Elohim, just as the manna in the wilderness was called "bread from heaven" [Exodus 16:4], but Christ is the true bread from heaven [John 6:51]. 'Tis further to be noted that in Psalms 82:5 the judges of Israel are called "the foundations of the earth." They are so because they are the rulers of God's people. They that have the care of the welfare of God's people are in effect "the foundations of the earth," for the whole earth is for

-- 517 --

them; all things are theirs. But Christ, when he comes, he will judge the whole earth indeed, and set to rights all things through the whole system.

Psalms 83:13. "Like a wheel."] "That they might be in continual motion, unquiet, unsettled, and giddy in all their counsels and resolves." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 320.

Psalms 84:3. "Even thine altars, O Lord."] No. 349.Works, 15, 335.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1105–106.

Psalms 84:5–6.] See Evans, Christian Temper, vol. 2, p. 18.John Evans' sermon in vol. 2 of the Practical Discourse concerning the Christian Temper: Being Thirty Eight Sermons upon the Principal Heads of practical Religion, especially as injoined and inforced by Christianity (2nd ed., 2 vols. London, 1725), entitled "Preference of the soul to the body, and diligence for its welfare" (pp. 1–25), includes a discussion of "the diligent use of all appointed means of life" in which he urges the use of "every proper opportunity for reading and hearing, for meditation and prayer, and communicating at the Lord's table." Evans points to this passage as a description of some Jews living at a distance from Jerusalem, who "out of love to the temple worship, and in obedience to God," passed through the desert valley of Baca, demonstrating the labor and pains needed for their best interest (pp. 18–19). Evans (1680–1730), a divine of presbyterian orientation in London, was a successful preacher.

Psalms 84:6.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1107–8.

Psalms 84:7. "They go from strength to strength."] "I.e. their company increases by the accession of more out of every town as they pass through, till they become very numerous. Those that were near stayed, till those that were further off called them, saying, Come, 'let us go up to the house of the Lord' (Psalms 122:1–2)." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 322.

Psalms 84:9. "Behold, O God our shield."] The word "behold" is not hen,הֵן ecce, but raah,רָאָה aspice. See 2 Chronicles 6:42, and Psalms 132:10.

Psalms 86:11. "Unite my heart to fear thy name."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1118.

-- 518 --

Psalms 86:16. "Son of thy handmaid."] Note on Psalms 116:16.

Psalms 87:7. "All my springs are in thee."] By "springs" here is meant prolific springs, or fountains of posterity, for the children of Zion that are born of God are here spoken of, as may be seen in the three preceding verses. Thus this and such like words are used in the Old Testament, as Psalms 68:26. "Bless ye God in the congregations, even the Lord, from the fountain of Israel." (And 'tis observable that there, in the preceding verse, "singers" and "players on instruments" are spoken of, as here.) Isaiah 48:1, "Hear ye this, O ye house of Jacob, which are called by the name of Israel, and are come forth out of the waters of Judah." Deuteronomy 33:28, "Israel then shall dwell in safety alone; the fountain of Jacob shall be upon a land of corn and wine" (where the wordעַיִן translated "fountain" is the same as in this place). Proverbs 5:18, "Let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth." And in the Proverbs 5:16, "Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad." So the fountains of water, spoken of, Exodus 15:27, evidently represent the twelve sons of Jacob, the heads of the tribes, or the twelve tribes themselves, with regard to their progeny, and as so many fountains of posterity. The word there translated "wells" is the same that is used in this place. The words seem to be the words of God to Zion, or the church, speaking of the children that heJE deleted "she." has born in one place and another, says, "All my springs are in thee." 'Tis as much as to say, Although I have many children born in many places of many nations, yet thou art theJE deleted "father." mother of them all. Though I have many streams in many countries, yet the fountains from whence all those streams proceed are in thee. All are by the means of grace maintained in thee, and used by thee.

Psalms 88:13. "Prevent thee."] I.e. shall be so early as to [be] before thou beginnest thy usual works of the day, before thou beginnest to send thy light on the earth to cause the sun to shine upon it, to awaken and comfort men and other animals, before thou settest the wheels of the world going anew, as thou dost at the beginning of the day.

Psalms 89:8. "O Lord God of hosts, who is a strong Lord like unto thee, and to thy faithfulness round about thee?"] The words might have been better translated, "O Jehovah God of hosts, who is like thee? O mighty Jah, and

-- 519 --

thy truth round about thee." The wordוֶאֱמוּנָתְךָ translated "thy faithfulness" is aimunatheka. Amunah signifies "truth," and is a wordאֱמוּנָה of the same root and signification with amen.אָמֵן But we are told in the New Testament that Christ is "the Amen" [Revelation 3:14]. And he seems to be what the Psalmist has respect to in this when he speaks of God, "truth round about," even his personal reason, wisdom, light, and truth, which is the brightness of his glory that is round about him. We cannot make sense of the words if we understand it of the faithfulness of God considered merely as a property or virtue of the Divine Being.

Psalms 89:15.] There is the dreadful, and there is the joyful sound. The dreadful sound was at Mt. Sinai. The joyful sound is from Mt. Zion. When the people heard the former, they were far from beholding the glory of God's face. Moses only was admitted to see his back parts [Exodus 33:23]. The people were kept at a distance, and the light of God's glory that they saw was so terrible to them that they could not abide it. But they that know the joyful sound, they shall be admitted near, nearer than Moses, so as to see the glory of God's face, or brightness of his countenance, and that not only transiently, as Moses saw God's back parts, but continually. The light of God's glory shall not be terrible to 'em, but easy and sweet, that they may dwell in it and walk in it; and it shall be to them instead of the light of the sun. For the sun shall no more be their light by day, nor the moon by night; but God shall be their everlasting light. Compare this with Isaiah 2:5, and Revelation 21:23–24 (And see note in loc.), and Revelation 22:4–5.

Psalms 89:22.] By the "enemy" and the "son of wickedness" here seems especially to be meant the devil.

Psalms 89:27. "Also I will make him my first-born, higher than the kings of the earth."] The kings and princes of the earth are sometimes called the "sons of God," as Psalms 82:6; but God makes his Son the first-born of these sons. This is also true with respect to the thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers in heavenly places, who are also called the "sons of God" (Job 38:7), and seem sometimes mystically to be couched under this expression of "kings of the earth." See "Exposition on Revelation," no. 59.Works, 5, 149–58.

-- 520 --

Psalms 89:37.] The heavenly bodies, the sun, moon, and stars that God hath settled and fixed in heaven, and appointed to be for times and season, and for days and years, are here represented as "faithful witnesses in heaven"; that is, they give a faithful testimony with respect to times and seasons. They never cheat or fail us. So it is with respect to God's heaven, and Jesus Christ, the Sun of righteousness, the mediator of that covenant, the seed of David. As the sun and other heavenly bodies never cheat us, never fail the expectations of those that expect them in their season, so God's covenant never fails, and Christ never fails those that trust in him. We may as surely depend on the fulfillment of God's promises, as in the night we may surely depend on the due returns of the light of the sun in the morning, or as in winter we may surely depend on the returns of the benign influences of the sun in the proper season of spring.

Psalms 89:45. "The days of his youth hast thou shortened."] In Rehoboam's time, when the house of David was but in the days of its youth, yet it waxed old, and greatly decayed. And Rehoboam lost most of his kingdom in early days, in his youth, and soon after he began to reign. In the time of the captivity into Babylon, the kings of the house of David had the days of their youth shortened, it being when they were about thirty years old that Jehoiachin [2 Kings 24:15] and Zedekiah [2 Kings 25:7] were carried captives to Babylon. Christ suffered when about three or four and thirty years of age; the Christian church was exceedingly persecuted in early times.

Psalms 90. "A prayer of Moses, the man of God."] See sermon on the Psalms 90:11, the exposition of the text.No extant copy of this sermon has been located.

Psalms 90:1. "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations."] "Canaan was a land of pilgrimage to their fathers who dwelt there in tabernacles" (and had no inheritance, not so much as to set their foot on). "But then God was their habitation, and wherever they went, they were at home in him. Egypt had been a land of bondage to 'em for many years, but even then God was their refuge, and in him that poor oppressed people lived, and were kept in being."Henry, Exposition, 3 (1725), 335. (And he had been their protection and hiding place since they came out of Egypt.)JE deleted "Henry." That people never yet had had any settled dwelling in this world.

-- 521 --

Psalms 90:5–9.] There was a great mortality in the wilderness, whereby the whole congregation of the men perished in thirty-eight years' time; and there was no increase of the congregation, but just so many men of war at the end of those thirty-eight years as had been at the beginning [Deuteronomy 2:14], though the people had multiplied so exceedingly before.

Psalms 90:10.] See no. 203.Works, 10, 126–27.

Psalms 90:11. "According to thy fear."] Job 25:2, "Dominion and fear are with him," i.e. awful majesty, tending to possess the heart with fear and dread.

Psalms 91:1. "In the secret place of the Most High."] In the holy of holies, "in the secret of God's tabernacle," as it is called, Psalms 27:5. This God calls his "secret place" (Ezekiel 7:22), so that we may understand the secret place of heaven, which is the true holy of holies.

Psalms 91:11.] See no. 168.Ibid., 2, 98.

Psalms 92. Tide. "A psalm or song for the sabbath day."] By the contents of this psalm, it is evident that 'tis God's works of redemption, Christ's victory over his enemies, and its glorious consequences thereof, that are chiefly regarded by God in the appointment of the sabbath day.

Psalms 92:6.] The "brutish man" don't understand the depth of the divine thoughts in the sufferings and humiliation of Christ (Christ crucified is to such a stumbling block.), and in the sufferings of good men and the contrary prosperity of the wicked, spoken of in the next verse.

Psalms 92:15. "To show that the Lord is upright."] See SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1159.

Psalms 93:3.] The floods here probably imply: 1. The multitudes, peoples, and nations of the world which set themselves with great rage and tumult to threaten, exclaim against, and oppose the church of God, and if possible, to overwhelm and swallow it up, or carry it away (Revelation 17:15; Psalms 124:2–6, and Psalms 144:7). The wicked are compared to the "troubled sea"

-- 522 --

(Isaiah 57:20), and "the tumult of the people" to the noise of the waves of the sea (Psalms 65:7). The heathen, they rage against Christ and the church (Psalms 2:1). The church is said to be "tossed with tempests" (Isaiah 54:11), and "the floods of ungodly men" make the saints afraid (Psalms 18:4). 2. The evils and afflictions, in general, which befall God's [church] in this world, are compared to waters, deep waters, floods, waves, etc., including the sense of God's anger, Satan's temptation, the evidence of inward corruption, and grievous outward afflictions.

The preservation of the ship wherein Christ and his disciples were in a time of great storm, and Christ's stilling the storm [Mark 4:37–39], and Christ's walking on the water in the time of tempest [Mark 6:49], and saving Peter when beginning to sink [Matthew 14:28–31], are types of what is spoken of in this psalm. See SSS on Psalms 93:3–4.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1160–61.

Psalms 94:10.] "He that chastiseth the heathen" that are not his people, and with whom he han't that near concern, and that are ignorant of him and his law, shall he not much more correct the sinners and rebellious of Israel that are his own people, and are more especially under his care and government, to whom he has given his statutes and judgments, and that are under infinitely greater obligations to obey him? Amos 3:2, "You only have I known of all the families of the earth. Therefore will I punish you."

Psalms 94:11.] Special respect is here had to the thoughts of persecutors that the Psalmist had been speaking of; their thoughts are "vanity." They imagine a vain thing when they think to advance themselves, and to swallow up God's people, etc. He had been describing the vanity of their thoughts in the four preceding verses.

Psalms 94:12. "Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O Lord, and teachest."] The Psalmist has reference to what God's people suffered from the oppression and persecution of their enemies, spoken of in Psalms 94:3–6, which as from God's providence were his chastenings. In these persecutions judgment began at the house of God, as the apostle Peter observes (1 Peter 4:17).

Psalms 94:13. "Until the pit be digged for the wicked."] This is agreeable to what follows in that verse of the apostle Peter, "What shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?" [1 Peter 4:17].

-- 523 --

Psalms 94:15. "But judgment shall return unto righteousness."] That is, that judgment that begins at the house of God shall, as to them, return to covenant mercy, which is commonly called "righteousness" in the Old Testament.

Psalms 94:16–17.] As much as to say, There is notI.e. no one. to "rise up for me against the evildoers," but God. There was no other to be "my help," but the Lord.

Psalms 95:4. "In his hand are the deep places of the earth; the strength of the hills" (or the "height of the hills," as it is in the margin)Margin of the KJV.
