The literal translationיַיטִבפֶּנִים is, "makes the countenance good," which might be rendered "causes a healthy countenance," so that the meaning probably is that a cheerful mind is for a man's health, for "to have a healthy

-- 559 --

countenance" is a Hebrew phrase for enjoying health. See Psalms 42:11 and Psalms 43:5.

This sense is abundantly confirmed by Proverbs 17:22. "A merry heart doth good like a medicine," i.e. promotes health. And it may be noted that the wordיַיטִב "do good" there is the same which is here used and translated "makes cheerful." See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1607–8.

Proverbs 15:14. "The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge."] And so such an one is more ready to hear than to speak. "But the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness." I.e. he [is] eager upon foolish and sinful talk, and 'tis what he delights in. 'Tis to him as food that a man loves and is greedy of. In the Hebrew phrase,רָעָה a man is said to "feed upon" or "devour" words when he is forward to speak. So Proverbs 19:28, "An ungodly witness scorneth judgment, and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity." So Proverbs 20:25, "It is a snare to a man to devour that which is holy, and after vows to make inquiry."

Proverbs 15:21. "Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom, but a man of understanding walketh uprightly."] The literal translationיַיַשּׁר־לָכֶת תְּבוּנָה וְאִישׁ לַחֲסַר־לַב שִׂמְחה אִוֶּלֶת is, "Folly is joy to him that is without a heart, but a man of understanding will direct himself in walking." The meaning seems to be this. The wicked man, who has no principle of true virtue in his heart, commits sin with eagerness, and delight, and relish of heart; and therefore he goes on in ways of sin allowedly without hesitation. But a gracious man has a principle in his heart that directs and governs him, that abhors sin, and relishes and delights in righteousness, by which principle he is led and directed in the right way, as by a spiritual scent, distinguishing good from bad, and inclining him to that which is right. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1610–11.

Proverbs 15:25. "The Lord will destroy the house of the proud, but he will establish the border of the widow."] As by "the poor" in the Old Testament is oftentimes meant those that are poor in spirit, so here and perhaps in some other places, by "the widow" seems to be intended one that is so in

-- 560 --

a spiritual sense, or the soul to whom those things are dead that formerly it was wedded [to], as the soul that is weaned from the world and her own righteousness. True Christians are represented as being dead to the world, and the world to them; and so the Apostle compares the person that is weaned from his own righteousness to a woman that has lost her husband. Such widows as these the Apostle calls "widows indeed." 1 Timothy 5:3, "Honor widows that are widows indeed." And 1 Timothy 5:5, "Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day." It seems manifest that by "widow" in this place in Proverbs is meant a widow in this sense by the antithesis, the widow in the latter part of the verse being set in opposition to the proud in the former part.

Proverbs 15:30. "The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart, and a good report" (or "a good hearing," as itטוֹבָה שְׁמוּעָה might have been rendered) "makes the bones fat."] I.e. when we don't wish and hope for what we desire, or think it probable, but see it with our eyes, or hear it with our ears. See Proverbs 13:12.

Proverbs 15:31. "The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise."] I.e.MS: "i.e. that is." this is the way to dwell amongst 'em, and not to depart from 'em, because wholesome reproofs, or reproofs of life, are the proper means of reclaiming persons when they are departing, or are in danger of departing, from among the wise.

Proverbs 15:33. "The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honor is humility."] "The fear of the Lord," a disposition to stand in awe of him, to reverence, and adore, and trust in him, is the way to wisdom; and humility is the way to honor. The fear of the Lord and humility are near akin, and wisdom and honor are near akin. "The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom." I.e. a principle of true piety in the heart will wonderfully enlighten the mind in the doctrine of true wisdom, and will guide and direct one in its ways. See John 7:17, and Proverbs 8:9, and the places there quoted.

Proverbs 16:1. "The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the Lord."] Mr. Henry says, that "most read it, 'The preparations of the heart are in man, but the answer of the tongue is

-- 561 --

from the Lord.'" I.e. man contrives what and how he will speak, but the happy executing his design, and the success of it, is of God, as it is said, Proverbs 16:9. "Man's heart deviseth his way, but the Lord directs his steps." And in another place, "A man's way is not in himself. 'Tis not of him that walketh to direct his steps" [Jeremiah 10:23].Exposition, 3 (1725), 510–11.

Proverbs 16:4.] The Wise Man in the expression, "hath made all things," has not respect merely to the works of creation, but also the works of providence. Making and creating is commonly understood in this large sense in Scripture for bringing to pass. Yea, bringing to pass, though not by an immediate effecting, but only by permitting, ordering, and disposing, is called "making" in Scripture. The "making the wicked," here mentioned, is a work of providence. God makes men wicked in the same sense as he said in the ninth of Romans, to make them "vessels of wrath," to harden them, and fit them "to destruction" [Romans 9:22] (of which, see notes, in loc.), viz. by so disposing and ordering things in his providence that they, in consequence of his disposals, especially in his permission or withholding restraints, do continue in wickedness, or are hardened in it. They are distinguished from others in being impenitently and obstinately wicked, and are suffered to multiply wickedness, and heap up wrath. And God's end in it is to glorify himself in the day of their evil or ruin. God makes wicked men in no other sense than he creates darkness, which is not by any positive effecting,JE wrote this over "efficiency." but only ordering by withholding light, for darkness is only a negative. Isaiah 45:7, "I form the light, and create darkness. I make peace, and create evil. I the Lord do all these things." These things that are here said to be formed, made, and created are all works of providence, and some of them brought to pass by no positive efficiency, because negative things, works of providence, are said to be created (Numbers 16:30; Isaiah 57:19; Isaiah 41:20; Isaiah 45:8, and Isaiah 48:7, and Isaiah 54:16; Jeremiah 31:22). So that it don't appear that this scripture will justify such an expression as that, that God made some men to damn them. 'Tis most probable that the Wise Man, by "making the wicked," has respect to something that God doth respecting the wicked or reprobates that is distinguishing and peculiar to them. God's distinguishing dealings towards mankind might be expressed thus: That God maketh both the righteous and the wicked in the same sense, i.e. whom he will, he has mercy on and makes righteous, and whom he will, he hardens or leaves to wickedness. But if the

-- 562 --

Wise Man had respect only to the bringing the men into being, bearingConjecture for illegible word that Grosart overwrote. guilt and corruption, this is common to all. All in this sense are made wicked, in this sense alike. 'Tis probable that by "making the wicked" here is intended the same as is expressed, Romans 11:7–10, 2 Thessalonians 2:11–12, Psalms 81:12, Isaiah 6:9–10, which is a judicial proceeding and a punishment of sin, though it be a mere sovereign proceeding in God that he distinguishes some by not executing this punishment upon them.

Proverbs 16:6. "By mercy and truth iniquity is purged."] The wordיְכֻפֵּר rendered "purged" is jecup-par, which signified "atoned." Therefore by this saying the Wise Man would teach that the legal sacrifices in themselves are of no efficacy to atone for sin, and that nothing can avail to this but spiritual sacrifices, Christ's righteousness consisting in his obedience and faithfulness to God, and mercy to men. And nothing in us can avail as any evidence of our interest in his righteousness, but moral and spiritual dispositions and acts, spiritual offerings to God, whereby we imitate Christ's righteousness, and follow his example.

Proverbs 16:11. "Are the Lord's,… are his work."] I.e. just weights and balances are sacred things which God has appointed, as he did the vessels of the sanctuary, and which is as much of a sin to violate or alter as it would be to alter any of the sacred utensils of the temple from the divine pattern by which they were made. Hence the standard weights seemed to have been kept in the sanctuary, laid up there, as well as the ark and the sacred vessels. Hence we read of the shekel of the sanctuary. "All the weights of the bag," i.e. the just, true weights, are said to be God's "work," i.e. they are God's appointment, as that which God "appointed,"JE deleted "He was, according to an Hebrew idiom, said to have made." as though he had by an immediate command directed how it should be made, as he did how the vessels of the temple should be made. Yea, they are to be looked upon as sacred, as though God had made them with his own hands, as he did the tables of stone that were delivered to Moses in Mt. Sinai.

Proverbs 16:20. "He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good; and whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he."] Mr. Henry observes that "Some read the former part of the verse thus, 'He that attendeth to the word shall

-- 563 --

find good,'" which is a most literal translation,יִמְצָא־טוֹב עַל־דָּבָר מַשְׂכִּיל and is much confirmed by Proverbs 13:13.Exposition, 3 (1725), 512. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1623.

Proverbs 16:21. "The wise in heart shall be called prudent, and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning."] The literal translationלֶקֵח יסִיף שְׂפָתֵיִם וּמֶתֶק נָבוֹן יִקָּרֵא לַחֲכַם־לֵב is thus. "To the wise in heart, he that hath understanding shall be called; and the sweetness of the lips shall add to learning." The word "called" is from a wordקָרָא that is used for calling or inviting one to another, and for the calling together a company or congregation. And therefore the meaning seems to be this. They that have understanding shall be gathered about him that is wise of heart, to hear his instructions, and be benefitted by his conversation and his good instructions. His wise speeches, which shall be pleasant and entertaining to them, shall increase their knowledge.

Proverbs 16:22. "Understanding is a wellspring of life to him that hath it, but the instruction of fools is folly."] It might as well have been rendered, "is a wellspring of life in him that hath it," i.e. a fountain of good to others, tending to their life and happiness. What is communicated from them, the instructions they give, are wholesome and of vital influence. But as to what flows from fools, even the best instructions they give are folly, and tends to blind and corrupt the minds of those that are conversant with them, and to lead 'em to mischief and misery.

Proverbs 16:23. "The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips."] This is agreeable to what Christ says,MS: "Say." "A good man, out of the good treasure of his heart, bringeth forth that which is good.… How can ye, being evil, speak good things?… Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" [Matthew 12:35, Matthew 12:34].

Proverbs 16:27. "An ungodly man diggeth up evil."] He "takes a great deal of pains to find out something" wherewith to reproach his neighbor, and blast his reputation. "If none appear above ground, he will dig for it, by diving into what is secret, or looking a great way back, or by evil suspicions and surmises." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 513. The words immediately following in this and the next verse confirm this sense.

-- 564 --

Proverbs 16:30. "He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things; moving his lips, he bringeth evil to pass."] These expressions intimate the secret, subtile, sly, deceitful way of his injuring his neighbor. "He shuts his eyes," that is, he conceals his aim and design, as though he did not see or aim at the mischief that will follow, acts as it were as if he were asleep and thought no harm, had no more hand in the evil that befalls his neighbor than if he were all the while asleep. "He moveth his lips." I.e. he whispers. He puts his ill designs in practice in a very secret manner.

Proverbs 17:5. "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker."] I.e. him that in his providence has made him poor, and has made [him] in this respect to differ from others that are ready to mock him, and deride him on that account.

Proverbs 17:8. "Whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth."] I.e. "whithersoever it turneth" from the hands of the giver, "it prospers" to promote his designs, and to gain those to whom it is given to his interests.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. The wordsיַשְׂכִּיל יִפְנֶה אֶל־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר בְעָלָיו בְּעַינֵי הַשּׂחַד אֶבֶן־חֵן might have been translated more literally thus. "A gift is a precious stone in the eyes of its lord" (or its husband, or him that espouses it, i.e. of the judge that is fond of bribes). "It prospers to all that to which it looks," or to which it has respect. See SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1631–32.

Proverbs 17:12.] This is agreeable to what Christ said to his disciples. "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves. But beware of men" [Matthew 10:16–17].

Proverbs 17:13.] It was declared that the sword should never depart from David's house, because he rewarded Uriah with evil for his good services [2 Samuel 12:10]. Evil did not depart from the house of Eli, and the house of Saul and Jeroboam, and the houses of others that God advanced to the kingdom over Israel, because they rewarded God evil for good. The Jews rewarded Christ, and his apostles, and other disciples evil for good. Therefore evil never departed from them and their posterity. Their house was left to them desolate, and the guilt of Christ's blood was on them and their children.

-- 565 --

Proverbs 17:26.]Before this entry, JE deleted "Proverbs 17:26. to strike princes for equity." As, on the one hand, it is not good for judges to do injustice in judgment, and to punish the just, so, on the other hand, when they punish the wicked, and thereby do justice and equity, it is not good to rise up against 'em, and oppose, reproach, or in any respect injure 'em for that.

Proverbs 17:27.] Here see SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1641.

Proverbs 18:1.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1642–44.

Proverbs 18:4. "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook."] The sense seems to be this. The words of a wise man's mouth are like waters that come from a deep fountain or wellspring, and his words flow from his heart like a flowing brook, from a deep fountain that yields a sufficient, constant supply. The wisdom of his talk is not feigned or forced, but flows naturally, as having the fountain within him. They are not muddy, mixed, and adulterated, but clear, sweet, and refreshing, like waters from a deep fountain. See Proverbs 10:11 and Proverbs 20:5.

Proverbs 18:10. "The name of JEHOVAH is a strong tower."] It is so in several respects. 1. As Christ is the name of God, as he is often called, who is the idea, Logos, word, or name of God. 2. As that by which God has made himself known, the word and promises of God, and the whole revelation he has made of him is so. 3. As the name JEHOVAH itself is so, as that exhibits God's infinite perfection, his all-sufficiency, his immutability, and faithfulness. God's calling himself by this name, and sending Moses to the children of Israel in the manner he did with this name, implies in it the great promises of the covenant of grace to them.

Proverbs 18:21. "And they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof."] Itפִּרְיָהּ יֹאכַל יְאֹהֲבֶיהָ might have been as well translated, "Let them that love it" (i.e. life), "eat the fruit thereof," i.e. of the tongue. For the Hebrew tongue always uses the future for the imperative in the third person. This sense is confirmed by Psalms 34:12–13.

-- 566 --

Proverbs 18:24. "A man that hath friends must show himself friendly, and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."] The words might be translated more agreeably to the originalמֵאָח דָּבֵק אֹהֵב וְיֵשׁ לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ רֵעִים אִישׁ thus. "There is one of friends" (or one of those that are of that character), "who is so for the sake of showing himself friendly," i.e. a man of disinterested friendship, of pure benevolence, who is a friend not to gain anything, but to benefit the object of his love. "And he is a friend that sticks closer than a brother." Such a disinterested friend may be depended on. Christ is eminently such a friend, and perhaps the Spirit of God may have respect to him. Neither need it seem strange that some of these proverbs should have respect to him; so very evidently does Proverbs 18:10 of this chapter.

Proverbs 19:2. "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."] The former partלא־טוֹב נֶפֶשׁ בְּלֹא־דַעת גַּם of the verse might have been translated thus. "Also in the soul's being without knowledge, there is no good." I.e. if the soul be without grace, nothing that that man has, and nothing that happens to him, or that he is the subject of, can be of any benefit to him. "And he that hasteth with his feet sinneth." I.e. he that directly proceeds according to natural appetite and inclination without knowledge, without considering any other consequences, or any higher end than the immediate gratification of his inclinations, runs into nothing but mischief and ruin, and gets no good in the end. The wordחוֹטֵא "sinneth," here as in many other places, is used for coming to punishment and ruin.

Note on Deuteronomy 6:25.This reference is a separate entry.

Proverbs 19:3.] I.e. though men's wicked practices and their evil consequences are the fruits of their own folly and wickedness, yet they lay the blame of it to God and not to themselves. When they feel and fear the terrible consequences of their own sin and folly, then they fret against God, and find fault with his dealings with them, instead of condemning themselves.

Proverbs 19:22. "The desire of a man is his kindness."] That is, this is what in a peculiar manner recommends him to the affection of others, causes him to be beloved and desired, agreeable to many other passages in this book, as Proverbs 19:6 of this chapter, and Proverbs 18:16, and Proverbs 21:14, and Proverbs 17:8. To be a man

-- 567 --

beloved, in the Hebrew way of expressing it, is to be a man of desire, as when the angel says to Daniel, "O man, greatly beloved" [Daniel 10:19]. In the original,אִישׁ־חֲמֻדוֹת it is "O man of desire." By a like Hebraism, when the Wise [Man] would signify that a man's amiableness or desirableness in the eyes of others consists in his kindness, he says, "The desire of a man is his kindness."

"And a poor man is better than a liar." A poor man that has but little to give, and can show but little kindness, is better than a rich man that promises much, but only flatters and turns persons off with good words.

Or by "the desire of a man being his kindness" may be meant that his kindness is according to his sincere good will, though he may be poor, and able to help us but little. We ought in such a case to accept such a gift as manifests his hearty desire of our welfare, as God doth. For wherever there is "a willing mind, it is accepted according to what a man hath, and not according to what he hath not" (2 Corinthians 8:12), as Christ accepted what the poor widow threw into the treasury as a greater act of piety and charity than the abundance that was given by the rich, who, many of 'em, were hypocritical and so liars, as the expression is here, in their offerings (Mark 12:43–44).This paragraph is a later addition.

Proverbs 19:28.] Note on Proverbs 15:14.

Proverbs 20:24.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1675–76.

Proverbs 20:26. "He bringeth the wheel over them."] In allusion to the wheel then used in threshing, which dislodged the grains of corn from the stalk where they hung together, fast one by another, as in clusters. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1677.

Proverbs 20:30. "The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil," etc.] The former part of the verse, as well as the latter, relates to the benefit of correction. "The blueness of a wound," i.e. when the skin or flesh is made black and blue by the stripes of the rod of correction, this cleanses away sin.

Proverbs 21:1.] The turning of "rivers of water" here spoken of is not the cutting out a new channel or water course for the water to run in, but God's governing the water of a river in its course by its banks, and turning the

-- 568 --

stream hither and thither as he will, as God governs the waters of the sea, and stays its proud waves by the sands, saying, "Hitherto shalt thou come, and no further" [Job 38:11]. As the waters of the sea are great and very forceable, as though they would not be restrained, but yet God breaks their force, and brings them down by the sands. So the stream of many rivers is rapid, and the force of waters mighty, as though they would not be diverted from their course, yet they are under government. They don't go on in a direct course where it as it were seems resolute to go, but is continually restrained, and governed, and is turned from its course hither and thither. God stays and turns the mighty waters by the limits and bounds he has set everywhere, on both sides, throughout the whole course of the river from the head to the mouth. The water han't its own course where the strength of the stream bears, but God cuts out their course for them, and says, Thus far shalt thou go in this course, and then so far shalt thou go in that course. He governs the stream by sands and rocks that he places for limits. This is a very fit and beautiful comparison. As God thus governs the course of the mightiest streams of water, so he governs the hearts of the greatest and mightiest of men.

Proverbs 21:4. "The plowing of the wicked is sin."] The marginal readingI.e. of the KJV. seems preferable, viz. "The light of the wicked is sin." This appears by the Hebrew concordance to be by far the most general signification of the word.See נור, נִיר, נֵר in Buxtorf, Lexicon Hebraicum el Chaldaicum (6th ed.), p. 432, where the primary meaning is "Lucerna, Lumen," that is, lamp or light. See also Taylor, Hebrew Concordance, I, entry 1134 under ניר. By "the light of the wicked" we must understand the show, the proud profession, and appearance they make of great excellency, and their good opinion of themselves by which they shine in their own eyes (This agrees with the signification of the lamps of the foolish virgins [Matthew 25:3].), and their glory, joy, and expectation. So the same word as applied to the wicked is to be understood, in Job 18:6 and Job 21:17, and from time to time in this book, as Proverbs 13:9, and Proverbs 20:20, and Proverbs 24:20. And this agrees well with the former part of the verse. The word properly signifies a candle or lamp. The lamps of the foolish virgins imply all those things that I mention: their self-conceit, their show and profession, their hope and expectation, and their joy and comfort.

Proverbs 21:5. "Hasty."] I.e. with that sort of haste that is spoken of, Proverbs 20:21 and Proverbs 28:20, Proverbs 28:22.

-- 569 --

Proverbs 21:6. "Is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death."] The literal translationמְבַקְשֵׁי־מָות נִדָּף הֶבֶל is this. "Is a vanity dispelled, they seeking death." "A vanity dispelled," i.e. their work, their contrivances, and what they get by it vanishes away, like a vapor that is dispelled, or like smoke that is driven away by the wind. Psalms 68:2, "As smoke is driven away." There the same wordנָדַף is used. So again the same word in Psalms 114, "The wicked shall be as the chaff which the wind drives away." So Isaiah 19:7, "Shall wither, and be driven away, and be no more." "They seeking death," i.e. they that thus get riches by a lying tongue.

Proverbs 21:12. "The righteous man wisely considereth the house of the wicked, but God overthroweth the wicked for their wickedness."] A more literal translationלָרָע רְשׁעִים מְסַלֵּף רָשָׁע לְבֵית צַדִּיק מַשְׂכִּיל would be, "The righteous man, wisely considering the house of the wicked, overthroweth the wicked for their wickedness." I.e. he as it were passes sentence upon them, as those that are to [be] overthrown, which is by an Hebraism called "overthrowing them." See Jeremiah 1:10.

Proverbs 21:15. "It is joy to the just to do judgment, but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity."] The wordsאָוֶן לְפעֲלֵי וּמְחִתָּה מִשְׁפָּט עֲשׁוֹת לַצַּדִּיק שִׂמְחָה would be more literally translated, "To do judgment shall be joy to the just" (i.e. it shall issue in their joy and happiness); "but horror shall be to the workers of iniquity," i.e. working iniquity instead of joy shall issue in the sorrow and amazement of the unjust.

Proverbs 21:16. "Congregation of the dead."] Hebrew, rephaim. See Job 26:5. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1685–86.

Proverbs 21:24. "Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath."] The wordעוֹשֶׂה rendered "dealeth" is guosheh, doeth, maketh, or worketh. The meaning seems to be this. If a man's behavior and practice be haughty, bitter, and wrathful, his true character is determined by it. It demonstrates him to be a "haughty scorner," a proud enemy to God and men, whatsoever good principles he may pretend to act from, whether

-- 570 --

superior wisdom, justice, religious zeal, sense of honor, hatred of wickedness, or any other. This is a very important observation, because there is no ill thing which men do so often pretend to proceed from good principles, and christen with good names, as those things that proceed from pride, and spite, or false zeal.

Proverbs 21:27. "How much more when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?"] The wordבְזִמָּה properly signifies a wicked design or device, as Absalom's vow, Jezebel's fast, and the Pharisee's long prayers, when [they] make a show of devotion, that they may the more easily and effectually compass some covetous or malicious design. When holiness is pretended, but some wickedness intended, then especially the performance is abomination (Isaiah 66:5). See more fully, SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2. col. 1690.

Proverbs 21:28.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1690–91.

Proverbs 22:1. "A good name."] I.e. a good character, including a good report. But that real character that is just ground for such a report, the favor that is better than silver or gold, is properly the favor of God.

Proverbs 22:2.] I.e. though there is so great a difference between them, and one has so much more [than] the other, yet both are equally dependent on God for all good. The rich, notwithstanding all his riches and sufficiency, after all is as much dependent on God's help, and his pleasure, and providence, for his well-being as the poor man. They are on a level in this respect. See Proverbs 29:13.

Proverbs 23:2. "And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite."] I.e. "put a knife to thy throat," and then thou will have before your eyes a representation of the danger you are in. A man that has a knife at his throat, ready to cut it, would be uneasy and very careful for his safety, being in great danger of his life. So would the Wise Man have men, that are "given to appetite," be under such temptation as that mentioned in the foregoing verse.

Proverbs 23:4.] The wordsהֲדָל מִבִּינָתְךָ לְהַעֲשִׁיר אַל־תִּיגַע literally translated are thus. "That there may not be labors to be rich, cease from thine own wisdom," which makes the sense

-- 571 --

and connection with the following words much easier and plainer. "Cease from thine own wisdom," so natural to thee, whereby you are so apt to imagine that this is the way to be happy. If you trust to your own heart or its natural dictates, you will find riches deceitful, as well as the "meat" of the ruler's table, spoken, Proverbs 23:3.

Proverbs 24:2.] "Their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief."] I.e. the things which they are in pursuit of, and their hearts and tongues are so busy about, will end in their own mischief and destruction.

Proverbs 24:8.] "He that thinketh to do evil shall be called a mischievous person."] The latter part in the originalיִקְרָאוּ בַּעַל־מְזִמּוֹת לוֹ is, "They shall call him a master," or "patron," or "husband of mischief." I.e. though his wickedness be only in thought, yet he allows himself in it, and that be his manner. He shall have his character from it. Wickedness is to be looked upon as his trade and business, what he is espoused to, that which he allows, patronizes, and is a practitioner of. The next verse confirms this sense.

Proverbs 24:9.] "The thought of foolishness is sin."] The meaning seems to be this. A mischievous device tends to the ruin of him that is the author of it. The wordזִמַּת translated "thought" is the same that is used in the latter part of the foregoing verse, "shall be called a mischievous person." In the Hebrew,בַּעַל־מְזִמּוֹת it shall be called the "master" (or author) "of mischievous devices." "Mischievous devices" is a word of the same radix with that here translated "thought." And whereas 'tis said to be "sin," that often signifies calamity or ruin. See note on Deuteronomy 15:9.

Proverbs 24:17–18.] He that, when he is wronged, will revenge himself, takes his vindication of himself out of God's hands; and so God will leave it with him. Whereas if he receives the injury with meekness, God will plead his cause, a remarkable instance of which we have in Moses. See Numbers 12, throughout.

Proverbs 24:21. "My son, fear thou the Lord and the king."] By this it appears that when Solomon says "my son" in this book, he han't respect to his natural son that was to be his successor in the kingdom, but only speaks in the

-- 572 --

style of a teacher to whosoever shall hear or read his instructions, especially those that are young. For he tells us he wrote these proverbs to give "the young man knowledge and discretion" (Proverbs 1:4).JE's exposition of the text in his sermon on Proverbs 24:13–14, first preached May 1734, with the doctrine, "The directest way that young people can take to spend their youth pleasantly, is to walk in the ways of religion and virtue," echoes this entry. See Works, 19, 81–82.

Proverbs 24:21–22. "Meddle not with them that are given to change,… who knoweth the ruin of them both?"] The true sense would have appeared if the last part of the Proverbs 24:21 had been translated thus, which is the most literal sense of the words.אַל־שִתְעָרָב עִםשׁ־וֹנִים "Meddle not with men that are for another," or "for a second," shonim,שׁוֹנִים i.e. for another kind, such as would change their king, and have a new one. "Who knows the ruin of them both?" I.e. the ruin of these innovators, and of the new king they set up.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. Here JE deleted "See the Ruin of Shenechem a word of the Same Radix as Shonim." See how the word sheni,שֵּׁנִי "second," is used, Ecclesiastes 4:15–16. See the note.

Proverbs 24:23. "The wise."] I.e. judges. See Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19, and Job 12:17.

Proverbs 24:26. "Shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer."] I.e. shall respect and love the judge that passes a just sentence. The foregoing verses confirm this sense, especially Proverbs 24:24. The originalיִשָּׁק שִׂפָתַיִם is, "His lips shall be kissed." 'Tis not said by whom. 'Tis as much as to say, He shall be greatly approved, and have great favor with God, and men, and all elect beings.

Proverbs 25:1.] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1725.

Proverbs 25:2. "The glory of God."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1725–26.

Proverbs 25:11. "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver." "A word fitly spoken," i.e. when both the thing spoken is good, tending to a good purpose, and when it is spoken in an agreeable manner. This is like gold conveyed or given under the appearance, representation, or

-- 573 --

similitude of silver. The words are the silver, and the sense and fruit is gold. Words are signs, representations, and a kind of pictures of things. The thing signified, and end intended, is the substance. When a word is fitly spoken, the words themselves are agreeable and pleasant. For "the lips of the righteous know what is acceptable" (Proverbs 10:32). Their words "are gracious" (Ecclesiastes 10:12). In their tongue "is the law of kindness" (Proverbs 31:26). So "the tongue of the just is as choice silver" (Proverbs 10:20). So the picture or representation is silver, and the sense, substance delivered, and fruit of what is spoken, is better, that is gold. The lips of the wise conveys fruit that feeds those [that] hear them. Proverbs 10:21, "The lips of the righteous feed many." And the fruit that they are fed with is golden fruit. It is nothing meaner than grace. They "minister grace to the hearers" (Ephesians 4:29). This is better than gold. Proverbs 20:15, "There is gold, and a multitude of rubies, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel." 'Tis said, Proverbs 15:4, that "a wholesome tongue is a tree of life." And the fruit that this tree bears is golden fruit. And when the words are "fitly spoken," the leaves of the tree are silver. When a man uses eloquence and pleasant words to express those things that are wise and pious, the words or representations, though they are very agreeable and pleasant, are not better than the things spoken or represented, nor yet near so good. The speech or representation is silver, but the thing represented is gold.

The fruit, as it comes from the giver, looks like silver, but in the use it is found to be gold. The appearance of the fruit is pleasant and acceptable, but when the fruit is eaten, 'tis much pleasanter. The husk or shell is silver, but the pulp and kernel is gold. 'Tis contrariwise when eloquence and sweet words are used to an ill purpose. Then there is the appearance, or representation, or picture of silver, but the substance is a baser metal or earth, as this same Wise Man himself observes. Proverbs 26:23, "Burning lips and a wicked heart" (i.e. a wicked intent and design) "are like a potsherd covered with silver dross." There is the representation and appearance of silver, but the substance is earth. This last mentioned place is a great confirmation that this interpretation, which has now been given of Proverbs 25:11, is the true one. Note: This proverb is remarkably verified in the words spoken to us by God, in the representations under which he signifies and communicates divine and heavenly things to us, as, for instance, the types and similitudes in which the glorious things of the gospel were signified, such as the tabernacle, temple, the ark, mercy seat, golden altar, candlestick, the glorious robes of the

-- 574 --

priests, etc. These pictures and representations were beautiful and precious, but the things signified far more so.See Stephen J. Stein, "'Like Apples of Gold in Pictures of Silver': The Portrait of Wisdom in Jonathan Edwards' Commentary on the Book of Proverbs," Church History 54 (1985), 324–37.

Proverbs 25:15. "By long forbearing, the prince is persuaded."] I.e. "patience to bear a present heat, without being put into a heat by it, and to wait for a fit opportunity to offer our reasons, and to give them time to consider of it." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 544.

Proverbs 25:23.] The angry or displeased "countenance" of him that hears the reproach, not of the person reproached.

Proverbs 25:25.] "Good news" from our friends at a distance who have been gone long from us. Heaven is "a far country," a far country especially to sinners who have gone far off from God to the very borders, and seems to be a far country indeed to an awakened, convinced sinner. The gospel is glad tidings from thence.

Abraham's servant brought to Rebecca "good news from a far country." Joseph's brethren, when they returned to Canaan to their kindred there, after Joseph had made himself known to 'em in Egypt, and Joseph sent by them an account of his being alive, and his riches and glory and plentiful supplies for them, and invited them to come down to him, and partake of his wealth and glory, they brought "good news from a far country" to them who before were sorrowful and ready to perish with famine. Moses brought to the children of Israel in Egypt, who were in great affliction there, and almost worn out with cruel bondage, good news from Mt. Sinai near the land of Midian. The spies, when they brought an account of the exceeding fertility of the land of Canaan, brought "good news from a far country" to them that were faithful in Israel. Cyrus sent good news from the Persian court to the poor captive Jews in Chaldea, as we have an account, Ezra 1. Darius's messengers brought good news from the same court to the Jews in Judea (Ezra 6). Ezra came with good news to Jerusalem, when he brought from thence Artaxerxes' commission and decree (Ezra 7). Nehemiah came to Jerusalem with good news from the same court (Nehemiah 1). Esther's messengers brought good news from Shushan, to the Jews in Judea and in all the distant provinces, of Esther and Mordecai's advancement, and of great salvation for the Jews.

-- 575 --

Naomi, when in the land of Moab, heard good news from Canaan, when she heard "how the Lord had visited his people in giving them bread" (Ruth 1:6). All these are types of the good news sent us from heaven in the gospel of Jesus Christ, which gospel was "good news from a far country" also in another sense, viz. as it is preached to the Gentiles who were far off, aliens and strangers, far off from the church of God, and sent from Jerusalem and the land of Canaan to the remote parts of the world.This paragraph is a later addition.

Proverbs 25:26. "A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and corrupt spring."] I.e. "it is a public grievance of ill consequence to many, like the muddying of a fountain, and the corrupting of a spring.

"First, for the righteous to fall into sin in the sight of the wicked." The originalמָט will bear such an application of the word "falling."

"Secondly, for the righteous to be oppressed, and run down, and trampled upon by the violence or subtilty of evil men, to be displaced and thrust into obscurity. This is the troubling of the fountain of justice, and corrupting the very springs of government. See Proverbs 28:12, Proverbs 28:28, and Proverbs 29:2.

"Thirdly, for the righteous to be cowardly, to sneak and truckle to the wicked, to be afraid of opposing his wickedness, and basely to yield to him. This is a reflection upon religion, a discouragement to good men, and strengthens the hands of sinners in their sins, and so is like 'a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring.'" Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 546.

Proverbs 26:1. "As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honor is not seemly for a fool."] Not only as incongruous and disagreeable, but as hurtful and pernicious, it is as prejudicial to mankind, to human society, as to have nature put out of its proper course. Snow and frost in summer would kill the growth of the earth; and rain in harvest would hinder men's proper labors, and spoil the fruits of their labor. So when wicked men are advanced to places of honor and power, it discourages virtue and industry, and destroys a people's prosperity and joy, and brings sorrow and death on the face of public society.

Proverbs 26:4–5.] We must not answer a fool "according to his folly," in that to talk foolishly and wickedly as he does. We must not answer railing with

-- 576 --

railing. If he boasts him, we must not boast ourselves to match him. But sometimes we must "answer a fool according to his folly," in that respect, that our answer may be adapted to his folly, such as his folly deserves, such as tends to lay open his folly to his view, and show him the absurdity of it.

Proverbs 26:9. "As a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools."] A fool, by undertaking to deliver wise sayings, disgraces himself. A wicked man, by making a showing of spiritual wisdom by religious talk, does but aggravate his guilt. Their words will be their condemnation; out of their own mouths shall they be judged.

Proverbs 26:10. "The great God, who formeth all things, both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth the transgressors."] This verse does with great emphasis denote the certainty of the punishment of sinners. It is strongly asserted in the repetition of the assertion, as is used in Hebrew, and it is confirmed by two things. First, by God's greatness. As God is infinitely great, and able to recompense his enemies, so he will do it. And as his majesty is infinite, so he will vindicate his affronted, contemned majesty. Second, by God's forming all things. As God has created and governs the world, and has all things in his hands, so he will surely be avenged on the ungodly.

Proverbs 26:14.] The door, turning on the hinges, moves indeed, but not out of its place, moves backwards, makes no progress. So a "slothful" seeker of heaven goes backwards and forwards, goes by fit and starts, or goes round like a horse in a mill, but gets never to heaven or true goodness. As the door is fastened to the hinges, so the slothful seeker is tied fast to the world and his own righteousness, which hinder his getting forward, or doing anything, in religion to any purpose.

Proverbs 26:16. "The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason."] Slothful men commonly are busybodies, apt to judge and censure, to meddle not only with private but public affairs. They are apt to think themselves great politicians, and sufficient to judge and determine of all sorts of affairs. Slothful men have so little to do with themselves, and with their own business, that they are ignorant of themselves, great strangers at home.

Proverbs 26:18–19.] The man spoken of is he that glories in his craftiness, outwitting, overreaching other men, and making a sport of their deceiving

-- 577 --

and deluding them, and bringing them into their snares. They make light of the mischief they do to their neighbors; they make a jest of it, as a man that is distracted, who throws mortal weapons, never reflects upon the mischievous consequences of what he does, has no sense of guilt, nor serious concern for himself, nor his neighbor.

Proverbs 27:3.] The fool wanteth judgment and understanding to allay and moderate the rage of his wrath, so that when it falleth, it falleth with the whole strength and weight of it. The more wisdom a man hath, the more can he give check to passion. They can oppose wise considerations, the frailties of nature, their own slips, their need of pardon from God. At least they will not trust such a furious passion, and let it out without restraint. See Proverbs 29:11, and Proverbs 17:12, and Proverbs 11:2; James 3:13 and James 3:17.

Proverbs 27:4. "Before envy."] It had better have been translated, "jealousy." The wordקִנְאָה is the very same which Solomon makes use of, Canticles 8:6. "Jealousy is cruel as the grave; the coals thereof are as coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame."

And again the same word is used in Proverbs 6:34–35. "For jealousy is the rage of a man; therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts."This paragraph is a later addition.

Proverbs 27:5.] That is "secret love" that durst not show itself towards us, when we have many or powerful enemies, for fear of offending them. Open rebuke or plain reproach is from that virtue and true friendship that is not afraid of doing its part for fear of offending us. The latter is the fruit of the faithfulness of a friend; the former is a sign of unfaithfulness. So that both these things are condemned in those that pretend to be friends to others, viz. neglecting to do the part of a friend to them for fear of their enemies, and neglecting to do the part of a friend to them for fear of themselves. Both usually go together. He that han't faithfulness and courage enough to reprove us when he sees what is amiss in us, is not likely to stand by us when opposed by potent enemies.

Proverbs 27:7.] This is to show that there is not so much difference between the rich and the poor as to comfort in outward enjoyments as the world is ready to imagine. See Ecclesiastes 5:12.

-- 578 --

Proverbs 27:10.] This verse implies that in a time of calamity, it is not best to trust to a brother, and run the venture of being burdensome to him, merely because he is near akin to us. 'Tis better to trust to tried friendship in a neighbor than to kindred in our nearest relations.

Proverbs 27:11.] See Psalms 127:4–5.

Proverbs 27:14. "He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning."] I.e. with extraordinary earnestness, forwardness, not naturally, but with contrivance, affectatiously, and immoderately.

"It shall be counted a curse to him." It is no sign of real friendship, but on the contrary, it looks suspicious. It savors of ill design. Such flatterers are pursuing their private designs, and seeking their own interest, and not the interest of them they flatter, and very often are seeking their own interest on the ruins of the other. See Proverbs 27:14.This is a later interlineation. And such commendations do a person no good, but are a disadvantage, excite envy, tempt others to detract, engage 'em to espy faults and blemishes, and often are a temptation to pride, and so deceive men, and lead into a great snare.This paragraph is a later separate entry.

Proverbs 27:18.] By the honor here spoken of, respect is had to wages or reward, as 1 Timothy 5:17. Compare this whole verse with that and 1 Corinthians 9:7.This remainder of this entry is a later addition. This verse may be spoken to masters for their direction, or it may be spoken to servants and those in mean employments, to direct and encourage them to be diligent and faithful, because as God takes care of such, and requires that they shall eat the fruit, as he has made provision in his law, that the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn shall not be muzzled [Deuteronomy 25:4]. So he will hereafter reward their faithfulness with honor and glory, agreeable to what the Apostle says, Colossians 3:24.

Proverbs 27:21. "As the refining pot," etc.] I.e. his praise tries him, as gold is tried in the fire. That this is the meaning is manifest by Proverbs 17:3. "'Rara virtus est humilitas honorata,' said Barnard. To find humility with honor is to find a phoenix. Let an obscure person be lifted up to honor, and how steady and well-composed soever he was before, 'tis a thousand to one but his eyes will dazzle and his head run round when he is upon the lofty pinnacle of praise and honor. Put the best gold in the fining pot of praise, and it's a great wonder if a great deal of dross don't appear. Isaiah 39:2, The

-- 579 --

vain glory of Hezekiah rose like a froth or scum upon the pot when heated by prosperity. It was such a fining pot to Herod, as discovered him to be dross itself (Acts 12:23)." How did prosperity alter Hazael (2 Kings 8:13) and Israel (Jeremiah 2:2, Jeremiah 2:7, Jeremiah 2:31). Flavell's Touchstone of Sincerity, ch. 4, §3.John Flavel, The Touchstone of Sincerity: Or The Signs of Grace, and Symptomes of Hypocrisie, Opened in a Practical Treatise upon Revelation 3:17, Revelation 3:18 (London, 1679), 69–71. Flavel (1630–1691) was a prolific Presbyterian divine ejected by the Act of Uniformity.

Proverbs 27:23–27.] In these verses we have the Wise Man's advice to contentment with the common enjoyments of life that are to be had in the way of that labor and industry which God has appointed for the generality of mankind, and good husbanding therein, without forsaking such a way of living to make haste to get riches and honor, and to reach and grasp after great things in the world. We are directed to the former way, as what is most to be depended on for a quiet and comfortable enjoyment of the blessings of this life, and for the continuance of them in our families.

Proverbs 28:3.] This is to represent how merciless the tyranny and cruelty of such often is who are advanced to dominion from a low state, beggars on horseback and servants, when they reign.

Proverbs 28:5. "Evil men understand not judgment."] I.e. they don't understand that which is right. The word mispatמִשְׁפָּט commonly signifies that which is right, as I have shown in what I have written on "Justification," in "Controversial Papers," pp. 153–54.JE writes, "So the word Mishpat is sometimes used to signify one's right or due or desert, just in the same manner as Tzedhek" ("'Controversies' Notebook: Justification," Works, 21, 349). What Christ says to the Jews, Luke 12:57, confirms this sense. "Yea, and why even of your own selves, judge ye not what is right?" See Proverbs 8:9, and places there referred to. (See Ecclesiastes 8:5–6.) "But they that seek the Lord understand all things." How agreeable is this to that of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 2:15.

Proverbs 28:10.] This is agreeable to many other scriptures which represent that they that persecute the righteous to cause 'em to forsake their religion, shall fall into the pit which they have digged. "But the upright shall have good things in possession." Instead of falling into the pit which the wicked have digged for them, they that are upright and faithful in time of trial and persecution shall have a crown of life and joy. See Proverbs 28:15.

-- 580 --

Proverbs 28:12.] See Proverbs 28:28.

Proverbs 28:19.] The translation would have been more beautiful if itישְׂבַּע־רִישׁ רֵיקִים וּמִרַדֵּף יִשְׂבַע־לָחֶם אַדְמָתוֹ עֹבֵד had been more literal, thus: "He that tilleth his land shall be filled with bread. He that followeth vain persons shall be filled with poverty."

Proverbs 28:20. "Innocent."] The wordנָקָה signifies unpunished as well as innocent. The former seems to be the true sense. See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Proverbs 28:26 "Trusteth his own heart."] His own wisdom, resolutions, stability, and merit, and so goes presumptuously on, proceeding without caution and circumspection.

Proverbs 29:9.] This represents what is often the state of things in a time of persecution. If the enemies of religion rage or smile, yet there is no dependence upon it. Their smiles are flattering and deceitful. The opposition is not at an end; so there is no rest. The persecutor is still secretly carrying on his malignant designs.

Proverbs 29:13. "Meet together."] See note on Proverbs 22:2.

Proverbs 29:18. "No vision."] I.e. no light of divine revelation.

Proverbs 29:20. "Hasty in his words."] I.e. forward to speak, to profess, to instruct, judge, and dictate, and manifest himself in his talk. The words in the originalבִּדְבָרָיו אָץ signify as much as "swift in his words." This proverb seems to be much of the same import with that, Proverbs 26:12. "Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope of a fool than of him." For it is the manner of the humble to be swift to hear, slow to speak, but the manner of those that [are] conceited of their wisdom and religion, and are spiritually proud, to be slow to hear, but swift to speak.

Proverbs 29:24. "He heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not."] When anything was stolen, and there appeared considerable grounds of suspicion that any person was guilty, they were wont to put him upon his oath, and adjure him with a curse, whether he knew ought of the matter. See Leviticus 5:1, 1 Kings 8:13

-- 581 --

1 Kings 8:31. And this is that "cursing" that the Wise Man here speaks of. "He heareth" the voice of swearing, or "cursing, and bewrayeth it not," and so sins against his own soul, for he brings that curse upon himself.

"He heareth cursing."] Proverbs 30:9.This reference is a separate entry.

Proverbs 30:1.] "Ithiel'אִיתִיאֵל signifies 'God with me,' and 'Ucal'אֻכָּל signifies 'the mighty one.'" Probably they are names given to the Messiah (Henry),Exposition, 3 (1725), 560. the same that is spoken of in the Proverbs 30:4. See also SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1780–82.

Proverbs 30:4.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1782–84.

Proverbs 30:9. "And take the name of my God in vain."] Proverbs 29:24.

Proverbs 30:15.] The "two daughters" of the horseleach here spoken of are probably ambition and sensuality.

Proverbs 30:15–16. "There are three things," etc.] This is said to the reproach of worldly-minded men, or those whose hearts are under the power of these "two daughters" of the horseleach, ambition and sensuality, that they are like "the grave," etc. These things were designed images and types of worldly-minded men; and therefore they show how mean and hateful they are, and how dreadful their case is upon other accounts. They are like "the grave"; they are in a state of death. Their souls are like sepulchers full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness. They are like the "barren," greedy, taking in, sucking up the strength of the earth, theJE deleted "sweetness of world." best the world can afford, and yet bringing forth no fruit, and on whom the seed of the word is spread in vain. They are like the "earth." They are earthly, vile, and base in their nature, as the dirt we tread under our feet. They are like the "fire," by the rage of their lusts consuming all things, full of violent principles of enmity against God and men, that render 'em dangerous and exceeding harmful to those that come near 'em.

Proverbs 30:19–20.] The "way of a man with a maid" and "the way of an adulterous woman" are here distinct instances. In the criminal intercourse "of

-- 582 --

a man with a maid," the maid was liable to a discovery by some effects that were left in her body, at least it is so generally.JE deleted "among that people in that country." But the man might conceal his wickedness; it might be hid as much as the way of a serpent on a rock. And when a married woman is guilty of adultery, then the woman may conceal her wickedness, as well as the adulterer his. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1789–90.

Proverbs 30:27.] See "Scripture," no. 462.Works, 15, 552–53.

Proverbs 31:1. "King Lemuel."] SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1799.

Proverbs 31:23.] By this it appears that by "elders" in Scripture is not meant merely the elder sort of people in age.

-- 583 --

Ecclesiastes

Ecclesiastes.] Concerning Solomon's writing this book after repentance in old age, see SSS, "Prolegomena."Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1809–12. See also notes on Ecclesiastes 7:23–29 and Ecclesiastes 7:23.

Ecclesiastes 1:4. "One generation goeth away, and another cometh; but the earth abideth forever." I.e. abideth such as it used to be, no better, mere vile earth still.

Ecclesiastes 1:4–7.] See no. 389, first three paragraphs of that number.Works, 15, 373–74. See how Solomon's argument justifies the Apostle's argument concerning sacrifices, Hebrews 10:1–3, note.This sentence is a later addition.

Ecclesiastes 1:5–11. "The sun also ariseth," etc.] These kind of vicissitudes in earthly things shows the great imperfection of earthly good in these respects. 1. 'Tis good that is sought by this labor of the creature, by the labor of the sun, and wind, and streams; they are laboring for good. But by their restlessness, their still continuing to labor, it appears that they don't fully attain their end. They don't attain any sufficient good. If they did, they would leave off laboring, as having attained what they labor for. As what the rivers aim at by their running is to fill up the sea, but by their still continuing to run, they go back to the same place and run the same course, it appears they do not do it (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

2. By their doing the same work over and over, it appears that they not only don't attain any sufficient good, but they don't make progress towards it. There is nothing new, as Ecclesiastes 1:9–10. The rivers not only don't fill up the sea, but they don't gain upon it. There is the like arguing, Ecclesiastes 6:7. "All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled."

3. It shows the unsatisfying nature of earthly good thus, that when one kind has been enjoyed a little while, there is need of change. After the

-- 584 --

light of the sun has been enjoyed a little while, then something else is sought; night and darkness is desired. After summer has been enjoyed a while, and the wind blowing from the south, then winter is desired, and the wind from the north. Man can't live upon one sort of earthly enjoyment, but he must have change continually.

4. And as it shows the unsatisfying nature of earthly good, so it shows its exceeding fleeting, fading nature. It is an evidence of this great imperfection in it, that after it has been enjoyed a little while, it don't only perish in the enjoyment, but turns to ill, to that which is irksome, so that the contrary is desired. After the light of the sun has been enjoyed a little, 'tis troublesome; and darkness is desired. After we have been awake a little while, it is burdensome: we want to sleep, and then we are weary of that, and want to be awake again. When, [for] a man, that which gratifies his appetite presentlyMS: "it presently." grows irksome, he desires no more of it for the present.

Ecclesiastes 1:6.] See no. 90.Works, 15, 76.

Ecclesiastes 1:6–9.] See no. 461.Ibid., 551–52.

Ecclesiastes 1:11. "No remembrance."] Two things the Wise Man aims to show are never attained to by all the constant labors that we see under the sun. 1. Nothing satisfying and that can give rest from any further labor on that account. And 2. Nothing stable, and permanent, or sufficient to afford any rest on that account. Things obtained soon vanish away, are forgotten, and buried in oblivion and darkness.

Ecclesiastes 1:13. "This sore travail hath God given to the sons of men to be exercised therewith."] By this we may argue two things. 1. That it was the design of the Being that constituted the world that some men should employ themselves in study as well as some in manual labors. 2. That the labor and weariness that attends study is a fulfillment of that curse, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread" [Genesis 3:19], as well as the fatigue of the business of the husbandman.

Ecclesiastes 1:15. "That which is crooked cannot be made straight."] After all my attainments in knowledge and wisdom, yet all signified nothing to remove

-- 585 --

or avoid the troubles and sorrows of the world, to mend it or make it better, or to find out any way to remove the vexation, or to seek satisfaction from it. All the philosophy and politics in the world can't amend the corrupt nature of mankind, prevent death, or give satisfaction and prevent sorrow while a man lives. See Ecclesiastes 2:14–16.

Ecclesiastes 1:18.] The more knowledge and discerning a man has, the more does he see of the sin, and folly, and misery, and helplessness of mankind. It seems to have been so with Solomon in a remarkable manner by the account he here gives us of his observations that were the fruit of his increase of knowledge. See more fully, SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1824.

Ecclesiastes 2:2. "And of mirth, what doth it?"] I.e. what is got by it?

Ecclesiastes 2:8. "Peculiar treasure," etc.] Solomon speaks here of the "peculiar treasure" of other kings. Solomon had the royal treasures of many countries or provinces in his possession that David his father had gotten by his conquests. David's hand "found as a nest" (as is said of the king of Assyria, Isaiah 10:14) the treasure of many kings. King[s'] treasures were the peculiar treasures of the countries or provinces they ruled; the most precious things that were in all the country were doubtless to be found there. We read of Hezekiah's "house of precious things, his silver, and gold, and spices, and precious ointment" (1 Kings 20:13).This sentence is a later addition.

Ecclesiastes 2:16.] "Scripture," no. 91.Works, 15, 76.

Ecclesiastes 2:24.] See note on Ecclesiastes 5:18.JE deleted Pierpont's entry immediately above this reference; it reads, "Ecclesiastes 2:24: Som say this is ye language of a Epicure: Post mortem nulla volupt:."

Ecclesiastes 3:9. "What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboreth?"] Seeing things thus will have their course, their appointed changes and vicissities, no contrivance or labor of men can prevent it.

Ecclesiastes 3:11. "So that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end."] "He hath set the world in their heart." He has given 'em the world which he hath made to view and contemplate, and

-- 586 --

they see the particular changes that come to pass in it. They observe the present rotations of the wheels of God's chariot, but they cannot find out the grand design of God in the whole series of rotations, from the beginning to the end of the whole journey. Things seem to labor in vain, to be in a perpetual revolution, going and returning to the same place again, without making any progress or anything new brought forth (See Ecclesiastes 1.); but there is a progress. There is a grand scheme which God is continually prosecuting, a grand design which God constantly aims at in all the revolutions, from the beginning to the end, but men cannot find it out. In these days of the world, much more of it is discovered than had been in preceding ages; but till Christ came into the world, the grand mystery had been kept secret from ages and generations, from men and angels, from the beginning of the world (Ephesians 3:9–11).

"He hath made everything beautiful in his time; also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God doth from the beginning to the end."] Instead of "heart," it should have been translated "middle." God "hath set the world in the middle of things." God has not set us at the beginning nor at the end of things. We see but the middle of God's works, not the beginning of them. Then we should have seen how wisely and beautifully they were contrived in the divine counsels, how he made everything beautiful in its time. We see not the end and final issue of things. Then we should see by the excellent and glorious issue that all was orderedMS: "order." most fitly and beautifully. The same wordכֵבָב is used for "middle" or "midst," Jonah 2:3, "in the midst of the sea." So again the same word for "the midst of the sea" in Exodus 15:8; and the same word is used in 2 Samuel 18:14, "in the midst of the oak."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ecclesiastes 3:14–15.] The design of the Wise Man in these verses seems to be to show that God hath settled things in a stated course, according to fixed laws and an established method, that is unalterable, that was the same in all times past, is now, and will continue to be in time to come. These wordsאֶת־נִרְדָּף יְבַקּשׁ וְהָאֱלהִימ which are rendered, "God requireth that which is past," might have been translated, according to the two Buxtorfs, "God requireth or seeks the consequence, or the thing that is consequent," i.e. what shall follow from the course of things, as he has settled 'em by his decree and the

-- 587 --

stated methods of his providence.Johannis Buxtorf, Lexicon Hebraicum el Chaldaicum (6th ed. London, 1646), 680. What shall follow he seeks and requires, and 'tis in vain for any to seek anything diverse from it. The words most literally translated are, "God requireth the thing that is pursued or followed after," i.e. God required, as by a law, the consequence that is pursued or sought by things that now are in their present state and course. See SSS.This reference and the preceding sentence are a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1845–47.

Ecclesiastes 3:16–17.] The Wise Man argues a divine judgment of all mankind from the injustice of human judges.

Ecclesiastes 3:21.] "Spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of a beast that goeth downward to the earth."] Here reference seems to be had to the ordinary manner of their dying. Man, when he expires, ordinarily lies on his back with his face upward, so that when his breath goeth forth, it goeth upward. Beasts ordinarily expire in the contrary posture.

Ecclesiastes 3:22.] See note on Ecclesiastes 5:18.

Ecclesiastes 4:13–14.] See catalogue of texts in the Old Testament that suppose a future state, pp. 17 ff.See footnote on Job 4:21 entry.

Ecclesiastes 4:15–16.] "I considered all the living which walk under the sun, with the second child that shall stand up in his stead. There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them. They also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit."] To "walk with" is a phrase sometimes used to signify taking contentment in acquiescing, in men's manifesting themselves pleased with [something]. So Psalms 35:14, "I walked as though he had been my friend or brother." Amos 3:3, "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?" The word קֵץ, "an end," is a word sometimes used to signify a final obtaining or accomplishingMS: "accomplish." of one's purposes, or desires, or expectations. So Ecclesiastes 4:8, "Yet there is no end of his labor." Ecclesiastes 12:12, "In making many books there is no end." Job 6:11, "What is my strength, that I should hope? And what is mine end, that I should prolong my life?" So

-- 588 --

another wordאַחֲרִית that is translated "end" has the same signification in Proverbs 23:18. "For surely there is an end, and thine expectation shall not be cut off." So that the sense of these verses seems to be this: I considered how it commonly is with mankind in this world, how they seem to be mightily pleased with the new king that stands up, instead of the old one that they found fault with for his moroseness and austerity, stiffness in his own way, and refusing to be admonished. They won't rest satisfied very long. They afterward grow weary of their new king, for mankind are so unsteady and capricious, so given to change and fond of novelty, they never know when they are well. No such thing is to be expected as their finally resting in what they obtain as the completing of their desires and expectations. As it was with those that went before, the former generation grew weary of their old king; so it shall be with this that comes after. They won't continue to rejoice in this "second child that stands up in his stead."

Ecclesiastes 5:1. "And be more ready to hear than to give the sacrifice of fools."] I.e. be more ready to hearken to and obey what God has to say to you and command you than to offer to him the sacrifice of the wicked and disobedient, which is agreeable to that in 1 Samuel 15:22. "To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." And that in the Psalms 40, "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ear hast thou opened" Psalms 40:6]. And to Psalms 50 and Isaiah 1.

Ecclesiastes 5:6. "Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin."] "We must not vow that, which through the frailty of the flesh, we have reason to fear we shall not be able to perform, as those that vow a single life, and yet know not how to keep their vow." Henry.Exposition, 3 (1725), 587. See on the whole verse, SSS.This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1864–66.

Ecclesiastes 5:13–14.] What is asserted in these verses is parallel with Proverbs 11:24. "There is that withholdeth more than is meet, and it tendeth only to poverty."

Ecclesiastes 5:18. "It is good and comely for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy the good of all his labor which he taketh under the sun."] That rejoicing or comfort in the enjoyments, which the Wise Man has here respect to, and

-- 589 --

in Ecclesiastes 2:24, and Ecclesiastes 3:12–13, Ecclesiastes 3:22, and Ecclesiastes 8:15, and Ecclesiastes 9:7–9, cannot be a carnal mirth or rejoicing, for so he would contradict himself. For he says in Ecclesiastes 7:3, "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better." And Ecclesiastes 7:6, "As the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool." And Ecclesiastes 2:2, "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doth it?" So that it is, must be, a virtuous and spiritual comfort, peace, and contentment that must be here spoken, opposite to that darkness in which a wicked man always enjoys his outward good things, spoken of in the preceding verse, which is peculiarly the gift of God, agreeable to what is said in the next verse (See note on that verse.), and is attended with doing good in life (Ecclesiastes 3:12), that joy which God gives to him "that is good in his sight" (Ecclesiastes 2:26, taken with the two preceding verses).

Ecclesiastes 5:19–20.] The sense of these verses seems to be this: It is the fruit of the peculiar favor of heaven when God gives a man wealth, and gives power to use and enjoy it aright with a spirit of true contentment, thankfulness, and rest of soul in God, the author of his mercies. And when God is pleased, of his sovereign grace, to give such a spirit of spiritual rest and joy with outward enjoyments, he shall not much lay to heart the shortness and sorrows of his life, "because God answers him in the joy of his heart." This spiritual joy will be a sufficient support against the afflictions of life and the expectations of death. He can't mean that in his outward mirth he will not think much of death, but will cast it [out] of his thoughts, for this would be directly repugnant to Ecclesiastes 7:2–6. See note on Ecclesiastes 7:18.

Ecclesiastes 6:3. "And also that he have no burial."] That is, that his memory be not honored. He dies in shame, and his name rots, as is said of the wicked, "He goes out like a snuff in a stink." Thus having no burial is explained in Isaiah 14:20. See no. 316.Works, 15, 292–93. See note on Ecclesiastes 6:4.This reference is a later addition.

Ecclesiastes 6:4.] The name seems sometimes to be put for the departed soul. At least the spirit of God seemed to have intended, as by having "no burial" in the preceding verse, it seems to mean that God takes no care of the departed spirit that is not gathered, as the dead body is evidently put for the departed soul in the last verses of the Isaiah 66. As

-- 590 --

that Logos, and Wisdom of God, and Divine Mind that dwelt in the temple was called God's "name," so the mind of man is called his "name." See note on Ecclesiastes 7:1. See note on Genesis 23:4.This reference is a later addition.

Ecclesiastes 6:7. "All the labor of man is for his mouth."] See note on Hebrews 10:1–3.

Ecclesiastes 6:8. "For what hath the wise more than the fool?"] "A fool may have as much worldly wealth, and may enjoy as much of the outward pleasure of it, as a wise man. Suppose 'em to be equal in their possessions, what can a wise man, a scholar, a wit, a politician, squeeze out of his estate more than supplies for back and belly, and that a half-witted man may do? A fool can fare as well, and relish it, can dress as well, and make as good a figure in any public appearance, as a wise man." "What hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living?" As much as to say, Yea, not only are riches so empty of happiness that no wisdom of man can extract happiness out of them, let him never so much of it; but one that is without them, that is poor in the world, that knows how "to walk before the living," has a far better portion. He has more comfort and less vexation with his little, a more contented calm spirit, a better peace and tranquility. (This from Henry, in part.)Exposition, 3 (1725), 590.

Ecclesiastes 6:9.] It is better to have a thing in possession than to have it to seek.

"Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire." He is happier, though poor, that makes the best of what he has and is content with his portion, as it is with him that knows how "to walk before the living" (See the foregoing verses.), than he that is always coveting and affecting a variety of imaginary satisfactions, which is commonly the case with rich men that know not how "to walk before the living." See on the whole verse, SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1878.

Ecclesiastes 6:10. "That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it is man."] There is a certain sphere in which God hath placed man, certain limits by which his attainments in the world, and the degree of his worldly happiness is circumscribed, which limits men have come to in time past; and 'tis a vain imagination for any to expect to exceed those limits. Whatever men attain to, still they are but men. He that made him gave him

-- 591 --

his name, "Adam,"אָדָם which implies that he is dust; and let him be never so greedy, aspiring, busy, and restless, and grasping in his pursuits, and vast in his expectations, he never will be any more. Man in his first transgression was ambitious of getting above his limits, of being as God; and this disposition is common among men. But he that is mightier than man hath set his limits; and 'tis in vain to contend with him, as it follows. "Neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he." God will make it to be known that men are but men (Psalms 9:20). See SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1878–79.

Ecclesiastes 6:11.] Thisלָאָדָם מַה־יֹּתַר הָבֶל מַרְבִּים הַרְבֵּה יֵשׁ־דְּרִים כִּי might have been translated thus: "Seeing that it belongs to many affairs that they increase (or multiply) vanity, what is man the better?" I.e. what is he the better for having his affairs and possessions multiplied, and his worldly things increased?

Ecclesiastes 7:1. "A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of one's birth."] These things are probably here mentioned together because that on the day of a child's birth they used perfumed ointment to anoint the child with (Ezekiel 16:9), and on the day of death the righteous and wise leave a good name behind them. Their dead bodies are loathsome, and soon putrefy, and are unsavory; but they die in a perfume. Their good name they leave behind them is as though their bodies sent forth a sweet savor, better than the most precious ointment, when they died. Proverbs 10:7, "The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot."

The manner of the Wise Man's expressing himself is such as would lead us to suppose that the day of death is better than the day of one's birth on account of the good name that a good man leaves behind, which is better than the most precious ointment that a child can be anointed with at its birth, as if it would be worth the while to die for the sake of that good name to follow one, which cannot be the Wise Man's meaning. For a good man has a good name while he lives as well as after he is dead; and is it not better to live and enjoy that good name and loving favor, that is better than silver and gold, than to die for a good name that one can't enjoy after death? See Ecclesiastes 9:5–6. Therefore something further is meant than is expressed. There is respect had here to that future immortal honor and glory that the soul enters into at death, whereby it

-- 592 --

partakes with Christ of his new name and new honor. The soul of a departed saint is glorified immediately on its departure, made perfectly beautiful and excellent with a spiritual sweetness, fragrancy, and honor, which is fitly compared [to] the precious ointment with which the child is anointed as soon as born. Precious ointments were used for beauty, fragrancy, and honor. And the soul of a saint, going out of the prison of the body and this dark world into a world of perfect light and liberty, is like a child's coming forth out of the womb where it was pent up in darkness and pollution.

It is observable that in the Old Testament, where a future state and immortality is but darkly revealed, what remains of a dead person in this world is often made use of to represent the soul that remains in a state of perception.This paragraph is a separate entry. So is the dead body frequently, as when it is said of some that their iniquity shall be upon their bones, and that their bones shall be full of the sin of their youth, etc. So also Ecclesiastes 6:3, Proverbs 30:17. And sometimes the name that a person leaves behind him, as Proverbs 10:7, where it is said, "The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot," both the name and dead body are mentioned together as manifestly representing the state of the departed soul, in the Proverbs 6:3–4, and is more evident by Proverbs 6:5, which is a confirmation that by the good name in this chapter the Wise Man means the glory of the departed soul. See note on Proverbs 6:3 and Proverbs 6:4.This reference is a later addition.

Probably also here is reference to the precious ointments used in embalming dead bodies to make 'em as if everlasting, to which the everlasting life and happiness of the soul may fitly be compared and preferred. What has been observed on this verse is much confirmed by Psalms 112:6 and Proverbs 10:7. See SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. This reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, II (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1880–81.

Here is also respect, and perhaps a principal respect, to the spices and ointments with which they were wont to embalm dead bodies.This sentence is a later addition.

Ecclesiastes 7:6.] The mirth of fools, it makes a blaze and a noise, but soon goes out, and is of a destructive nature, as the blaze of thorns turns them to ashes.

Ecclesiastes 7:7. "Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad, and a gift destroyeth the heart."] The wise is a name or title for a judge. See Proverbs 24:23, with

-- 593 --

other parallel scriptures there referred to in my note.
